q: Rhoda, a retired nurse, offers her minivan to the Hillcrest Middle School chess club for a weekend tournament, but only on the condition that the club's faculty advisor, Mr. Okafor, does the driving. She takes no payment; the school buys the gas. On the way, Okafor rear-ends Petra's car. Petra sues Rhoda, arguing that Okafor was driving as Rhoda's agent. Under Gorton v. Doty, how should the court rule?
o: For Petra: the condition that Okafor drive gave Rhoda consent and control.
For Rhoda: agency requires that the agent be paid or that the parties form a contract.
For Rhoda: a person who lends a car is a bailor, and a bailor is never a principal.
For Petra, but only because the school paid for the gas, which made the trip a business venture.
oe: Correct. In Gorton the teacher's car was lent on the express condition that the coach drive it. Designating the driver supplied control, and his driving supplied his consent. No contract or compensation is needed, and ownership raises a prima facie presumption that the driver is the owner's agent.
Gorton holds the opposite: “it is not essential … that there be a contract between principal and agent … nor … that they, or either, receive compensation.”
That is Justice Budge's dissent. The majority found more than “mere passive permission” because Rhoda dictated who would drive.
Who paid for gas is not what creates agency. The condition that Okafor drive is what gives Rhoda control.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Consent and control

q: Variation: Rhoda hands the keys to the school's principal and says, “Use it however you need this weekend.” The school picks the driver. Is Okafor now Rhoda's agent?
o: Probably not: an unconditional loan to the school leaves Rhoda no control.
Yes: ownership alone makes any permissive driver the owner's agent as a matter of law.
Yes: Rhoda consented to the use of her car, and consent is the only element of agency that matters.
No, because a school district can never be a principal or an agent.
oe: Correct. The planning lesson of Gorton is that an owner who wants to avoid agency should lend the car outright, with no conditions, or insure. Without a manifestation that the driver act for her and subject to her control, the elements are missing.
Ownership raises only a rebuttable presumption in Gorton. It isn't a conclusive rule, and the facts here rebut it.
Agency also needs the agent to act on the principal's behalf and subject to her control. Passive permission is not enough.
Entities can be principals and agents. The issue is the missing control, not the school's status.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — No condition attached
pre: Rhoda, a retired nurse, offers her minivan to the Hillcrest Middle School chess club for a weekend tournament, but only on the condition that the club's faculty advisor, Mr. Okafor, does the driving. She takes no payment; the school buys the gas. On the way, Okafor rear-ends Petra's car. Petra sues Rhoda, arguing that Okafor was driving as Rhoda's agent. Under Gorton v. Doty, how should the court rule?

q: Hollis signs a contract describing himself as an “independent consultant” to Grand Lake Bistro's management company and expressly “not an agent of the Bistro.” In practice he sets the Bistro's hours and prices, picks its vendors, signs its checks, and sees its confidential investor data. While still doing all this, he secretly lines up investors for a competing restaurant. The Bistro sues for breach of fiduciary duty, and Hollis moves to dismiss because he wasn't its agent. What result?
o: Motion denied: actual practice, not the contract's label, decides agency.
Motion granted: the written contract expressly disclaims agency, and courts enforce such disclaimers.
Motion granted: a subagent hired through a management company can owe no greater duty than that company.
Motion denied, but only because planning a competing business is itself a tort whether or not he was an agent.
oe: Correct. MJ & Partners v. Zadikoff: the court looks at whether the principal could control the manner and method of the work and whether the agent could subject it to liability, judged by actual practice. A contract label doesn't control (R3d § 1.02), and an agent owes fiduciary duties.
Disclaimers are evidence but not controlling when the parties' conduct shows the elements of agency.
Zadikoff made this argument, and it failed at the pleading stage.
Preparing to compete is not wrongful in itself. The fiduciary claim depends on his being an agent.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Labels and actual practice

q: A professional cycling league's member teams sign an agreement making the league's Integrity Officer “wholly independent of the teams” in disciplinary matters; the teams can't direct, overrule, or remove the officer during a term. A rider sues the officer and the league to stop a doping hearing, and the case turns on whether the officer acts as the league's agent in discipline. What result under Rose v. Giamatti?
o: No agency in discipline: the teams gave up control in that area.
Agency exists, because the teams created the office and pay the officer's salary.
Agency exists for all purposes once it exists for any purpose.
No agency, because a league is an unincorporated association that cannot have agents.
oe: Correct. In Rose the clubs made the Commissioner independent of their control in discipline, “analogous to that of an independent contractor.” Without control there is no agency, though the officer could still be the league's agent for other purposes.
Creating and paying a position doesn't supply control. Rose turned on the clubs' surrender of control over discipline.
Rose recognizes that a person can be an agent for some purposes and not others.
Unincorporated associations can act through agents. The missing element was control, not capacity.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — No right of control

q: Variation: The agreement lets a majority of the teams remove the Integrity Officer at any time, for any reason, and amend the officer's powers by majority vote. Does the analysis change?
o: It may: a power to fire or redirect the officer is a form of control.
No: control means day-to-day supervision of physical conduct, which the teams still lack.
No: once the parties call the office independent, that label controls the analysis.
Yes: the removal power makes the officer an employee of each of the teams individually.
oe: Correct. The casebook asks exactly this after Rose. Control need not be exercised over every detail, and a power to remove or amend at will is evidence that the principal can direct the result.
Control of physical conduct is the test for employee status (vicarious tort liability), not for agency itself.
Labels don't control. R3d § 1.02.
At most it supports agency for the league. It says nothing about employment by each team.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Power to remove
pre: A professional cycling league's member teams sign an agreement making the league's Integrity Officer “wholly independent of the teams” in disciplinary matters; the teams can't direct, overrule, or remove the officer during a term. A rider sues the officer and the league to stop a doping hearing, and the case turns on whether the officer acts as the league's agent in discipline. What result under Rose v. Giamatti?

q: Northfield Feed lends a small rural elevator company, Prairie Co-op, ever-larger sums. Northfield also holds a right of first refusal on Prairie's grain, prints its own name on Prairie's forms, must approve Prairie's dividends and major capital spending, calls daily with directions, criticizes Prairie's salaries, and calls Prairie in an internal memo a business that “needs strong paternal guidance.” Prairie collapses owing local farmers $2 million. Are the farmers likely to recover from Northfield?
o: Yes: taken together, the controls made Northfield Prairie's principal.
No: a creditor can never be liable as a principal because a loan is an arm's-length contract.
No: agency exists only when both parties intend it and call their relationship agency.
Yes, but only because Northfield's name on the forms created apparent authority by itself.
oe: Correct. A. Gay Jenson Farms v. Cargill: R2d § 14O makes a creditor that takes over management of its debtor's business liable as principal. The nine factors are each common for lenders, but together they showed control, Prairie acted for Northfield's benefit, and Northfield directed its affairs.
Section 14O expressly allows creditor liability when the creditor assumes control.
Agency can arise although the parties didn't call it agency or intend its legal consequences.
The forms were one of nine factors. The case rests on actual agency from de facto control, not on the forms alone.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Creditor as principal

q: Variation: Northfield's only rights are to audit Prairie's books and to veto any single purchase or sale over $250,000. Northfield never calls with directions and never weighs in on salaries or operations. Is Northfield likely a principal?
o: No: veto rights over large deals protect a loan without running the business.
Yes: any veto right is a form of control, and control is all that agency requires.
Yes: an audit right is the most important of the Cargill factors and shows control.
No, because a lender is always treated as a mere supplier under § 14K.
oe: Correct. R2d § 14O comment a: a creditor who merely vetoes purchases or sales above specified amounts doesn't become a principal. Liability comes when the creditor takes over management and directs what contracts may be made.
Protective, negative controls are typical for lenders. Compare Martin v. Peyton, where veto rights didn't make lenders partners.
An audit right was one factor among nine and is common in ordinary lending.
Section 14K separates agents from suppliers who buy and resell. It is a different question.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Mere veto rights
pre: Northfield Feed lends a small rural elevator company, Prairie Co-op, ever-larger sums. Northfield also holds a right of first refusal on Prairie's grain, prints its own name on Prairie's forms, must approve Prairie's dividends and major capital spending, calls daily with directions, criticizes Prairie's salaries, and calls Prairie in an internal memo a business that “needs strong paternal guidance.” Prairie collapses owing local farmers $2 million. Are the farmers likely to recover from Northfield?

q: Marisol runs her own produce brokerage. She contracts to deliver 5,000 bushels of apples a month to Orchard Juice at a fixed price of $9 a bushel, buys the apples in her own name from growers she chooses at whatever price she can negotiate, and sells to several other juicers too. A grower she failed to pay sues Orchard Juice, claiming Marisol was its agent. Which fact most strongly shows Marisol is a supplier, not an agent?
o: Orchard pays a fixed price regardless of what Marisol paid the growers.
Orchard buys a large share of Marisol's apples every month on a standing order.
Marisol and Orchard put their arrangement in a signed, written contract.
The unpaid grower had never heard of Orchard Juice when it sold to Marisol.
oe: Correct. Under R2d § 14K comment a, the most important indicator of a supplier is a fixed price regardless of the supplier's cost. Acting in her own name, taking title, and running an independent business in similar goods point the same way.
Volume suggests a close relationship but doesn't separate an agent from a supplier. Warren in Cargill sold 90% of its grain to Cargill and was still found an agent.
A writing exists in both agency and sale relationships. It isn't an indicator either way.
That goes to whether a principal was disclosed, not to whether Marisol was an agent at all.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Agent or supplier

q: Theo, age 16, authorizes his 15-year-old cousin Lena to sell Theo's electric guitar to Ravi for $600. Lena makes the sale exactly as told. The next week Theo wants the guitar back. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Theo can avoid the sale: a minor principal's appointment is voidable.
The sale binds Theo, because Lena did exactly what Theo authorized her to do.
The sale is void, because an agent must have full contractual capacity to act.
Theo can avoid the sale only because Lena is a minor; an adult agent would bind him.
oe: Correct. The principal must have contractual capacity, so a minor principal's appointment (and the deal made through it) is voidable as if he acted in person (R3d § 3.04). The agent needs only enough mental capacity to act; her own minority doesn't matter (§ 3.05).
Authority doesn't cure the principal's lack of capacity. Theo could avoid the deal if he had made it himself.
An agent doesn't need contractual capacity, only mental capacity to act.
It is the principal's capacity that matters. An adult agent wouldn't change Theo's power to avoid.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Capacity

q: Over coffee, Dana orally tells her longtime friend Ike, “Go ahead and sell my lake lot; anything over $150,000 is fine.” Ike signs a written contract selling the lot to Basil for $160,000 as “agent for Dana.” Their state has an equal-dignities statute. Dana backs out. Basil sues to enforce. What is Dana's best defense?
o: The authority to sign a land contract had to be in writing, and it wasn't.
There was no consideration for Ike's promise to act as Dana's agent.
Ike never signed a formal agency contract with Dana before acting for her.
Friends can't be agents for each other unless one of them is paid for it.
oe: Correct. Generally no writing is needed to create agency, but some states require that the agency agreement be written when the agent is to enter contracts within the statute of frauds, such as land sales. R3d § 3.02: if the law requires a signed writing, the principal isn't bound without it (subject to estoppel).
Consideration isn't required for agency. Gratuitous agents are common (Gorton; R3d § 1.04(3)).
Agency needs consent, not a contract.
No such rule exists. Compensation isn't required.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Formalities

q: Wendell mails a letter to his nephew Abe: “I appoint you to collect the rent from my tenants while I'm abroad.” Abe never receives the letter and never collects or tries to collect anything. A tenant pays $1,200 to a stranger who claims to be Wendell's collector. Was Abe Wendell's agent when the tenant paid?
o: No: Abe never accepted the undertaking, so agency never formed.
Yes: the principal's written manifestation creates the agency as soon as it is mailed.
Yes, because a family relationship creates agency by operation of law.
No, because collecting money requires a notarized power of attorney.
oe: Correct. Botticello (citing R2d § 1 cmt. b) lists three elements: a manifestation by the principal, acceptance of the undertaking by the agent, and an understanding that the principal controls. Abe neither knew of nor accepted the undertaking. Agency is consensual on both sides.
Agency needs the agent's assent too, by words or conduct (R3d § 1.01).
Family relationships don't create agency (Botticello: marriage alone isn't proof).
No such formality is generally required.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Three elements

q: Customer Gil sues Midtown Motors on a contract signed by Fran, who Gil says was Midtown's agent. Midtown offers no evidence either way. At the close of Gil's case, the only evidence is that Fran wore a Midtown polo shirt once. Who bears the burden on agency, and what is the likely result?
o: Gil must prove agency by a preponderance; on this record he likely fails.
Midtown must disprove agency once Gil shows that Fran acted in its name.
Gil must prove agency beyond a reasonable doubt, which he can't do here.
Neither party; agency is a question of law the court decides without evidence.
oe: Correct. Agency is never presumed. The party asserting it bears the burden, though it may be proved circumstantially (Cargill; Mill Street; Hoddeson; Botticello).
The burden stays on the proponent.
The standard is a fair preponderance of the evidence.
Whether agency exists is usually a fact question that depends on the evidence.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Burden of proof

q: A tax-preparation chain hires seasonal preparers. It sets the client fees and the deadlines for each return, but lets each preparer decide when to work, where, and how to organize the return. A client argues the chain is a principal; the chain answers that it never controlled the preparers' physical actions. Which statement is correct?
o: Control of the result or objectives is enough; physical control isn't needed.
Without control of the preparers' physical conduct there can be no agency.
Agency exists only if the principal can dictate when and where the agent works.
Control is irrelevant to agency; the relationship rests on consent alone.
oe: Correct. The principal “need not exercise physical control over the actions of its agent” so long as it may direct “the result or ultimate objectives” (Green v. H & R Block, noted after Rose). Physical control matters for whether an agent is an employee (vicarious tort liability), not for whether agency exists.
That confuses agency with the master–servant (employee) relationship.
Hours are one factor in the employee analysis (Humble, Hoover), not a requirement for agency.
Control is one of the three elements.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Degree of control needed

q: Silver Realty, a broker hired by Paula to sell her house, has Paula's permission to use cooperating agents. Silver engages Juan, at another firm, to show the house. Juan learns that a buyer will pay $40,000 more than its offer, but tells Paula nothing. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Juan is Paula's subagent and fiduciary, and Silver answers to Paula for him.
Juan owes duties only to Silver, because Paula never hired him herself.
Silver has no responsibility for Juan, because Paula authorized subagents.
Juan is Paula's coagent, so Silver has no role in supervising his conduct.
oe: Correct. A subagent is appointed by an agent, with actual or apparent authority to do so, to perform functions the agent undertook for the principal. Both relationships are agency relationships, the subagent “stands in a fiduciary relation to the principal,” and the appointing agent answers to the principal (R2d § 5; R3d §§ 1.04(8), 3.15).
A subagent is also the principal's agent and fiduciary.
Authorization makes the appointment proper; the appointing agent still answers for the subagent.
Coagents are agents of the same principal, often appointed by her. Here Silver appointed Juan to help perform its own undertaking, which is the subagent pattern.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — Subagents

q: Which of these agents is a general agent under R2d § 3?
o: A store manager who runs purchasing, staffing and sales year-round.
A broker hired to find a buyer for one specific parcel of land.
A friend asked to buy a single concert ticket at the box office.
A courier hired to deliver one set of signed closing documents.
oe: Correct. A general agent is authorized to conduct a series of transactions involving a continuity of service. A special agent handles a single transaction or a series without continuity of service. The distinction matters for inherent authority (R2d § 161; Nogales).
A single transaction makes this a special agent.
A single transaction: a special agent.
A single errand: a special agent.
topic: Wk 1 · Creating an agency — General and special agents

q: St. Brendan's parish hires member Luis to re-roof its rectory. For two earlier projects the parish let Luis bring on his son as a helper and paid the son. This time the parish council privately decides that if Luis needs help he should use a parishioner named Carl, but no one tells Luis. The job can't safely be done by one person. Luis hires his son, who falls on the first morning. Is the son a parish employee for workers' compensation?
o: Yes: past practice and the job's needs gave Luis implied authority to hire him.
No: the council decided Carl would be the helper, and an agent has no authority beyond the principal's actual wishes.
Yes, but only because the son reasonably believed that Luis could hire him.
No: implied authority exists only in emergencies, and this wasn't one.
oe: Correct. Mill Street Church v. Hogan: implied authority focuses on the agent's reasonable belief, from the principal's present or past conduct, that the principal wants him to act. Prior similar practice is among the most important factors, and necessity (one person couldn't do the work) supports it. The council's secret decision doesn't matter.
Actual authority is measured by the principal's manifestations as the agent reasonably understood them, not by the principal's uncommunicated decisions.
The son's belief is relevant to apparent authority, not actual authority.
Emergency is one source of implied authority. Past conduct and necessity are others.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Implied authority from past practice

q: Paul, who owns an apartment building, tells his manager Ann in writing: “Hire a landscaping company for the summer, up to $4,000.” Ann hires GreenCo for $3,800. Paul later says he meant to use his brother-in-law's firm. Is Paul bound?
o: Yes: Ann acted with express actual authority.
No: express authority is ineffective if the principal didn't really mean it.
Only if GreenCo knew about Paul's written instruction before signing.
No, unless Paul later ratifies the contract with GreenCo.
oe: Correct. Express authority is conveyed explicitly in words, oral or written. It is effective even if the principal granted it by mistake, and the question is all or nothing: did the principal clearly grant authority for this act?
Express authority is effective even if granted mistakenly or because of a misrepresentation.
Actual authority depends on the principal's manifestation to the agent, not the third party's knowledge.
Ratification is needed only when the agent lacked authority.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Express authority

q: Variation: Paul gave Ann no instructions about cleaning. The building's hallways are filthy, and Ann hires a part-time janitor at the going rate. Is Paul bound?
o: Yes, probably: hiring a janitor is incidental to managing the building.
No: without an express instruction, the agent has no actual authority at all.
No: only apparent authority could bind Paul, and the janitor never met him.
Yes, but only if the janitor knew that Ann was the building's manager.
oe: Correct. This is the casebook's second Ann hypothetical: implied actual authority covers acts incidental to, usually accompanying, or reasonably necessary to accomplish the authorized task (R2d § 35; R3d § 2.01–2.02).
Implied actual authority fills in what express instructions leave out.
Apparent authority is analyzed after actual authority. Here actual (implied) authority likely exists.
Actual authority doesn't depend on the third party's knowledge.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Incidental authority
pre: Paul, who owns an apartment building, tells his manager Ann in writing: “Hire a landscaping company for the summer, up to $4,000.” Ann hires GreenCo for $3,800. Paul later says he meant to use his brother-in-law's firm. Is Paul bound?

q: Variation: Paul told Ann, “Do not hire a janitor; I'll clean myself.” Local custom lets apartment managers hire janitors. Ann hires one anyway. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No actual authority, but Paul may be bound by apparent authority.
Ann had implied authority from custom, which overrides Paul's instruction.
Paul can't be bound, because his agent violated a direct order.
Ann is personally bound and Paul isn't, as a matter of law.
oe: Correct. Between principal and agent, an express instruction controls over custom, so there is no actual authority. But placing Ann in a position that customarily carries the power to hire janitors can create apparent authority, and third parties need not inquire into undisclosed limits (R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
Custom fills gaps; it doesn't override an express contrary instruction between principal and agent.
Violating an order defeats actual authority but not necessarily apparent or inherent authority.
Whether Paul is bound depends on apparent authority. Ann may also be liable to Paul for disobeying.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Express limit vs. custom
pre: Paul, who owns an apartment building, tells his manager Ann in writing: “Hire a landscaping company for the summer, up to $4,000.” Ann hires GreenCo for $3,800. Paul later says he meant to use his brother-in-law's firm. Is Paul bound?

q: Gemma authorizes her agent Raj to buy a used delivery van for her bakery “for no more than $20,000.” Raj finds one for $18,500. The seller insists on a cashier's check and tells Raj to pick the van up at its lot. Raj pays and drives it to the bakery. Which statement is correct?
o: Raj had implied authority to pay for and take delivery of the van.
Raj needed separate express authority before making any payment.
Raj could buy the van but not take possession; only Gemma could accept delivery.
Raj had authority only if the seller knew about Gemma's $20,000 limit.
oe: Correct. One recognized category of implied actual authority is the authority to pay for and accept delivery of goods where there is authority to purchase.
Payment is incidental to an authorized purchase.
Accepting delivery is incidental to a purchase.
Actual authority depends on the principal's manifestation to the agent.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Implied authority to complete the task

q: Attorney Ortiz represents Kemp in a dispute. Kemp is unreachable on a hiking trip when Ortiz learns that the last day to file a notice preserving Kemp's claim is today at 5 p.m. Kemp's instructions say nothing about such notices. Ortiz files. Did Ortiz act with authority?
o: Yes: implied authority covers emergency action to preserve the client's rights.
No: an agent has no authority to act without the principal's specific approval.
Only if Kemp later ratifies the filing after returning from the trip.
Yes, but only because lawyers have inherent authority over every procedural step.
oe: Correct. The slides list emergency action as a source of implied actual authority (e.g., “I must act by 5 pm today in order to preserve the client's rights”).
Implied authority covers acts the principal would reasonably want, including emergencies.
Ratification isn't needed when there was implied actual authority.
The source of authority here is the emergency rule for implied authority, not a special rule for lawyers.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Emergency authority

q: An exam question asks whether Principal is bound by a contract that Agent signed with Third Party. Following the course's order of analysis, after deciding that an agency relationship exists, which question should you ask first?
o: Did Agent have express actual authority?
Did Principal ratify the contract?
Is Principal estopped to deny the contract?
Did Agent have inherent agency power?
oe: Correct. The slides say to analyze authority in this order: (1) actual authority, express then implied; (2) apparent authority; (3) ratification; (4) operation of law (inherent authority and estoppel). Also confirm that authority wasn't terminated before the agent acted.
Ratification comes third, after actual and apparent authority.
Estoppel comes last, under operation of law.
Inherent authority is part of the last category.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Order of analysis

q: Agent Mona, acting within her express authority for disclosed principal Hart Industries, signs a supply contract “Hart Industries, by Mona Ruiz, Purchasing Manager.” Hart later fails to pay. Can the supplier recover from Mona personally?
o: No: for a disclosed principal, the agent isn't a party absent agreement.
Yes: every agent who signs a contract is jointly liable with the principal.
Yes, because Hart breached and Mona personally negotiated the contract.
Only if Mona was a general agent rather than a special agent.
oe: Correct. The agent binds the principal when acting on its behalf, with authority, before termination, and is generally not bound herself (R3d § 6.01).
That is the rule for unidentified (partially disclosed) and undisclosed principals, not disclosed ones.
Negotiating for a disclosed principal doesn't make the agent a party.
General or special status doesn't decide the agent's personal liability.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Agent not a party

q: A candidate's longtime aide, whom the candidate lets hire staff and approve vendors for the campaign committee, tells a polling firm that the candidate “fully backs” a $150,000 polling contract with the committee. The candidate personally reviews the poll questions, uses the results in speeches, and tells the firm “great work.” The committee is insolvent. Is the candidate personally liable?
o: Likely yes: he assented and ratified, personally and through his aide.
No: campaign committees are separate entities whose debts never bind the candidate.
No, because agency is presumed not to exist between a candidate and his own staff.
Yes, but only because the candidate signed the polling contract himself.
oe: Correct. Karl Rove & Co. v. Thornburgh: members aren't liable merely as members, but are liable when (treating the member as principal and the association as agent) they authorize, assent to, or ratify a contract. The aide, whom Thornburgh controlled, could bestow that assent, and Thornburgh's own conduct added to it.
Unincorporated committees are governed by nonprofit association law, under which members can be liable.
Agency is never presumed, but it can be proven, and control showed it in Rove.
He didn't sign. Liability rested on assent through his agent and his own conduct.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Liability through one's agent

q: Orchard Co. appoints Bea as its exclusive sales agent for two years. After six months, Orchard emails Bea: “Your authority to sell for us ends today.” The next morning Bea signs a sale with a buyer who knows nothing of the email. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Bea's actual authority ended with the email, even if Orchard breached.
Bea's actual authority continues for the full two years the contract guaranteed.
The email was ineffective, because ending authority requires mutual agreement.
The email ended both Bea's actual authority and her apparent authority at once.
oe: Correct. Either party can end actual authority by a manifestation to the other, notwithstanding any agreement (R3d § 3.06 cmt. a): the power exists even without the right, and Orchard may owe contract damages. Apparent authority lingers until the third party has notice.
A contract term affects the right to terminate, not the power.
Agreement is one way to end authority; unilateral notice is another.
Terminating actual authority doesn't automatically end apparent authority; the third party must have notice.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Termination events

q: Ezra authorizes his niece to sell his antique clock. Ezra dies Tuesday morning, and the niece hears the news at noon. That afternoon she sells the clock anyway, because the buyer was already on the way. Did she have actual authority?
o: No: the death of an individual principal terminates actual authority by operation of law.
Yes: authority lasts until the estate revokes it in writing.
Yes: authority survives the principal's death for any sale the agent had already arranged.
No, but only because the clock was a family heirloom.
oe: Correct. Actual authority ends by agreement, by either party's manifestation, by the death or loss of capacity of an individual principal (or the end of an entity principal), by the agent's death, or by statute (R3d § 3.06 cmt. a). The slides list the principal's death as an operation-of-law termination.
Death of the principal is an operation-of-law termination; no revocation is needed.
The sale wasn't made until after Ezra died, and the niece knew of the death when she made it.
The nature of the property is irrelevant.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Death of the principal

q: Which of the following does NOT terminate an agent's actual authority?
o: The third party's lack of notice that the agent was fired.
Completion of the single task the agent was hired to do.
The agent's serious breach of the duty of loyalty to the principal.
Passage of a reasonable time when the parties set no duration.
oe: Correct. The third party's lack of notice is relevant to apparent (lingering) authority, not actual authority. Actual authority ends on agreement, notice by either party, an event such as fulfilling the purpose, lapse of a reasonable time, changed circumstances, the agent's breach of fiduciary duty, unilateral termination, or operation of law.
Fulfilling the relationship's purpose ends authority.
The agent's breach of fiduciary duty is a listed termination event.
Lapse of a reasonable time ends authority.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Other termination events

q: For years, Delta Supply has sold to Kurt, purchasing agent for Mapleton Hardware, on Mapleton's credit. Mapleton fires Kurt but tells no suppliers. A week later Kurt orders $8,000 of goods from Delta in Mapleton's name and disappears with them. Is Mapleton liable to Delta?
o: Likely yes: Kurt's apparent authority lingered until Delta had notice.
No: Kurt's authority ended when he was fired, and a principal is never liable for a former agent.
No, because Kurt acted for his own purposes rather than Mapleton's.
Yes, but only if Mapleton later accepts and keeps the goods.
oe: Correct. Terminating actual authority doesn't end apparent authority; it continues until the third party has notice that authority ended (Ackerman, quoting Tomlinson). Mapleton should have notified its suppliers.
That ignores lingering apparent authority.
Apparent authority can bind even when the agent acts for himself, if the third party reasonably believes he acts for the principal.
Accepting the goods would be ratification, but liability here rests on apparent authority.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Lingering apparent authority

q: Which pair correctly states whose belief matters for each type of authority?
o: Actual: A's belief from P's words to A. Apparent: T's belief from P's words to T.
Actual: P's subjective intent. Apparent: what A told T about his authority.
Actual: the third party's belief. Apparent: the agent's own belief.
Both depend only on what the principal subjectively intended.
oe: Correct. The slides frame it by relationship: principal–agent gives actual authority; principal–third party gives apparent authority. Mill Street: implied authority is actual authority proven circumstantially; apparent authority is a matter of appearances on which third parties rely.
Actual authority is measured by the agent's reasonable understanding, and apparent authority must trace to the principal, not the agent.
That reverses the two.
Neither test turns on the principal's secret intent.
topic: Wk 1 · Actual authority & termination — Perspective of the test

q: Ridgeway Foods' vice president tells new hire Nadia that she will report to regional manager Cole and “should see Cole about your duties and pay.” Cole writes Nadia that she will be “Area Lead” and later tells her she'll get a 1% commission on her team's sales. Only Ridgeway's president can set pay. Nadia works two years without the commission and sues. Under Lind v. Schenley, can a jury find Ridgeway bound?
o: Yes: Ridgeway held Cole out as its spokesman on pay.
No: only the president could set salaries, so Cole had no authority of any kind.
No: apparent authority can't arise from statements made by the agent himself.
Yes, but only if Nadia's commission would be smaller than Cole's own salary.
oe: Correct. In Lind, the company's instruction to see Kaufman about salary and his position as Lind's superior were the principal's manifestations; evidence that Kaufman lacked actual authority was irrelevant to apparent authority. Lind also changed position by taking on the job.
Lack of actual authority doesn't defeat apparent authority.
True, but here the manifestations came from the company: the VP's instruction and Cole's position.
The Lind dissent stressed that the commission would quadruple Lind's pay, but the majority rejected unreasonableness as a matter of law.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Position as manifestation

q: Variation: Instead, a Ridgeway board member who has nothing to do with hiring offers Nadia $250,000 in cash plus $250,000 in stock to join, far beyond anything Ridgeway pays anyone at her level. Is apparent authority likely?
o: Unlikely: an unusual offer from someone who doesn't hire puts her on notice.
Likely: any director of a corporation has apparent authority to set employees' pay.
Likely, because Nadia relied on the offer by accepting the job.
Certain, because the board member made the offer in writing.
oe: Correct. Lind distinguished Gumpert v. Bon Ami on this ground: a director, who doesn't ordinarily hire, offering an unusual cash-and-stock package should alert the employee to inquire. A commission to a salesman used to commissions doesn't.
Directors act as a board and don't ordinarily hire employees individually.
Reliance doesn't help if the belief in authority was unreasonable.
A writing from the agent doesn't create apparent authority; the question is whether the principal's manifestations make the belief reasonable.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Unusual offer by a non-hiring officer
pre: Ridgeway Foods' vice president tells new hire Nadia that she will report to regional manager Cole and “should see Cole about your duties and pay.” Cole writes Nadia that she will be “Area Lead” and later tells her she'll get a 1% commission on her team's sales. Only Ridgeway's president can set pay. Nadia works two years without the commission and sues. Under Lind v. Schenley, can a jury find Ridgeway bound?

q: Plaintiff Gwen attends a mediation with her lawyer, Burke, and is seen conferring with him throughout the final hours of talks. Burke tells defense counsel several times that he has authority to settle, then makes a global offer of $900,000, which the defendants accept before the deadline. Gwen never told anyone that Burke's authority was limited. A week later Burke says he misunderstood her wishes. Is the settlement enforceable?
o: Yes: Gwen's own conduct held Burke out, and the defense reasonably relied.
No: retaining a lawyer never gives the lawyer apparent authority to settle a case.
No: an oral settlement isn't enforceable until it is put in writing and signed.
No: Burke misunderstood his instructions, so he had no authority of any kind.
oe: Correct. Ackerman v. Sobol's two prongs: (1) the principal's conduct held the agent out (or knowingly let him act) and (2) the third party reasonably and in good faith believed he had authority. Attendance, conferring, and silence when a reasonable person would object (R3d § 1.03 cmt. b) are manifestations; Burke's assurances only bolster reasonableness.
Retention alone isn't enough, but Gwen did much more than retain Burke.
Ackerman held oral settlements enforceable even if meant to be memorialized later.
An agent's misunderstanding defeats actual authority, not apparent authority.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Attorney's authority to settle

q: Variation: Gwen never attends any session, never communicates with the defendants, and has given Burke no settlement authority. The only evidence of authority is Burke's own repeated statements that he has it. What result?
o: Probably no settlement: hiring a lawyer and his own claims aren't enough.
Settlement enforceable: defense counsel may always rely on opposing counsel's assurances.
Settlement enforceable, because the ethics rules make the lawyer the decision-maker on settlement.
Settlement enforceable by ratification, because Gwen later learned of it.
oe: Correct. Ackerman says retaining an attorney doesn't by itself create apparent authority to settle. Apparent authority must be traceable to the principal; “an employee-agent cannot confer authority upon himself merely by claiming it” (Nogales instruction).
Assurances support reasonableness only when the principal has made some manifestation.
Rule 1.2(a) gives the client, not the lawyer, the decision whether to settle.
Learning of a deal isn't ratification; she must affirm it with knowledge.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Absent client, agent's word only
pre: Plaintiff Gwen attends a mediation with her lawyer, Burke, and is seen conferring with him throughout the final hours of talks. Burke tells defense counsel several times that he has authority to settle, then makes a global offer of $900,000, which the defendants accept before the deadline. Gwen never told anyone that Burke's authority was limited. A week later Burke says he misunderstood her wishes. Is the settlement enforceable?

q: Trent, a junior clerk at Bellwether Shipping with no purchasing duties, tells a forklift dealer he is Bellwether's “purchasing director,” shows a business card he printed himself, and signs a $60,000 order in Bellwether's name. Bellwether has never dealt with the dealer. Is Bellwether bound by apparent authority?
o: No: Bellwether made no manifestation, and Trent's claims can't create one.
Yes: every employee has apparent authority to buy equipment for the employer.
Yes, because the dealer reasonably believed the business card Trent showed.
No, but only because the order was over $50,000.
oe: Correct. Apparent authority must rest on the principal's manifestations to the third party (R3d § 3.03). Unilateral agent representations are insufficient, and the principal isn't bound by an agent's false statement of his own authority unless he had authority to make it (R3d § 6.11(1)).
Employment alone doesn't hold out a clerk as a purchasing agent.
The belief must be traceable to the principal; Trent made the card himself.
Amount may bear on reasonableness, but the decisive problem is the absence of any manifestation by Bellwether.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Agent's own statements

q: For three years, Linden Farms has paid every invoice for seed that its foreman, Mo, ordered from Agri Supply, though Linden's internal rule says the owner must approve purchases over $2,000. Agri never knew of the rule. Mo orders $3,500 of seed. Linden refuses to pay. What is Agri's best argument?
o: Apparent authority from Linden's course of honoring Mo's orders.
Actual authority: Mo reasonably believed he could ignore the owner-approval rule.
Ratification: by paying Mo's earlier orders, Linden ratified this one in advance.
Estoppel: Agri detrimentally relied on Mo's statement that he was the foreman.
oe: Correct. Prior acts the principal allowed or honored are a classic basis for apparent authority. The principal's secret limit doesn't bind a third party without notice (R2d § 160).
The internal rule was communicated to Mo, so he couldn't reasonably believe he had actual authority beyond it.
Ratification relates to a specific prior act with knowledge. Paying past orders doesn't ratify a new one.
Estoppel needs the principal's intentional or careless conduct and the third party's detrimental change of position. The stronger theory is apparent authority from the course of dealing.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Prior acts

q: Coastal Pharmacy fires its buyer, Lana, and on May 1 mails each of its regular suppliers a letter announcing that Lana no longer works there. Supplier Medline receives the letter May 3 but files it unread. On May 20, Lana orders $5,000 of goods in Coastal's name from Medline. Is Coastal bound?
o: No: a reasonable time after the letter arrived, Medline had notice.
Yes: written notice is effective only once the third party actually reads it.
Yes: apparent authority lasts until the principal files a public notice of termination.
No, because firing an agent automatically ends every form of authority at once.
oe: Correct. Apparent authority ends when the third party has notice that authority ended. Notification occurs when the principal states the fact to the third party or a reasonable time after a writing stating it is delivered (Ackerman, quoting Tomlinson). Failing to read delivered mail isn't a defense.
Notification by delivered writing is effective after a reasonable time.
Public filing matters for partnerships (statements of dissociation); direct notice works here.
Firing ends actual authority only; it is the notice that ends apparent authority.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Termination of apparent authority

q: Hal gives his agent a signed power of attorney to sell his boat, then revokes it orally but lets the agent keep the document. The agent shows it to a buyer who has never heard of the revocation and sells the boat. What theory most strongly protects the buyer?
o: Apparent authority from a writing of prior authority left with the agent.
Actual authority, because the power of attorney was never physically destroyed.
Inherent authority, because holding a power of attorney makes the agent a general agent.
No theory: an orally revoked power of attorney protects no one who relies on it.
oe: Correct. A power of attorney or letter of authority the agent still holds after revocation is one of the listed types of apparent authority: the principal's writing is the manifestation, and the third party had no notice of revocation.
Revocation ended actual authority regardless of the document.
A power to sell one boat creates a special agency. The theory here is apparent authority.
The written instrument remains a manifestation to third parties until they have notice.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Writings of prior authority

q: Seller authorizes its traveling salesman to sell tractors but secretly forbids him to give any warranty. Salesmen of tractors customarily give a 90-day parts warranty. The salesman sells a tractor with a 90-day warranty to a buyer who knows nothing of the restriction. Is Seller bound by the warranty?
o: Yes: a secret limit on an incidental term doesn't bind a buyer without notice.
No: the express prohibition means the salesman had no authority to give it.
No: a warranty binds the seller only if the seller itself signs it.
Yes, but only if the buyer asked to see the salesman's written instructions.
oe: Correct. R2d § 160 makes the principal liable when an agent makes a contract within apparent authority while violating orders on incidental terms that the third party doesn't know about. The customary authority of the position supports the buyer's belief.
He had no actual authority, but apparent authority remains.
No such rule exists.
A third party need not inquire into undisclosed limits on customary authority.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Secret limits on incidental terms

q: Which statement about reliance is most accurate under the course materials?
o: Reliance is uncertain for apparent authority but always required for estoppel.
Apparent authority always requires detrimental reliance, but estoppel never does.
Neither doctrine considers the third party's reliance or belief at all.
Reliance matters only when the principal was undisclosed at the time of contracting.
oe: Correct. The outline notes some uncertainty whether T must change position for apparent authority (Lind found the requirement satisfied anyway); estoppel always requires detrimental reliance (R2d § 8B; R3d § 2.05).
Reversed: detrimental reliance is the core of estoppel.
Reasonable belief is central to apparent authority, and reliance is central to estoppel.
An undisclosed principal makes no manifestation to the third party, so reliance on it isn't possible; reliance matters for apparent authority and estoppel.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Reliance

q: After Lind v. Schenley, a client asks how to prevent mid-level managers from binding the company to compensation promises. What is the best advice?
o: Tell employees in writing who sets pay, and confirm big promises with that person.
Add a limit to managers' job descriptions kept in the confidential HR file.
Tell managers privately, in a staff meeting, never to discuss pay with recruits.
Nothing can be done, because managers always have inherent authority over pay.
oe: Correct. The casebook's planning lesson: firms should put compensation authority limits in writing and communicate them, and employees should confirm significant promises with someone who has actual authority.
Secret limits don't defeat apparent authority with third parties who don't know of them.
An uncommunicated instruction affects actual authority only.
The company can defeat apparent authority by communicating limits to the people dealing with the managers.
topic: Wk 2 · Apparent authority — Planning after Lind

q: Holloway Brewing buys a tavern but keeps the former owner, Finch, as manager; Finch's name stays on the sign and the liquor license. Holloway forbids Finch to buy anything except bar snacks; all drinks and supplies must come from Holloway. Finch buys $3,000 of cigars and mixers on credit from Vendor, who has never heard of Holloway. Vendor later discovers Holloway's ownership. Under Watteau v. Fenwick, is Holloway liable?
o: Yes: Holloway is liable for purchases usual for a tavern manager.
No: Vendor didn't know of Holloway, so there was no manifestation and no apparent authority.
No: Finch's purchases were forbidden, so there was no actual authority and nothing else binds Holloway.
Yes, but only because Vendor relied on Holloway's credit when it sold the goods.
oe: Correct. Watteau: once the defendant is shown to be the real principal, it is liable for acts usual for such an agent “notwithstanding limitations, as between the principal and the agent.” Otherwise principals could hide behind managers. This is R2d § 195 inherent agency power.
True, there's no apparent authority. But that is exactly why Watteau rests on inherent agency power.
Watteau bound the principal without actual or apparent authority.
Vendor relied on Finch's credit; it had never heard of Holloway.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Undisclosed principal's secret limits

q: Variation: Holloway never knew Finch was buying cigars or mixers. Under R3d § 2.06(1), which replaced inherent agency power, is Holloway likely liable?
o: Probably not: § 2.06(1) requires that the principal had notice of the conduct.
Yes: the Third Restatement codifies Watteau without any change in result.
Yes: § 2.06(1) makes an undisclosed principal strictly liable for its agent's purchases.
No, because the Third Restatement doesn't recognize undisclosed principals at all.
oe: Correct. R3d § 2.06(1) makes an undisclosed principal liable to a third party justifiably induced to change position only if the principal, having notice of the agent's conduct, didn't take reasonable steps to notify them. The casebook notes the Watteau defendants likely wouldn't be liable under it.
The Third Restatement rejects “inherent agency power” and narrows the result.
Section 2.06(1) is estoppel-like, tied to the principal's notice.
It recognizes them (§§ 1.04(2), 6.03) and even lets them ratify (§ 4.03).
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Under the Third Restatement
pre: Holloway Brewing buys a tavern but keeps the former owner, Finch, as manager; Finch's name stays on the sign and the liquor license. Holloway forbids Finch to buy anything except bar snacks; all drinks and supplies must come from Holloway. Finch buys $3,000 of cigars and mixers on credit from Vendor, who has never heard of Holloway. Vendor later discovers Holloway's ownership. Under Watteau v. Fenwick, is Holloway liable?

q: A record label assigns its promotions agent to book singers for live “compare the recording” recitals. Its secret instruction: book singers only for recitals that local dealers will later pay for. The agent books a soprano for a ten-city tour, with no such condition. The label cancels. Under Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison, is the label bound?
o: Yes: the uncommunicated, unusual limit doesn't bind the singer.
No: the agent disobeyed an express instruction, so the label is bound only if it ratifies.
No: estoppel can't apply, because the label itself never spoke to the singer.
Yes, but only because the singer was famous and the label wanted her.
oe: Correct. Judge Hand held Edison bound: a principal who selects an agent with discretion “has by that fact vouched to some extent for his reliability,” and delegated authority exists to avoid constant recourse by third parties to the principal. Best theories: apparent authority from the position (R3d § 1.03) or inherent power.
Disobedience defeats actual authority, but the singer could rely on the customary scope of the position.
Hand agreed estoppel was a fiction here, but held the principal bound anyway.
Her fame didn't matter; the customary scope of the agent's role did.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Customary scope of authority

q: Kerr Oil's regional marketing manager regularly grants truck-stop operators volume and promotional discounts. He tells one operator that Kerr will give it a 2¢/gallon across-the-board discount if it builds a restaurant. Kerr's policy forbids across-the-board discounts, which the operator doesn't know. Which statement best describes R2d § 161 as Nogales explained it?
o: A general agent's usual but forbidden acts can bind P even without apparent authority.
Inherent authority is simply another name for apparent authority.
Section 161 applies only to special agents engaged for a single transaction.
Section 161 binds the principal only if the third party relied on the principal's own words.
oe: Correct. Nogales: inherent authority “may make the principal liable because of conduct which he did not desire or direct, to persons who may or may not have known of his existence or who did not rely upon anything which the principal said or did.” Section 161 applies even where there is no apparent authority (cmt. b).
Nogales stresses that it is distinct: it arises from the agency relation itself, not the principal's manifestations.
Section 161 applies to general agents.
Section 161 doesn't require reliance on the principal's statements.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Inherent vs. apparent authority

q: Variation: At trial, the court instructs the jury (without objection) that only actual or apparent authority can bind Kerr, and refuses the operator's instruction paraphrasing § 161. The jury returns a verdict for Kerr. On appeal, what likely result?
o: Affirmed: the instruction conflicted with one given without objection.
Reversed: refusing any correct statement of the law is automatic reversible error.
Reversed, because inherent authority makes the principal liable as a matter of law.
Affirmed, because Arizona courts don't recognize inherent authority at all.
oe: Correct. That is how Nogales came out. Although the court explained inherent authority at length, there was no reversible error. A lesson in preserving objections at trial.
Nogales affirmed despite recognizing the doctrine.
Inherent authority still depends on facts, such as reasonable belief and lack of notice.
The court described inherent authority favorably; it affirmed on procedural grounds.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Jury instructions
pre: Kerr Oil's regional marketing manager regularly grants truck-stop operators volume and promotional discounts. He tells one operator that Kerr will give it a 2¢/gallon across-the-board discount if it builds a restaurant. Kerr's policy forbids across-the-board discounts, which the operator doesn't know. Which statement best describes R2d § 161 as Nogales explained it?

q: Which situation is NOT one of R2d § 8A comment b's three contract settings for inherent agency power?
o: An impostor who was never the principal's agent sells the principal's goods.
A general agent makes a deal similar to authorized deals, in violation of orders.
An agent makes an otherwise authorized deal but secretly for his own benefit.
An agent authorized to sell goods for cash sells them on credit.
oe: Correct. Inherent power arises “solely from the agency relation,” so an impostor has none. The three settings are (1) a general agent does something similar to what he's authorized to do but in violation of orders; (2) an agent acts purely for his own purposes in a transaction that would be authorized if properly motivated; and (3) an agent authorized to dispose of goods departs from the authorized method.
That's the first setting (§§ 161, 194).
That's the second setting (§§ 165, 262).
That's the third setting: departing from the authorized method of disposition (§§ 175, 201).
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Three situations of inherent power

q: Why does the Second Restatement put the risk of an agent's disobedience on the principal rather than on third parties?
o: Agents are chosen, trusted and controlled by the principal, so it should bear the loss.
Third parties are always better placed than principals to check an agent's instructions.
Principals always carry insurance against their agents' contracts.
Agents are usually judgment-proof, so courts must find some solvent defendant.
oe: Correct. R2d § 8A's rationale; Hand in Kidd adds that selecting an agent with discretion vouches for him, and delegation exists to spare third parties constant recourse to the principal.
The opposite: third parties usually can't see secret instructions.
Insurance isn't the stated rationale for inherent contract authority.
Risk spreading appears in tort rationales, not as the basis for § 8A.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Rationale

q: Professor Paula tells her research assistant Allie, “Hire another assistant for the summer at $19 an hour.” The going rate on campus is $20, and Allie hires Zelda at $20. Paula refuses to pay more than $19. Under the casebook's analysis, who likely wins?
o: Zelda: a hire at the going rate is within the customary scope of hiring.
Paula: an agent who exceeds an express pay limit by even $1 binds no one.
Paula, because Zelda should have asked to see Allie's written instructions.
Zelda, but only because Paula later let her work for a week.
oe: Correct. The book's Allie/Zelda problem suggests Zelda likely wins: Allie was placed in charge of hiring, and a hire at the going rate is within the customary scope of that role.
Exceeding express instructions defeats actual authority but not other theories.
Third parties need not inquire into undisclosed limits.
That would be a ratification argument; the book's analysis rests on authority.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Hiring at the going rate

q: Variation: Paula told Allie only to “find candidates and send them to me for approval.” Allie instead hires Zelda on the spot at $20. Zelda never had contact with Paula. Likely result?
o: Paula likely isn't bound: Allie had no authority to hire at all.
Paula is bound: anyone tasked with recruiting may also hire.
Paula is bound by inherent authority, because Allie is a general agent.
Paula is bound because Zelda accepted the job in good faith.
oe: Correct. The book notes that if Allie was only to send candidates for Paula's approval, there's no authority to hire.
Recruiting and hiring are different powers.
Allie's role was a narrow, special agency to find candidates.
Good faith alone doesn't create authority.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Agent only to recommend
pre: Professor Paula tells her research assistant Allie, “Hire another assistant for the summer at $19 an hour.” The going rate on campus is $20, and Allie hires Zelda at $20. Paula refuses to pay more than $19. Under the casebook's analysis, who likely wins?

q: Under R3d § 2.06(2), an undisclosed principal tries to rely on an instruction it gave its agent that limited authority below what a third party would reasonably have believed had the principal been disclosed. Can it?
o: No: § 2.06(2) bars relying on limits below what T would reasonably believe.
Yes: undisclosed principals are never bound beyond the agent's actual authority.
Yes, if the principal put its limiting instruction in writing.
Only if the third party later learns of the principal's identity.
oe: Correct. That's R3d § 2.06(2). It, together with § 2.06(1) and positional authority under § 1.03, replaces much of what inherent agency power did.
Section 2.06(2) prevents exactly that.
A writing doesn't change the § 2.06(2) result.
Discovery of the principal doesn't revive the secret limit.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Undisclosed principal can't hide instructions

q: M/M Records lets its A&R managers sign artists but has a firm policy: no guaranteed advances. A manager signs an artist with a guaranteed $50,000 advance. How could M/M best have protected itself, per the casebook?
o: Limit authority in its contracts, tell artists, or require countersignature.
Rely on the internal policy, since its A&R managers are bound to follow it.
Hire only general agents, who know the company's policies best.
Sue the artist for accepting a guarantee the manager had no power to give.
oe: Correct. The book's suggestions for M/M: limit authority in writing, tell the artists, or require countersignature, so that third parties have notice and can't reasonably believe the manager has the power.
An internal policy controls actual authority only.
General agents carry more inherent authority, not less.
The artist did nothing wrong if it lacked notice of the limit.
topic: Wk 2 · Inherent authority & undisclosed principals — Planning against guarantees

q: Mira and her husband Ned own a vineyard as tenants in common. Mira has told Ned she won't sell “for less than $400,000.” Ned, without telling Mira, signs a lease with an option to buy the whole vineyard for $400,000 to Ostrander. Mira collects her share of the rent for two years and watches Ostrander replant vines. Ostrander exercises the option. Is Mira bound?
o: No: Ned wasn't her agent, and taking rent didn't ratify his deal.
Yes: a spouse who manages the couple's business is presumed to be the other's agent.
Yes: Mira ratified by accepting rent and watching the improvements for two years.
No, and Ned isn't liable either, because the whole deal fails.
oe: Correct. Botticello v. Stefanovicz: marriage or joint ownership doesn't make one co-owner the other's agent, and “won't sell for less than $X” isn't an agreement to sell for $X. Because Walter never purported to act on Mary's behalf, there was nothing for her to ratify (R2d § 98 cmt. f). Ned himself is liable on his promise to convey full title.
Agency must be proven; marital status alone doesn't prove it.
Those acts were equally consistent with Ned's own half interest, and ratification requires intent to ratify with full knowledge.
Ned contracted to convey full title and is liable on that promise.
topic: Wk 2 · Ratification — Co-owners and spouses

q: A car buyer signs a “Buyer's Order” that the salesman also signs. The form states in bold: “NOT VALID UNLESS ACCEPTED BY SALES MANAGER OR OFFICER.” No manager or officer ever signs or learns of the order. Months later prices rise and the dealer refuses to deliver at the order price. The buyer argues the dealer ratified by silence. What result?
o: No contract: no one with authority knew of the order, so silence can't ratify.
Contract formed: the dealer's months of silence ratified the salesman's acceptance.
Contract formed by estoppel, because the salesman represented that the order was accepted.
Contract formed, because the salesman's knowledge is imputed to the dealer for ratification.
oe: Correct. Ercanbrack: silence can be affirmance only when one would naturally be expected to speak and only after the principal has information about the transaction. “Ratification of an act about which the principal knows nothing is inherently impossible.” The buyer also knew from the form that the salesman lacked authority.
Silence counts only if the principal knew.
Only an officer's representation could support estoppel; the salesman's couldn't.
The book asks why it wasn't imputed: knowledge needed to ratify is different from imputed notice (R3d § 5.03).
topic: Wk 2 · Ratification — Knowledge required

q: Variation: The dealer's general manager reads the Buyer's Order, takes the buyer's $2,000 deposit, and orders the truck from the factory in the buyer's specifications, but never signs the form. Can the buyer now enforce the order?
o: Likely yes: acting on the deal with knowledge can ratify it.
No: only a manager's signature on the form can ever bind the dealer.
No, because ratification is never available when the agent lacked authority.
Yes, but only up to the amount of the buyer's deposit.
oe: Correct. The most common implied ratification is accepting the benefits of the contract with knowledge. Ercanbrack distinguished Albright, where the company built the truck and took deposits.
Ratification can be implied from conduct.
Ratification exists precisely to adopt unauthorized acts.
Ratification adopts the whole transaction; partial ratification isn't allowed.
topic: Wk 2 · Ratification — Dealer acts on the order
pre: A car buyer signs a “Buyer's Order” that the salesman also signs. The form states in bold: “NOT VALID UNLESS ACCEPTED BY SALES MANAGER OR OFFICER.” No manager or officer ever signs or learns of the order. Months later prices rise and the dealer refuses to deliver at the order price. The buyer argues the dealer ratified by silence. What result?

q: Without authority, agent Rhea sells her principal's warehouse to Buyer for $2 million, with seller financing at 2% interest. The principal likes the price but not the financing, and writes Buyer: “I ratify the sale at $2 million, but not the 2% loan.” What is the effect?
o: It must ratify the whole deal or none of it.
The sale is ratified at $2 million, and the financing term is void.
The letter ratifies the sale, and the loan term stands only if Buyer later agrees to drop it.
Partial ratification is permitted if the principal acts promptly.
oe: Correct. Ratification requires acceptance of the entire transaction (R3d § 4.07). The principal's attempt to adopt only favorable terms fails.
No partial ratification.
Ratification can't split the transaction. The principal either adopts the whole deal, financing included, or none of it.
Promptness doesn't permit partial ratification.
topic: Wk 2 · Ratification — No partial ratification

q: Without authority, agent Kai agrees to sell his principal's painting to Lowe for $50,000. Before the principal learns of it, Lowe emails Kai: “I've changed my mind; consider my agreement withdrawn.” The principal then tells Lowe, “I ratify.” Is Lowe bound?
o: No: ratification must come before the third party withdraws.
Yes: ratification relates back to when Kai made the deal, before Lowe withdrew.
Yes, as long as the principal ratifies within a reasonable time.
No, but only because Kai was a special agent.
oe: Correct. R3d § 4.05(1): ratification must precede the third party's withdrawal. The slides list withdrawal as a bar alongside illegality and a material change in circumstances.
Relation back doesn't apply when the third party withdrew before ratification.
Timeliness can't overcome a prior withdrawal.
The agent's type is irrelevant to the withdrawal bar.
topic: Wk 2 · Ratification — Third party withdraws first

q: Agent Tess, without authority, contracts to sell her principal's beach house to Hugo. Before the principal learns of it, a hurricane destroys half the house. The principal, now eager to sell, ratifies. Hugo objects. What result?
o: Hugo isn't bound: the material change blocks ratification unless he agrees.
Hugo is bound, because ratification relates back to before the hurricane.
Hugo is bound, but the price is reduced by half to reflect the damage.
Hugo isn't bound, because ratification is never allowed for real estate.
oe: Correct. R3d § 4.05(2); the slides list a material change in circumstances as a bar.
Relation back is limited where it would be unfair to the innocent third party.

Neither Restatement allows an undisclosed principal to ratify.
Both Restatements allow it if the seller consents to the substitution.
Only the Second Restatement allows it; the Third forbids it.

Pia is liable, because ratification affects only the third party's rights.
Pia is liable for the cost of the extra 100 laptops only.
Pia is liable unless she paid for the extra laptops herself.

Ratification also affects the principal–agent relationship.
The principal ratified the whole deal.
Irrelevant; ratification adopts the act.

No: ratification always releases the agent completely from liability.
No, because the principal ratified with full knowledge of the facts.
Yes, but only if the supplier consents to the principal's suit.

Section 4.02(b) is an exception.
Knowledge makes ratification effective but doesn't override § 4.02(b).
The supplier's consent is irrelevant.

o: The principal, knowing all the material facts, stays silent while T performs.
The principal hasn't heard of the deal and so says nothing about it.
The principal hears a vague rumor of a deal, with no details, and says nothing.
The principal objects promptly in writing as soon as it hears of the deal.

No knowledge, no ratification.
Ratification needs knowledge of all material facts.
Objecting is the opposite of ratification.

q: Salesperson Ivy, while selling for Brightway Homes, learns from a buyer that a lot has a buried fuel tank. She doesn't tell Brightway. Later Brightway sells the lot to another buyer, who sues. Brightway argues it never knew of the tank. Under R3d § 5.03, is Ivy's knowledge imputed?
o: Yes: an agent's knowledge of material facts is imputed to the principal.
No: knowledge is imputed only if the agent actually passes it on.
No: imputation applies only to notifications sent in writing.
Yes, but only if Ivy was a general agent rather than a special agent.
oe: Correct. R3d § 5.03 imputes the agent's notice of material facts to the principal, unless the agent acts adversely to the principal for her own or another's purposes (§ 5.04), and even then it is imputed to protect a good-faith third party.
Imputation doesn't depend on actual communication.
A notification to an authorized agent is effective (§ 5.02), but imputation of knowledge (§ 5.03) doesn't require a writing.
Materiality to her duties is the test, not her general or special status.

q: An agent without any authority buys $10,000 of office furniture in the principal's name. The principal never ratifies, but its employees use the furniture for a year. Neither apparent authority nor estoppel applies. Does the seller have any claim against the principal?
o: Yes, possibly in restitution for the principal's unjust enrichment.
No: without authority or ratification, the seller can sue only the agent.
Yes, on the contract, because using the furniture is automatic ratification.
No: restitution claims against principals are barred by agency law.
oe: Correct. R3d § 2.07 provides restitution as a fallback when authority fails and the principal has been unjustly enriched.
Restitution is an independent route against an enriched principal.
Use might support ratification only with knowledge and intent; the question assumes none.
Section 2.07 expressly allows them.

q: At Grayson's Appliance showroom, a man in a dark suit who is not an employee approaches Dina, shows her a refrigerator, takes her $900 in cash, and promises delivery. Grayson's has no record of the sale. Dina sues Grayson's on an apparent authority theory. What result under Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.?
o: No apparent authority, but Dina may recover by estoppel based on the store's negligence.
Dina wins on apparent authority, because a reasonable customer would think he worked there.
Dina loses entirely, because a principal is never liable for someone who isn't its agent.
Dina wins automatically, because stores are strictly liable for what happens on their premises.
oe: Correct. “The law cannot permit apparent authority to be established by the mere proof that a mountebank in fact exercised it.” But a proprietor owes customers reasonable vigilance; if its lack of surveillance let a non-agent conspicuously act as its salesman, it can't rely on his lack of authority. Hoddeson got a new trial on that theory.
The belief must be traceable to the principal's manifestations, not to the impostor's conduct.
Estoppel based on the proprietor's negligence remains available.
Liability turns on negligence and reliance, not strict liability.

q: Variation: The impostor had Dina sign an order form, but she paid nothing, and when no refrigerator arrived she simply bought one elsewhere at the same price. Can she hold Grayson's to the “contract” by estoppel?
o: Probably not: without a detrimental change of position, estoppel fails.
Yes: signing the order form was enough reliance to support estoppel.
Yes, because estoppel never requires any reliance by the third party.
No, because estoppel applies only to undisclosed principals.
oe: Correct. The casebook asks this: with only an executory contract and no money paid, there's no detrimental change of position, which estoppel requires.
Signing a form with no resulting loss isn't a detrimental change of position.
Estoppel always requires detrimental reliance.
Estoppel applies where a person is “not otherwise liable,” regardless of disclosure.

o: That she changed her position in reliance on the appearance of authority.
That the impostor was in fact an employee of the store all along.
That the store intended to defraud her when it let him on the floor.
That the store later ratified the sale by accepting the money.

If he were an employee, she wouldn't need estoppel.
Negligence is enough.
Ratification is a separate doctrine.

q: Pension trustee Morales may collect contributions but not settle disputes; only the full board can. Over three years he signs eight settlement agreements with Employer, each stating that it binds the Fund and that cashing the check ratifies it. The Fund cashes every check, and copies of several agreements are in its files. Employer learns of the board's exclusive authority only in year three. The Fund later sues for a full audit of the settled years. What result?
o: The Fund is bound, by apparent authority, estoppel, and ratification.
The Fund isn't bound: Morales lacked actual authority, and Employer could have read the trust agreement.
The Fund isn't bound, because its clerks never read the agreements that came with the checks.
The Fund is bound only by agreements that its trustees personally signed.
oe: Correct. Trustees v. Steven Scott found the Fund bound to all 15 agreements: its continual cashing of checks created an appearance of authority; Employer relied to its detriment; and knowledge (inferred from the files) plus failure to repudiate supported ratification. Clerical staff's failure to read the agreements was no excuse.
Lack of actual authority doesn't defeat the other three theories.
Knowledge was inferred from the agreements in the Fund's files.
The theories didn't depend on the trustees signing.

q: Variation: Focus on the apparent authority and estoppel theories alone. For a settlement Morales signed after Employer received the trust agreement showing the board's exclusive power, is Employer's reliance reasonable?
o: No: after notice of the real limits, reliance is unreasonable.
Yes: reliance built on a long course of dealing can never become unreasonable.
Yes, because the Fund kept cashing the checks after that date.
No, and the Fund is free of every agreement Morales ever signed.
oe: Correct. The court held reliance unreasonable after June 1995, when Steven Scott received the Trust Agreement; ratification then carried the remaining agreements.
Notice of the agent's real scope ends reasonable reliance.
That supports ratification, not the reasonableness of reliance on apparent authority.
Earlier agreements remained binding.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts estoppel with apparent authority?
o: Estoppel only protects the relying party and can rest on carelessness; apparent authority binds both sides.
Both doctrines make the principal a full party to the contract, with rights against the third party.
Apparent authority can rest on negligence alone, but estoppel requires an express manifestation.
Neither doctrine requires the third party's belief in the agent's authority to be reasonable.
oe: Correct. Under apparent authority both sides are bound; under estoppel the person is liable to those who detrimentally changed position because of a belief it intentionally or carelessly caused, or failed to correct with notice (R2d § 8B; R3d § 2.05).
Estoppel only protects the relying party.
Reversed.
Both require a reasonable (justifiable) belief.
topic: Wk 3 · Estoppel — Estoppel vs. apparent authority

q: Oscar learns that his former business associate is telling suppliers he buys “for Oscar's company,” and that suppliers are shipping on that basis. Oscar never authorized this and did nothing to create the impression, but he says nothing for months. A supplier who shipped $15,000 of goods sues Oscar. What theory fits best?
o: Estoppel: knowing of the belief, Oscar failed to correct it.
Apparent authority, because Oscar's silence was itself a manifestation of consent.
Ratification, because Oscar knew of the purchases and didn't object.
No theory: a person is liable only for agents he appointed.
oe: Correct. R2d § 8B(1)(b) and R3d § 2.05(2): a person not otherwise liable is liable to those who justifiably and detrimentally change position if, knowing of the belief, he didn't take reasonable steps to correct it.
Apparent authority arises from manifestations to the third party; Oscar's failure to correct a belief he didn't create fits the estoppel provision.
Ratification adopts specific acts; Oscar never affirmed any.
Estoppel reaches people who failed to correct a belief they knew of.
