q: Dov buys $120,000 of lobster from Maine Catch, signing as “Purchasing Director, Harbor Seafood Exchange.” No such company exists. Dov's real company, Coastline Brokers, Inc., had filed a d/b/a certificate stating it does business as “Harbor Seafood Exchange.” Maine Catch never checked the records. Coastline doesn't pay. Is Dov personally liable?
o: Yes: the agent must disclose his principal's identity, and Dov didn't.
No: the public d/b/a certificate gave Maine Catch constructive knowledge of the principal.
No: Dov signed in a representative capacity, so only the business can be liable.
Yes, but only for the part of the debt incurred after Coastline was dissolved.
oe: Correct. Atlantic Salmon v. Curran: “unless otherwise agreed, a person purporting to make a contract … for a partially disclosed principal is a party to the contract.” Actual knowledge is the test, not means of discovering, so a d/b/a filing isn't enough, and a trade name with no rational connection to the real principal doesn't identify it.
The court rejected the “means of discovery” argument; the third party need not search records.
Signing as an officer of an unidentified or nonexistent entity doesn't protect the agent.
Liability rests on the failure to disclose the principal, not on the timing of the entity's dissolution.
topic: Wk 3 · Agent's liability on the contract — Unidentified principal

q: Agent Rosa tells a printer, “I'm ordering for Lark Publishing, Inc.,” shows her Lark business card, and signs the order “Lark Publishing, Inc., by Rosa Diaz, agent.” She has actual authority. Lark doesn't pay. Can the printer sue Rosa?
o: No: she disclosed her principal and acted with authority.
Yes: agents are always jointly liable with their principals on contracts they sign.
Yes, because Rosa's own signature appears on the order.
Only if Lark turns out to be insolvent.
oe: Correct. R3d § 6.01: for a disclosed principal, the principal and third party are parties; the agent isn't, unless the agent and third party agree.
Only for unidentified and undisclosed principals.
Signing in a representative capacity for a disclosed principal doesn't make her a party.
Insolvency doesn't change the agent's status.
topic: Wk 3 · Agent's liability on the contract — Disclosed principal

q: Variation: Rosa says, “I'm buying for a publisher I can't name yet,” and signs only her own name. Lark is later revealed as the principal and doesn't pay. Who is liable?
o: Both Rosa and Lark.
Only Lark, because the printer knew Rosa was acting as an agent.
Only Rosa, because Lark was never identified when the contract was made.
Neither, because a contract for an unnamed buyer is too indefinite.
oe: Correct. R3d § 6.02: when the principal is unidentified, the principal and third party are parties, and the agent is a party unless the agent and third party agree otherwise.
Knowing there is a principal isn't enough when its identity is unknown.
Lark becomes liable once identified, if Rosa had authority.
The contract is enforceable; the question is who is a party.

o: Lark must indemnify Rosa for the debt.
None: by contracting in her own name, Rosa took on the debt herself.
None, because an undisclosed principal is never liable on its agent's contracts.
Rosa may recover only half the bill from Lark.

Acting for an undisclosed principal with authority triggers the principal's duty to indemnify.
Undisclosed principals are liable on authorized contracts (R2d § 186).
Indemnity covers the whole loss incurred within authority.

o: Damages for breach of the implied warranty of authority, including her lost bargain.
Nothing: an agent who fails to bind his principal is never personally liable.
Only her out-of-pocket costs of preparing for the deal, never the lost bargain.
The truck itself, because Benny's contract binds the employer anyway.
oe: Correct. R3d § 6.10: one who purports to contract on behalf of another, lacking power to bind, impliedly warrants authority and is liable for the third party's loss, including the expected benefit, unless the principal ratifies, the agent disclaims the warranty, or the third party knows the agent lacks actual authority.
Section 6.10 makes him liable.
Section 6.10 includes the expected benefit.
Without authority or ratification, the employer isn't bound.

q: Variation: Before signing, Benny told Nell, “I'm not sure the boss will go along, so no promises.” Nell signed anyway. Is Benny liable on the warranty?
o: No: Benny's warning defeats the warranty claim.
Yes: the implied warranty of authority can never be disclaimed.
Yes, because the employer refused to ratify the sale.
No, because a vehicle sale needs a signed writing by the owner.

It can be disclaimed.
Refusal to ratify is what triggers the warranty, but the disclaimer defeats it.
That isn't the reason; the disclaimer is.

q: Kim signs a five-year lease for “Sunrise Yoga, LLC,” knowing the LLC hasn't been formed yet. The LLC is never formed. Is Kim liable on the lease?
o: Yes: one who contracts for a principal he knows doesn't exist is a party.
No: only the LLC can be liable, and it never came into being.
No, because the landlord should have checked the state's LLC records.
Yes, but only if Kim later forms some other LLC.

The person acting for a nonexistent principal is the one bound.
The burden isn't on the landlord, and § 6.04 applies regardless.
Liability doesn't depend on later formation.

q: Agent Lou, acting with authority for undisclosed principal Grove Inc., contracts to buy 1,000 tons of gravel from Quarry. Quarry later learns of Grove and refuses to deliver, saying it never agreed to deal with Grove. The contract doesn't exclude undisclosed principals, and nothing suggests Quarry would have refused to deal with Grove. Can Grove enforce it?
o: Yes: none of the exceptions applies, so Quarry is bound to Grove.
No: a third party may always refuse to deal with a principal it didn't know about.
No, because only the agent is a party to an undisclosed-principal contract.
Yes, but Grove must pay a premium for being substituted in.
oe: Correct. R2d § 302 (and § 292 for disclosed principals); R3d § 6.03: the undisclosed principal and third party have the same rights and defenses as if the principal contracted personally.
Only in the listed situations, or if the agent falsely denied acting for a principal and P or A knew T wouldn't deal with P (R3d § 6.11(4)).
The undisclosed principal is a party unless excluded.
No premium rule exists.

q: Variation: Quarry had asked Lou, “You're not buying for Grove, are you? We don't sell to Grove,” and Lou answered, “No.” Can Quarry avoid the contract?
o: Yes: Lou's false denial lets Quarry avoid the contract.
No: an undisclosed principal's rights can never be defeated.
No, because Lou acted with actual authority from Grove.
Yes, but only by suing Lou for damages, not by avoiding the contract.
oe: Correct. R3d § 6.11(4).
Fraud on the third party is an exception.
Authority doesn't excuse the misrepresentation.
Avoidance is available.

o: Mateo is liable: an agent stays liable for his own torts.
Mateo isn't liable: respondeat superior shifts all of the liability to the employer.
Mateo isn't liable, because he was following his employer's instructions.
Mateo is liable only if his employer turns out to be insolvent.

It makes the employer liable too; it doesn't release the employee.
Following instructions isn't a defense to one's own tort.
His liability doesn't depend on the employer's solvency.

q: A security firm hires a guard with two prior assault convictions without checking his background. The guard assaults a shopper for reasons wholly personal to him. The shopper sues the firm. Which theory best fits the firm's possible liability?
o: Direct liability for negligently selecting or supervising the guard.
Vicarious liability, because every tort by an employee is within the scope of employment.
Liability under § 7.08 for torts committed with apparent authority.
No liability, because a principal is never liable for an agent's intentional torts.

Section 7.08 covers torts the agent commits while dealing with third parties on the principal's behalf, like fraud. A personal assault isn't that.

Did P ratify the tort? Was A paid for the work done?
Did A act with apparent authority? Did T rely on that authority?
Is P insured against the loss? Is A solvent enough to pay?

Those belong to the apparent-agency alternative route, not the core sequence.
Insurance and solvency aren't steps in the analysis.

No: the agreement disclaims control, and courts enforce such labels.
No, because the operator never actually received instructions about the car.
Yes, but only because the oil company's brand appears on the station's signs.

Humble owned the station and products, paid utilities, controlled hours, could terminate at will, and could assign duties; “the business was Humble's business,” like a store clerk paid by commission.
Labels are informative, not dispositive.
It's the right to control, not actual control, that matters.
Branding is common to independent dealers too (Hoover). The control terms decide it.

Liability, because the oil company owns the station the dealer operates.

Branding and training are consistent with an independent dealer.
Ownership of the premises leased to the dealer isn't control of operations.
A lessee could be an agent if control existed; here it didn't.

q: Which of the following is NOT a factor listed in R2d § 220(2) for deciding whether a worker is a servant?

Who supplies the tools and the place of work.
Whether payment is by time or by the job.
Whether the work is part of the employer's regular business.

The § 220(2) factors are: extent of control over details; whether the worker is in a distinct occupation; whether such work is usually supervised in the locality; skill required; who supplies tools and place of work; length of employment; method of payment (time or job); whether the work is part of the employer's regular business; whether the parties believe they're creating a master–servant relation; and whether the principal is in business.
A listed factor (e).
A listed factor (g).
A listed factor (h).

An employee, because it can bind the company.
A nonagent service provider.
A servant under R3d § 7.07.

Power to bind makes it an agent; control of manner and means would make it an employee, and that's absent.
It's a fiduciary with power to bind, so it's an agent.

The employer is always the cheapest cost avoider, so efficiency alone decides.
The employer is morally at fault for every tort its employees commit.
Employees are fiduciaries, so their torts are legally the employer's own acts.

Friendly declined to rest on a purely economic, resource-allocation test.
Vicarious liability is liability without fault (Kerl).
Fiduciary status isn't the basis of respondeat superior.

Only the control the company actually exercised over the crew.
Only what the parties called their relationship in the contract.
Whether the crew member held a license to operate the equipment.

Actual exercise isn't required.
Labels are informative but not dispositive.
Licensing isn't the test.

o: No: unpaid work doesn't relieve the principal of liability.
Yes: only paid employees can trigger respondeat superior.
Yes, unless the charity happens to carry liability insurance.
No, but only if the volunteer signed a written volunteer agreement.

Insurance doesn't affect the rule.

q: A guest slips on a puddle in the lobby of a Starlight Inn owned by a licensee. The license requires approved building plans, Starlight signs, fees per room, quarterly reports, inspections, and training, but gives Starlight no say over room rates, hiring, wages, maintenance, or daily expenses. Is Starlight vicariously liable?
o: Likely not: the license protects the brand but doesn't control daily operations.
Yes: any franchisor that inspects its licensees thereby controls them.
Yes, because the guest relied on the Starlight name when booking.
No, because the license disclaims agency, and such disclaimers are conclusive.

Inspections to protect the brand don't amount to control of daily operations.
Reliance is relevant to apparent agency, a separate theory; the question asks about actual control.
Disclaimers aren't conclusive; the absence of control decides it.

q: A pizza franchisor's operating manual sets delivery-time zones, uniforms, grooming, driving and delivery techniques, sales quotas, bookkeeping, mandatory training, manager hours, and complaint handling, and allows random inspections. A franchisee's delivery driver causes a crash. The franchisor moves for summary judgment. Under Parker v. Domino's, what result?
o: Denied: the controls create a jury question on the right to control.
Granted: franchisors are never liable for their franchisees' employees.
Granted, because the franchisee sets its own menu prices.
Denied, and the franchisor is liable as a matter of law.

Is the franchisor vicariously liable?
o: No: the franchisor didn't control hiring or supervision, the aspect that caused harm.
Yes: the overall control reflected in the manual makes the franchisor a master.
Yes, because the franchisor could have terminated the franchise for poor hiring.
No, because franchisors are immune from such suits under federal trademark law.
oe: Correct. Kerl v. Rasmussen: Arby's had no control over hiring and supervision. Quality and operational standards protect the trademark; the power to terminate isn't control of daily operations; and the rationales for vicarious liability weaken in franchising.
Kerl rejected a general-control test in favor of an instrumentality-specific one.
A right to terminate isn't a right to control daily operations.
There's no immunity; the Lanham Act explains why quality controls aren't treated as control.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Franchising & apparent agency in tort — Specific instrumentality

q: A customer bites into a stone in a burger at a franchised burger restaurant. Only the national brand's signs are visible; a small notice by the register names the franchisee. The franchisor prescribes exact food-handling and preparation methods, and the customer chose the restaurant because she trusted the brand. The agreement disclaims agency. Can her claim against the franchisor reach a jury?

No: the disclaimer and the sign naming the franchisee defeat both theories.
Only on apparent agency, because franchisors never have actual control.
Only on actual agency, because apparent agency doesn't apply to physical injuries.

McDonald's reversed summary judgment on both theories: the franchisor controlled the precise part of the business that caused the injury, and its insistence on uniformity held out the franchisee as its agent and made reliance justifiable. One inconspicuous sign doesn't necessarily dispel the impression.
Neither was enough to defeat the claims at summary judgment.
The control over food handling supported actual agency too.

q: Variation: The customer testifies that she didn't know or care what brand the restaurant was; she went in only because it was the closest place open. What happens to the apparent agency claim?

It still succeeds, because the franchisor held out the franchisee as its agent.
It succeeds, because apparent agency in tort is strict liability.

A representation without reliance isn't enough under § 267.
Williams stressed it isn't strict liability.
Actual agency doesn't depend on the plaintiff's reliance.

Dimensions Health, can the hospital be vicariously liable?

No: an independent-contractor physician can never be a hospital's agent.
No: reliance must be the patient's own belief, and the patient was unconscious.
Yes, because hospitals are strictly liable for all care given on their premises.

That was Chief Judge Getty's dissent.
The majority stressed this isn't strict liability.

q: The Third Restatement doesn't carry forward R2d § 267. Which provisions does the casebook identify as its replacements for apparent agency in tort?

§ 4.01 (ratification), applied to the hospital's later conduct.
§ 8.01 (fiduciary duty) and § 8.08 (duty of care).

Yes: any brand affiliation creates agency under the civil rights statutes.
Yes, because the oil company had a nondelegable duty under § 1981.
No, because § 1981 never applies to retail stores.

Agency principles govern, and they require control.
Arguello rejected a nondelegable duty under § 1981.
Section 1981 and Title II can apply; the problem was agency.

q: Kerl explains that the rationales for vicarious liability weaken in franchising. Which observation supports that view?
o: The franchisee pays the franchisor, and the franchisor doesn't run the business.
Franchisors are almost always smaller businesses than their franchisees.
Franchisees are usually judgment-proof, so imposing liability is pointless.
Trademark law forbids franchisors from setting any operating standards.

The opposite is usually true.

Trademark law requires quality control to protect the mark.

q: Rideshare-van driver Petra, employed by Metro Shuttle, is paid $20 by a stranger to use her van to tow his stuck car. Metro's rules forbid using vans for anything but carrying passengers and specifically forbid towing; Metro has never tolerated violations. While towing, Petra hits another car. Is Metro vicariously liable?

Yes: Petra was using Metro's van during her shift, so she was within scope.

No, because vans are never treated as dangerous instrumentalities.
oe: Correct. Brill v. Davajon: the cab driver pushing a car for $1 against express rules “had departed from his employer's business.” No evidence showed such conduct was accepted practice, that the employer acquiesced in past violations, or that the money went to the company.
Using the employer's vehicle on shift isn't enough when the act is different in kind and serves only the driver.

q: Variation: Petra takes no money; she tows the car because Metro encourages drivers to “help stranded motorists — it's great PR,” and supervisors have praised drivers who did so. Is Metro likely liable now?
o: Possibly: encouragement and goodwill support a purpose to serve Metro.
No: violating a written rule always takes the act outside the scope of employment.
No, because Petra wasn't paid anything for the tow.
Yes, automatically, because a goodwill gesture is part of every driver's job.
oe: Correct. The casebook notes that without the $1 there's an argument that helping a motorist builds goodwill, and Brill distinguished cases where the employer acquiesced in rule violations.

Lack of payment from the stranger actually strengthens the purpose-to-serve argument.

q: A sailor returning drunk to his ship late at night crosses a private drydock, as the government's contract with the drydock owner allowed crew members to do, and for no reason turns valves that flood the drydock, sinking part of it. The sailor's act served no purpose of the government. Is the government liable under Bushey?
o: Yes: the risk was characteristic of the enterprise's activities.
No: conduct with no purpose to serve the employer is outside scope under R2d § 228(1)(c).
No: the drydock owner could cheaply have locked the valves, so it should bear the loss.
Yes, because the government is strictly liable for all acts of service members.
oe: Correct. Judge Friendly held the motive test “highly artificial.” A business “cannot justly disclaim responsibility for accidents which may fairly be said to be characteristic of its activities.” Seamen's drinking is well known and crew crossing the drydock might foreseeably cause damage; the precise act needn't be foreseeable.
Bushey acknowledged the motive test wasn't met and held the government liable anyway.
Friendly mentioned that efficiency argument but refused to rest liability on it.
Liability rested on enterprise risk, not blanket strict liability.
topic: Wk 4 · Scope of employment — Enterprise risk

q: Variation: On the way back to the ship, the same drunken sailor instead causes a traffic accident on a city street. Is the government liable under Bushey's reasoning?
o: No: a street accident is a risk the whole community shares.
Yes: anything a sailor does on shore leave is within the scope of employment.
Yes, because the sailor was on his way back to duty at the time.
No, because Bushey's rule applies only to property damage.
oe: Correct. Friendly's limits: no liability for setting fire to a bar or for a street accident on the way back, since those risks aren't characteristic of the enterprise; nor for shooting someone over a purely personal or domestic matter.
Bushey drew a line at risks no different from the community's.
Returning to the ship doesn't make an ordinary traffic accident characteristic of the enterprise.
The limit is about the kind of risk, not property versus injury.

q: A visiting team's pitcher, warming up in the bullpen, is heckled continuously for three innings by fans in the adjacent stands. At the end of the inning he throws a fastball hard at the hecklers; it passes through the screen and hits a fan. The fan sues the pitcher's club for battery. Under Manning v. Grimsley, can the club be liable?
o: Yes, if the throw responded to conduct presently interfering with his job.
No: an intentional battery can never be within the scope of employment.
No, because the club never paid the pitcher to throw at fans.
Yes, because the club is responsible for the stadium where it plays.
oe: Correct. Under the Massachusetts rule, the employer is liable for an employee's assault made in response to the plaintiff's conduct that was presently interfering with the employee's performance. Continuous heckling designed to rattle a pitcher qualifies; mere retaliation for past annoyance doesn't.
Intentional torts can be within scope; R2d § 228(1)(d) covers force that is not unexpectable.
The question is whether the act responded to interference with his job, not whether it was assigned.
A visiting club doesn't control the home stadium, and in any case liability turns on scope of employment.

o: Unlikely: one remark isn't conduct interfering with his job.
Likely: any interaction with fans is part of a ballplayer's job.
Likely, because punches by athletes are always “not unexpectable.”
Unlikely, but only because the pitcher had already left the field.
oe: Correct. Manning distinguished Miller v. Federated Dept. Stores, where a porter slapped a customer over a remark: one comment isn't “conduct” interfering with performance.
The rule requires present interference with job performance.
That isn't the Massachusetts test applied in Manning.
Being off the field matters, but the main problem is the lack of interfering conduct.

The town's insurance policy excludes intentional acts. What result under Lamkin v. Brooks?
o: The town is liable, but its insurer owes no coverage.
The town isn't liable, because the officer was outside town limits.
The town isn't liable, because intentional torts are outside scope as a matter of law.
The town and its insurer are both liable to the injured man.

The test: whether the conduct was “so closely connected in time, place, and causation to his employment-duties as to be regarded a risk of harm fairly attributable to the employer's business.” All contacts arose from police duties. The intentional-acts exclusion shifted who actually paid.
Being outside the jurisdiction doesn't automatically defeat liability.
Intentional torts can be within scope.
The exclusion defeated coverage.

o: It cuts against scope: purely personal conduct falls outside it.
None: anything an on-duty officer does is within the scope of employment.
It makes the insurer liable instead of the town.
It makes the town directly liable for negligent supervision as a matter of law.
oe: Correct. The book notes that without a bona fide intent to record the plate, a purely personal motive argues against scope; Lamkin also relied on the absence of prior bad blood.
Purely personal conduct falls outside even for on-duty officers.
The intentional-acts exclusion still applies.
Direct liability would require proof of negligence.

q: At a store owned by an oil company, a clerk ringing up a sale refuses a customer's out-of-state license, shouts racial slurs over the intercom, and makes obscene gestures. The customers sue the company under § 1981. Can the clerk's conduct be within the scope of employment?
o: Yes, it's a jury question: her job put her in position to do it.
No: racial slurs never serve the employer, so they're outside scope as a matter of law.
Yes, and the company is liable because it ratified her conduct by not firing her.
No, because § 1981 claims never use agency principles.

Factors: time, place and purpose; similarity to authorized acts; whether such acts are commonly done; departure from normal methods; whether the employer would expect it. Intentional misconduct doesn't automatically take conduct outside scope.
The court held it a jury question.
Arguello held counseling her wasn't ratification.
Agency principles govern § 1981 liability.

o: No: counseling her and calling it inappropriate isn't adoption.
Yes: keeping an employee after learning of misconduct always ratifies it.
Yes, because the company knew all the material facts.
No, because a corporation can never ratify an intentional tort.

Keeping an employee isn't by itself adoption of the conduct.
Knowledge is necessary but not sufficient.
Corporations can ratify torts; Conoco just didn't.

o: When it's an independent course of conduct serving no purpose of the employer.
Whenever it happens outside working hours or away from the workplace.
Whenever the employer has forbidden the act.
Whenever the act is an intentional tort.

Forbidden acts may be within scope.
Comment c says intentional torts may be within scope.

q: Which act is the Third Restatement's commentary most likely to treat as within the scope of employment?
o: A sales manager who sets prices agrees with a competitor to fix prices.
A cashier robs a bank on her lunch break.
A bookkeeper assaults a neighbor over a property-line dispute.
A warehouse worker steals a car from the parking lot of a different company to drive home.

Serious crime unrelated to the work is outside scope.
Purely personal conduct is outside scope.
Unrelated to the employer's purposes.

q: A chef at a ski resort, required to ski between the resort's two restaurants, takes a few extra runs and a jump on the way down and injures another skier. Under Clover v. Snowbird, what can a jury find?
o: That his deviation wasn't a total abandonment of his job.
That he was on a frolic as a matter of law, because skiing for fun is personal.
That the resort is liable regardless of scope, because skiing is ultrahazardous.
That scope doesn't matter, because he was an independent contractor.
oe: Correct. Clover: the jury could find the chef had resumed or never fully abandoned his employment. A detour is a minor deviation still within scope; a frolic is a substantial departure on the employee's own business. (Utah also rejected Bushey's foreseeability test.)
A minor deviation within the route required for work can be a detour.
Skiing isn't treated that way.
He was an employee.

q: Under R2d § 229, which fact would most strongly support treating an unauthorized act as within the scope of employment?
o: The harm came from a tool the employer furnished, used much as authorized.
The act was seriously criminal, such as an armed robbery.
The act was entirely outside the employer's line of business.
The employer had no reason to expect that such an act would be done.

Serious criminality cuts against scope.
That cuts against scope.
That cuts against scope.

q: The Class 4 slides propose a “better standard” for allocating liability. Which question does it ask?

Which party has more money with which to pay the loss?
Which party was morally more at fault for what happened?
Which party signed the contract first?

Irrelevant.

q: Homeowner Iris hires Apex Roofing, an established company with its own crews and equipment, to replace her roof. Iris gives no instructions about methods. An Apex worker carelessly drops a bundle of shingles on a passerby. Is Iris liable?
o: No: she isn't liable for an independent contractor's negligence.
Yes: a property owner is always liable for work done on her property.
Yes, because she chose the contractor and so vouched for it.
No, but only because roofing is ultrahazardous, which shifts liability to the contractor.
oe: Correct. That's the general rule in Majestic, Kleeman and Anderson; under R3d § 7.03 there is no vicarious liability for nonemployee agents except for apparent-authority torts.
No such blanket rule exists.
Choosing a competent contractor isn't negligence.
Roofing isn't ultrahazardous, and ultrahazardous activities would increase, not reduce, the principal's liability.

q: A city parking authority hires a demolition contractor to raze buildings on a busy downtown block. The crane operator swings a wrecking ball into a free-standing wall, which falls onto the neighboring building's roof. The neighbor sues the parking authority. Under Majestic Realty v. Toti, what result?
o: The authority may be liable, because the work was inherently dangerous.
The authority isn't liable, because the contractor alone controlled the work.
The authority is absolutely liable, because demolition is ultrahazardous.
The authority is liable only if it chose an incompetent contractor.
oe: Correct. Majestic adopted the rule that such demolition is inherently dangerous under Restatement of Torts § 416: work that necessarily creates a peculiar risk of harm unless special precautions are taken. Where reasonable minds could differ, it's a jury question.
Inherently dangerous work is an exception to the general rule.
Majestic distinguished inherently dangerous work (liability for the contractor's negligent failure to take precautions) from ultrahazardous activity (absolute liability).

q: How does an abnormally dangerous (ultrahazardous) activity differ from inherently dangerous work?
o: Abnormal danger can't be eliminated with care and brings absolute liability; inherent danger can be, with precautions.
They're identical terms for the same doctrine, used interchangeably by courts.
Inherently dangerous work brings absolute liability; abnormally dangerous activity requires negligence.
Only abnormally dangerous activities can involve independent contractors at all.
oe: Correct. Restatement of Torts § 520 and Torts 2d § 427A (abnormally dangerous) vs. § 416 (peculiar risk unless special precautions). Majestic drew this line.
Majestic distinguished them.
Reversed.
Both doctrines are exceptions to independent-contractor non-liability.

q: An oil refinery hires a sandblasting contractor to clean its storage tanks. Liability, because the refinery knew of the unsafe hood and did nothing.
Liability, because sandblasting is inherently dangerous work.
No liability, because the refinery never hired the employee and owed no one any duty.

Yes: no one can ever sue a principal over an independent contractor's work.
Yes, because the visitor wasn't a party to the contract.
No, and the refinery is absolutely liable regardless of the activity.

The exceptions protect third parties.
Third parties are the classic beneficiaries of the exceptions.

o: The principal buys an output and isn't placed to supervise inputs or safety.
Contractors are always wealthier than the principals who hire them.
Principals are blameless, and the law never imposes liability without fault.
Contractors always carry insurance, so principals never need to.
oe: Correct. Posner: the principal buys a result and lacks the expertise and control to manage how it's produced; employees surrender control over details in exchange for wages.
Wealth isn't the rationale.

Insurance is a planning tool, not the stated rationale.

Ruiz isn't liable, because she chose a reputable agency and gave proper instructions.
Ruiz isn't liable, because process servers are independent contractors.
Ruiz is liable only if she was negligent in choosing the agency.
oe: Correct. A duty is nondelegable when “the responsibility is so important to the community that the employer should not be permitted to transfer it to another.” Kleeman relied on the professional rules, clients' expectations, and lawyers' exclusive franchise.
Careful selection doesn't satisfy a nondelegable duty.
That's exactly the defense a nondelegable duty overrides.
That was the concurrence's narrower ground; the majority rested on nondelegability.
topic: Wk 4 · Torts of independent contractors — Nondelegable duty

q: What did Judge Bellacosa's concurrence in Kleeman worry the majority's rule would do?
o: That lawyers would bring process serving in-house and answer for retained experts.
That clients would become liable for their own lawyers' malpractice.
That malpractice liability for lawyers would effectively be abolished.
That lawyers would be barred from ever using outside vendors for any task.
oe: Correct. He would have decided the case on the narrower ground of fact issues about negligent selection (the agency's reputed sloppiness).
The rule runs the other way.
It expands liability.
The concern was cost and scope, not a prohibition.
topic: Wk 4 · Torts of independent contractors — Concurrence's concern

q: A developer hires a framing contractor but has its own site supervisor dictate exactly how scaffolding is erected each day. A scaffold collapses onto a pedestrian. Which exception most clearly applies?
o: The developer retained control of the manner of the work.
Nondelegable duty owed to the public.
Abnormally dangerous activity.
No exception applies; only the contractor can be liable.
oe: Correct. Retained control is the first Majestic exception: when the principal controls the manner of work, the reason for non-liability (no right to control) disappears.
Possible in some settings, but the facts point to retained control.
Scaffolding isn't abnormally dangerous.
Retained control makes the developer potentially liable.
topic: Wk 4 · Torts of independent contractors — Retained control

q: Majestic reserved a question about the incompetent-contractor exception. What was it, and what planning tool does the casebook suggest?
o: Whether “competence” includes solvency; require insurance or a bond.
Whether the contractor needed a license; require a license check first.
Whether demolition is ultrahazardous; avoid demolition work altogether.
Whether the authority was immune from suit; seek legislative immunity.
oe: Correct. Majestic reserved whether hiring a financially irresponsible contractor counts as hiring an incompetent one (Prof. Morris's suggestion). Planning: require the contractor's insurance or a bond.
Licensing wasn't the reserved question.
Majestic decided it was inherently dangerous.
Immunity wasn't the reserved issue.
topic: Wk 4 · Torts of independent contractors — Financial responsibility

q: Wen hires her neighbor Ty, a contractor, as her agent to buy lumber for her new deck. Separately, at a yard sale unrelated to the deck, Ty buys Wen's old snowblower for $50 without mentioning that it's a collectible model worth $600. Wen sues Ty for breach of fiduciary duty over the snowblower. What is Ty's best argument?
o: Ty's duties covered only matters connected with the agency, and this wasn't one.
Agents never owe fiduciary duties to principals who don't pay them.
Fiduciary duties exist only if the agency agreement expressly creates them.
Neighbors can't be in a fiduciary relationship with each other.
oe: Correct. R2d § 13: an agent is a fiduciary with respect to matters within the scope of his agency; R3d § 8.01: in all matters connected with the agency relationship. A fiduciary relation arises where confidence is reposed and accepted (Wolf v. Superior Court); the snowblower deal was at arm's length.
Gratuitous agents are still fiduciaries; compensation isn't required.
Fiduciary duties arise from the agency relationship itself; the agreement shapes their extent (R2d § 376).
Any agency relationship carries fiduciary duties within its scope.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Scope of the fiduciary relation

q: A uniformed customs inspector is paid $30,000 by a smuggler to ride along in his trucks so that police won't stop them. The government, which suffered no loss and couldn't have earned such a fee itself, seizes the money. The inspector sues to get it back. Under Reading v. Regem, who keeps the money?
o: The government: the uniform and position, not mere opportunity, earned the money.
The inspector: the government suffered no damage, so it has no claim at all.
The inspector: the government couldn't lawfully have earned such a fee itself.
The smuggler: the payment was illegal, so it must be returned to him.
oe: Correct. Reading: when the servant's position, rather than merely the opportunity, produces the money, he is accountable to his master. “It matters not that the master has not lost any profit nor suffered any damage, nor … that the master could not have done the act himself.” The theory is restitution of unjust enrichment.
Disgorgement doesn't require loss.
Reading says that doesn't matter.
The law doesn't return money to the briber; the question is between master and servant.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Profit from position

q: Variation: While stationed abroad, the inspector spends his off-duty evenings buying and reselling rugs at a profit, using nothing of the government's and no aspect of his position. Must he hand over the rug profits?
o: No: his service merely gave him the opportunity.
Yes: all profits made while employed belong to the employer.
Yes, because he was in uniform during the working day.
No, because he made the profits outside his home country.
oe: Correct. Reading distinguished cases where the service only provides the opportunity (gambling on the master's time, trading while stationed abroad) from those where the position is the real cause.
Only profits caused by the position or the principal's assets.
The uniform wasn't used to produce the rug profits.
Location isn't the test.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Opportunity only
pre: A uniformed customs inspector is paid $30,000 by a smuggler to ride along in his trucks so that police won't stop them. The government, which suffered no loss and couldn't have earned such a fee itself, seizes the money. The inspector sues to get it back. Under Reading v. Regem, who keeps the money?

q: Gus, general manager of a small machine shop, is paid a salary plus 3% of gross sales and has agreed to devote his full time to the shop. When he gets orders he thinks the shop can't fill profitably, he secretly sends them to other shops, charges the customers more, and keeps the difference. He argues the shop lost nothing because it couldn't have done the work. Must Gus account for the profits?
o: Yes: the decision belonged to the shop, so he had to disclose and account.
No: if the shop couldn't fill the orders, the business wasn't the shop's.
No, because his title was “manager” and not “consultant.”
Yes, but only the profits from orders the shop could have filled itself.
oe: Correct. General Automotive v. Singer: as an agent with broad powers, Singer owed utmost loyalty and had to account for secret profits. The decision belonged to the principal, not to the agent's own judgment.
The shop could have sub-jobbed them and kept the profit; the agent can't make that call alone.
Titles don't decide whether he competed; the nature of the business does.
All the secret profits had to be disclosed and accounted for (less agreed credits).
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Diverted business

q: The casebook describes General Automotive's default rule as a “penalty” or information-forcing default. What does that mean?
o: A harsh default pushes agents to disclose side business and bargain in advance.
The rule punishes principals who fail to monitor their agents.
The rule imposes criminal penalties on disloyal agents.
The rule applies only when the agent's contract has a penalty clause.
oe: Correct. A harsh default gives the party with information (the agent) an incentive to reveal it and negotiate, rather than guessing what the parties would have wanted.
It puts the burden on the agent.
It's a civil default.
It's a default that applies regardless.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Default rule as information-forcing

q: Lyle runs the regional division of a construction firm, hires staff, solicits and accepts subcontractor bids, and sets rates. He secretly owns a scaffolding company that wins over $1 million in subcontracts from his division. The firm's president once said he “didn't mind” employees having side businesses. Lyle's employment contract expired years ago, but he stayed on. Did Lyle breach his fiduciary duty?
o: Yes, as a matter of law: he never disclosed his interest.
No: the president's remark was consent to all side businesses.
No: his employment contract had lapsed, so he owed no duties.
No, because scaffolding wasn't within his area of responsibility.
oe: Correct. Rash v. J.V. Intermediate: agents must not act as or for an adverse party without consent and must deal openly, fully disclosing matters affecting the business. A general remark about side businesses isn't disclosure of this one. “This would be a different case altogether if Rash simply notified” the company.
Consent requires disclosure of the specific conflict (R3d § 8.06).
His fiduciary duties as an agent didn't depend on the expired contract.
He solicited and accepted the bids, so it was.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Undisclosed conflict

q: Why might a principal prefer suing a disloyal agent for breach of fiduciary duty rather than breach of contract?
o: Fiduciary duties are open-ended, need no proof of loss, and allow tort remedies.
Contract claims never allow money damages against a disloyal agent.
Fiduciary claims don't require any particular relationship between the parties.
Courts can't hear breach-of-contract claims brought against agents.
oe: Correct. The Rash slides: it may be easier to establish a fiduciary breach (no need to prove specific terms; Reading allows disgorgement without loss) and remedies may be greater.
Contract claims allow damages, but often less than fiduciary remedies.
They require a fiduciary relationship.
They can.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Fiduciary vs. contract claim

q: Variation: Suppose Lyle had fully disclosed his ownership of the scaffolding company, the firm let him keep bidding, and his contract (still in force) required him to devote his “full work time and efforts” to the firm. Which claim survives best?
o: A contract claim for failing to devote full time.
A fiduciary claim, because disclosure never cures self-dealing.
No claim of any kind survives full disclosure.
A claim for punitive damages for fraud.
oe: Correct. That's the slides' hypothetical: disclosure and consent cure the loyalty problem, but a best-efforts or exclusivity clause is a separate promise.
Disclosure plus consent is the cure (R3d § 8.06).
The contract claim may remain.
Full disclosure defeats fraud.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Disclosure and contract
pre: Why might a principal prefer suing a disloyal agent for breach of fiduciary duty rather than breach of contract?

q: A friend agrees, for free, to deposit Ana's paycheck while running errands, and a professional bookkeeper is paid to manage her accounts. Both lose money through carelessness. Which statement about their duty of care is most accurate?
o: The paid bookkeeper meets a professional standard; the friend a lesser one.
Neither owes any duty of care, because neither one guaranteed results.
Only the bookkeeper owes a duty of care; gratuitous agents owe none at all.
Both owe the identical professional standard of care to Ana.
oe: Correct. R2d § 379; R3d § 8.08: a sliding scale by skill and compensation; claiming special skill raises the standard. Compensation isn't required for a duty of care, but it can change the level expected.
Agents owe reasonable care.
Gratuitous agents owe care too, or must give notice they won't perform (R2d § 378).
The standard varies with skill and compensation.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Duty of care

q: Investor Bo tells his agent, “Sell my shares in Delta Corp. only if the price exceeds $50.” The price reaches $48 and the agent, sure it will fall, sells. The price climbs to $70. Which duty did the agent breach?
o: Obedience: he disregarded a reasonable instruction.
Accounting, because he sold the shares without permission.
None, as long as he acted in good faith.
Loyalty, because he profited personally from the sale.
oe: Correct. R2d § 385; R3d § 8.09. Breach makes the agent liable for the principal's resulting losses.
The accounting duty concerns keeping and rendering accounts and not commingling.
Good faith doesn't excuse disobeying a reasonable instruction.
Nothing suggests he profited; the breach is disobedience.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Duty of obedience

q: A property manager deposits tenants' rent checks for several owners into her personal checking account and pays each owner monthly from it. No money is lost. Has she breached a duty?
o: Yes: putting the owners' money in her own account breaches a duty.
No: without any loss to the owners there can be no breach of duty.
Only the duty of care, and only if she was negligent in some way.
No, as long as she keeps an accurate spreadsheet of who owns what.
oe: Correct. R2d §§ 382, 398: keep and render accounts; don't make the principal's things appear to be your own or mingle them.
Commingling is itself a breach.
The specific duty is accounting.
Records don't cure commingling.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Duty of accounting

q: An agent hired to buy land for her principal owns a suitable parcel herself. Under R3d § 8.06, what must she do to sell it to the principal without breaching the duty of loyalty?
o: Get the principal's informed consent after full disclosure and fair dealing.
Nothing, so long as the price she charges is fair market value.
Resign as agent first, and then sell the parcel to the principal.
Have a friend hold title temporarily so the principal doesn't see her name.
oe: Correct. Consent cures if the agent acts in good faith, discloses all material facts she knows or should know would affect the principal's judgment, deals fairly, and the consent concerns a specific act or a type expected in the ordinary course.
Fair price alone doesn't cure an undisclosed conflict.
Resigning to dodge disclosure doesn't solve the problem; disclosure and consent do.
Hiding ownership makes it worse.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Consent cures

q: Which remedy is NOT among those listed for a principal against a disloyal agent?
o: An order forcing the agent to keep working for the rest of the term.
Disgorgement of secret profits the agent made through the agency.
Imposition of a constructive trust on property the agent wrongly acquired.
Withholding the agent's compensation for an intentional breach of fiduciary duty.
oe: Correct. That isn't on the list, and courts generally won't compel personal service anyway. The listed remedies include contract and tort actions, disgorgement of secret profits, an accounting, a constructive trust, withholding compensation for intentional breaches, injunctions, and punitive damages (R2d § 399).
Listed.
Listed.
Listed.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Remedies

q: Agent Kaya, acting within her actual authority, pays a $2,000 shipping charge from her own funds to secure her principal's goods. What duty does the principal owe her?
o: A contractual duty to reimburse or indemnify her.
A fiduciary duty of loyalty owed to Kaya.
None: agents must bear their own expenses.
Only a moral duty, which no court will enforce.
oe: Correct. The principal's duties are contractual, not fiduciary: compensation if contemplated, reimbursement, indemnity, cooperation, non-interference, and good faith (R3d §§ 8.14–8.15).
Principals owe contractual duties, not fiduciary ones.
Indemnity covers payments within authority unless otherwise agreed.
The duty is enforceable.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Principal's duties

q: A buyer's agent learns that the seller's property is about to be rezoned in a way that will cut its value in half. Must the agent tell her principal, the buyer?
o: Yes: she must disclose facts the principal would want to know.
No: agents disclose only what the principal specifically asks for.
No, because the information came from a third party.
Only if disclosure would benefit the agent in some way.
oe: Correct. R3d § 8.11; R2d § 381.
The duty doesn't depend on a request.
The source doesn't matter.
The duty runs for the principal's benefit.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Duty of disclosure

q: A decorated war hero, after his discharge, is paid by a restaurant to appear at its grand opening. Using the Reading analysis, which argument most strongly supports letting him keep the fee?
o: He's out of service, and the fee rests on his personal fame.
Fiduciary duties never apply to military service.
Restaurants can't be parties to fiduciary-duty claims.
The government suffered no loss from his appearance.
oe: Correct. The book's Reading hypos (discharged soldier in uniform, war hero, memoirs, a CEO's book, celebrity royalties) test where profiting from position ends. R3d § 8.02 bars material benefits obtained through use of the agent's position while an agent.
Reading itself applied them to a soldier.
The issue is the agent's duty, not the restaurant's status.
Loss isn't required for disgorgement.
topic: Wk 5 · Agents' fiduciary duties — Where use of position ends

q: Selma, president of a legal publisher, secretly agrees to run a new division for a competitor. While still president she offers key editors jobs at the competitor, assures her parent company that no raid is likely, suggests delaying editors' raises so they'll be easier to lure, and brings a list of editors' names and salaries to a secret meeting where she and the competitor pick whom to recruit. Then she and 16 others resign. Did Selma breach her fiduciary duty?
o: Yes: she used her position to help a competitor raid staff.
No: officers may plan their departure and recruit colleagues freely until they resign.
No: salary information isn't confidential, so sharing it can't be wrongful.
Yes, but only because she didn't disclose her plans; disclosure would have cured everything.
oe: Correct. Bancroft-Whitney v. Glen: mere preparation isn't a breach, but the nature of the preparations matters. Misleading the parent, the delayed-raise suggestion, and giving a competitor a selective list of employees with salaries (a breach even if salaries aren't confidential) together breached the duty as a matter of law. The competitor was liable too for knowingly cooperating.
Officers may plan, but not use their position to strip the principal's staff for a competitor.
The court held it a breach even if salaries weren't confidential.
Disclosure doesn't immunize otherwise wrongful conduct.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Preparing vs. raiding

q: Before resigning from an accounting firm where she is an at-will employee, Neve leases office space, forms an LLC, and lines up a bank loan for her own firm, all on her own time and without using firm information or contacting clients or coworkers. Has she breached the duty of loyalty?
o: No: preparing to compete, without more, is allowed.
Yes: any preparation to compete while still employed is disloyal.
Yes, because she didn't tell the firm about her plans.
No, but only because she was at-will rather than on a fixed term.
oe: Correct. R3d § 8.04: no competing during the agency, but preparing to compete (lease, entity, financing) is allowed if not otherwise wrongful.
Preparation is allowed; actual competition and misuse of position aren't.
Nondisclosure of preparations is a breach only when particular circumstances make it harmful (Bancroft-Whitney).
At-will status doesn't change the preparation rule.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Permissible preparation

q: A house-cleaning service built its list of about 240 customers through costly cold-calling and custom pricing. After leaving, three former employees start a competing service and solicit only the old company's customers, using their knowledge of the list. What can the old company get?
o: An injunction against soliciting its customers, plus damages, but no ban on competing.
Nothing: former employees may compete with the company and solicit anyone they like.
An injunction shutting down the former employees' new business entirely.
Damages only for the period while the employees were still employed there.
oe: Correct. Town & Country v. Newbery: the customer list was the only trade secret; former employees may not solicit customers whose patronage was secured by years of effort and who aren't openly ascertainable. Forming a competing business on their own time wasn't itself actionable.
Not by exploiting a confidential, effort-built list.
Competition itself is allowed.
The remedy covered post-employment solicitation from the list.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Confidential customer list

q: An insurance agent leaves after his non-compete expires and solicits his former clients, using what he learned from the agency's client and policy-expiration lists. The lists sat in unlocked cabinets open to about 75 employees, and insurance buyers commonly shop around and use multiple agents. Under Corroon & Black v. Hosch, does the agency have recourse?
o: No: the lists weren't trade secrets, so he may solicit his old clients.
Yes: any customer list compiled by a business is a trade secret.
Yes: Town & Country protects every service business's customer list.
Yes, because the non-compete's expiration doesn't end an agent's duties.
oe: Correct. Applying the six Restatement of Torts § 757 factors (each of which must favor secrecy), the information was widely accessible, the money was spent developing the market rather than the list, and insurance customers are “nonroute” customers. “The law affords no recourse.”
Corroon held these lists weren't.
Town & Country involved a costly, confidential route-type list; Corroon distinguished it.
After termination, the agent may compete absent misuse of trade secrets.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Insurance client lists

q: Which is NOT one of the six Restatement of Torts § 757 comment b factors that Corroon used to decide whether information is a trade secret?
o: Whether the departing employee was paid a bonus.
The measures taken to guard the information's secrecy.
How easily others could properly acquire or duplicate it.
The effort or money spent developing the information.
oe: Correct. The factors: (1) extent known outside the business; (2) extent known by employees; (3) measures taken to guard secrecy; (4) value to the business and competitors; (5) effort or money spent developing it; (6) ease of proper acquisition or duplication.
A listed factor.
A listed factor.
A listed factor.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Six-factor test

q: A salesperson leaves her employer and, without taking any documents, contacts customers whose names she remembers. Under the Second and Third Restatements, which statement is accurate?
o: R2d § 396 allows remembered names; the R3d treats a memorized list as a breach.
Both Restatements forbid contacting any former customer at all.
Both Restatements permit using copied written lists after termination.
Neither Restatement addresses an agent's conduct after termination.
oe: Correct. The two Restatements diverge on memorized lists; both forbid using written lists and trade secrets.
After termination an agent may compete and solicit.
Neither does.
R2d § 396 and R3d § 8.05 address it directly.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Memory rule

q: After losing Corroon & Black, an insurance agency asks how to protect itself next time. What does the casebook suggest?
o: Use non-competes, confidentiality agreements, and real secrecy measures.
Rely on fiduciary duties, which last forever after termination.
Sue every departing agent for unfair competition.
Post the client list on the company website so ownership is clear.
oe: Correct. The book's planning note. The Uniform Trade Secrets Act also requires reasonable efforts to maintain secrecy.
Most fiduciary duties end at termination, apart from misuse of confidential information.
Without a protectable secret or covenant, there's no recourse.
That destroys any secrecy.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Planning after Corroon

q: Why did the Corroon court treat insurance customers differently from the cleaning-service customers in Town & Country?
o: Insurance buyers shop around and use several agents, unlike route customers.
Insurance is federally regulated, which preempts state trade-secret law.
The cleaning service had a non-compete and the insurance agency didn't.
Insurance agents, unlike cleaners, aren't fiduciaries of their employers.
oe: Correct. Route customers (milk delivery, cleaning, arguably professional services) stay with a provider; nonroute customers don't, so the list matters less.
No preemption was involved.
The insurance agency had one; it had expired.
They are agents; the issue was the list's status.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Route vs. non-route

q: In Bancroft-Whitney, why was the competitor (Matthew Bender) liable along with Glen?
o: It knowingly cooperated in Glen's breach.
Any company that hires a competitor's employees is automatically liable.
Bender had signed a non-compete agreement with Bancroft-Whitney.
As a competitor, Bender owed Bancroft-Whitney fiduciary duties.
oe: Correct. A third party who knowingly aids a fiduciary's breach can be liable. Bender's own letter referred to “a Fifth Columnist.”
Hiring alone isn't wrongful.
No such covenant was involved.
Competitors don't owe each other fiduciary duties.
topic: Wk 5 · Grabbing & leaving — Third-party liability

q: Four friends want to open a brewery. They want everyone to share equally in management, want no one personally liable for the business's debts, and are willing to file papers with the state. Which form on the course's chart fits best?
o: An LLC or an LLP.
A general partnership, because it requires no filing with the state.
A limited partnership, because limited partners have no personal liability.
A sole proprietorship owned by one friend on behalf of all four.
oe: Correct. On the chart, a general partnership needs no state action but has no limited liability; an LLP files a certificate, has one class, and gives limited liability with equal control; an LLC files articles, has one class (members), limited liability, and control by members or managers. LPs and LLLPs give control only to general partners.
General partners are personally liable.
Limited partners formally have no control, and someone must be a general partner with full liability.
A sole proprietor is personally liable and has sole control.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Entity chart

q: Rafa runs a food truck alone under the name “Rafa's Tacos,” with no filings other than a trade-name registration. A supplier sues for an unpaid $8,000 bill. Which statement is correct?
o: Rafa is personally liable for the debt.
Only the truck can be reached, because the business has its own registered name.
The supplier must first sue “Rafa's Tacos” as a separate entity.
Rafa is liable only if he signed a personal guarantee.
oe: Correct. A sole proprietorship is the default for one person: complete control, but business assets and liabilities aren't separate from personal ones. A trade name doesn't change that, and raising money is hard because there's no stock to sell.
A trade name isn't a separate entity.
There's no separate entity.
No guarantee is needed for a sole proprietor.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Sole proprietorship

q: Which consideration is NOT on the course's list of entity selection factors?
o: The number of trademarks the business will own.
Tax treatment.
The right to exit the business and cash out reasonably promptly.
Which fiduciary obligations might apply.
oe: Correct. The factors are: formation complexity; the right to manage; ability to raise money; paperwork and filing; avoidance of personal liability; tax treatment; the right to exit and cash out promptly; and the fiduciary obligations one may face.
A listed factor.
A listed factor.
A listed factor.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Selection factors

q: Under the original UPA (1914), a partnership couldn't hold title to real estate in its own name in some states and partners had trouble suing in the firm's name. What theory caused these problems, and how did RUPA respond?
o: The UPA's aggregate theory; RUPA § 201 makes the partnership an entity.
The UPA's entity theory; RUPA responded by adopting the aggregate theory.
Both acts use the aggregate theory; only corporations are entities.
The problems came from tax law, which RUPA changed by taxing partnerships.
oe: Correct. RUPA treats the partnership as an entity for nearly all purposes: it can sue and be sued (§ 307(a)), own and convey property (§§ 203, 302), and keep its own books (§ 408). Joint and several liability (§ 306(a)) and pass-through taxation are the aggregate residue.
Reversed.
RUPA § 201 says otherwise.
Partnerships still don't pay income tax; the change was to entity status.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Aggregate vs. entity

q: A supplier wins a $90,000 judgment against Birch & Pine, a RUPA general partnership with $40,000 in assets. Can the supplier immediately levy on partner Birch's personal bank account?
o: Generally no: it must first exhaust the partnership's assets.
Yes: partners are jointly and severally liable, so the creditor may take from any partner at once.
No: general partners are never personally liable for partnership debts.
Yes, but only for Birch's pro rata share of the judgment.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 307(c)–(d): the creditor needs a judgment against the partner too, and must generally exhaust partnership assets unless the partnership is in bankruptcy, the partner agreed, a court permits, or the partner is independently liable.
Joint and several liability is subject to the § 307 exhaustion rule.
General partners are personally liable (§ 306(a)), just not first.
Joint and several liability isn't limited to a pro rata share.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Exhaustion rule

q: Which statement about LLCs matches the course slides?
o: LLCs aren't corporations; they pair limited liability with pass-through tax.
LLCs are a kind of corporation governed by the corporation statutes.
LLC members are personally liable unless they also file an LLP statement.
LLCs must be managed by an elected board of directors.
oe: Correct. The C6 slide: the most widely used form combining limited liability and preferential tax treatment; operators mix and match features; the operating agreement informs the agency relationship; piercing the veil is one exception to limited liability.
LLCs have their own statutes (e.g., RULLCA).
LLC members have limited liability by default.
They're member-managed or manager-managed.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — LLCs vs. corporations

q: In a corporation, who are the corporation's agents owing fiduciary duties of care and loyalty, according to the course slides?
o: Its directors and officers.
Its shareholders, who elect the board.
Its creditors, who lend it money.
Only its outside lawyers and accountants.
oe: Correct. Shareholders elect directors, who hire officers responsible for day-to-day operations; D&O are agents of the corporation and owe it care and loyalty.
Shareholders own shares; they aren't the corporation's agents as such.
Creditors aren't agents.
Lawyers may be agents, but the slide refers to directors and officers.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Corporations' agents

q: Which item appears on the course's list of DISADVANTAGES of general partnerships?
o: Lack of indefinite life.
A single layer of taxation.
Simplicity.
Cost sharing.
oe: Correct. Disadvantages: lack of indefinite life, unlimited liability, potential for conflict, and expansion, succession and termination issues. Advantages: simplicity, a single layer of tax, more resources than a sole proprietorship, cost sharing, and a broader skill base.
That's an advantage.
That's an advantage.
That's an advantage.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Partnership pros and cons

q: Which statement about how agency law applies to general partners is correct?
o: Each partner is an agent and a fiduciary, and all are personally liable.
Partners are agents only if the partnership agreement appoints them as such.
Partners owe fiduciary duties only to the firm's outside creditors.
Partners are liable only for their own acts, never for their co-partners' acts.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 301(1) (agents), § 305(a) (vicarious tort liability), § 409 (fiduciaries), and § 306(a) (personal liability). Partners can be liable for fellow partners' and non-partner agents' acts.
Agency is a default incident of being a partner.
They owe duties to the partnership and the other partners.
They are jointly and severally liable for partnership obligations.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Partners as agents

q: A landlord leases space to a bakery for rent equal to 8% of the bakery's gross sales. The bakery fails, owing suppliers. Are the suppliers likely to hold the landlord liable as a partner?
o: No: rent measured by sales doesn't make the landlord a partner.
Yes: any payment tied to the business's performance makes the recipient a partner.
Yes, because the landlord owns the building that the business uses.
No, because landlords are immune from tenants' business debts by statute.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 202(c)(2)–(3)(C): sharing gross returns doesn't establish a partnership, and profits received as rent raise no presumption. The course stresses distinguishing partners from employees, lenders, franchisees, and landlords.
The statute lists exceptions.
Co-ownership of property alone doesn't establish a partnership, and here only the landlord owns it.
There's no immunity; the point is that the landlord isn't a co-owner of the business.
topic: Wk 6 · Entities & partnership basics — Distinguishing relationships

q: Salon owner Odette's receptionist, Bree, asks for a raise. A lawyer drafts a “partnership agreement”: Bree contributes no capital, keeps her $600/week wage plus 20% of net profits “if the business warrants,” has no say in management, isn't liable for debts, and can end things on 10 days' notice; Odette contributes everything and controls everything. They file a partnership tax return. The state says Bree is still an employee for unemployment-tax purposes. Who is right?
o: The state: in substance Bree's profit share is wages.
Odette: the written agreement and tax return conclusively establish a partnership.
Odette: sharing in net profits automatically makes someone a partner.
The state, but only because Bree's share was 20% rather than 50%.
oe: Correct. Fenwick: profit sharing is evidence but not conclusive (wages are an exception), and every other factor (intent, losses, capital, control, language, dissolution rights) pointed to employment. The burden is on the one alleging partnership.
The commission could challenge the label; substance controls.
Profit sharing only raises a presumption, rebutted when it's paid as wages.
The percentage wasn't decisive.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Label vs. substance

q: Two men with no lawyer and no writing buy wrecked cars to rebuild and sell. One, who can't read, borrows $10,000 against his own house to fund car purchases; they split the profits equally, even on cars the other bought and sold alone. The literate one keeps the books and treats the other as an employee, withholding taxes. Is there a partnership?
o: Yes: his capital and equal share of all profits point to co-ownership.
No: the payroll records show the parties understood an employment relationship.
No: a partnership requires a written agreement between the parties.
Yes, but only because the borrowed money was secured by his house.
oe: Correct. Zajac v. Harris: profit sharing is prima facie evidence unless paid as wages; Harris put in substantial capital, got half the profits even on deals Zajac did alone (inconsistent with a commission), and his illiteracy explained the payroll paperwork.
Unilateral bookkeeping by one party doesn't control, especially when the other can't read it.
No formalities are required (§ 202(a)).
The security wasn't decisive; the contribution and profit split were.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Capital and profits

q: Maria funds a catering company with $50,000; John runs operations. They agree profits split 70/30, John gets a fixed $1,500 a week, Maria has final say on decisions, everything is in Maria's name, and John won't be liable for debts, though they've talked loosely about “sharing the risk.” Is John likely a partner?
o: Likely not: the stipend and lack of control or liability point to employment.
Certainly yes: any profit share makes someone a partner, whatever else is agreed.
Certainly not: loose talk about sharing risk is legally irrelevant.
Yes, because John's 30% share of profits is more than nominal.
oe: Correct. The book's Gourmet Bites problem: profit share raises the presumption, but the fixed pay, Maria's control and ownership, and John's exemption from liability likely make him an employee, as in Fenwick.
It's a rebuttable presumption.
Loss sharing is a relevant factor; it just doesn't outweigh the rest here.
Size of share isn't decisive.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Funder and operator

q: A medical practice organized as a professional corporation has 13 regular employees plus four physician-shareholders who also serve as directors, share profits, and control the practice. A fired bookkeeper sues under the ADA, which covers employers with 15 or more employees. How should the court decide whether the physicians are “employees”?
o: Apply the common-law control test, weighing factors such as hiring, supervision, and profit sharing.
Count them as employees, because they have employment agreements with the corporation.
Count them as non-employees, because shareholders of a corporation are never its employees.
Ask whether they would be partners if the practice were organized as a partnership.
oe: Correct. Clackamas v. Wells: when Congress doesn't define “employee,” it means the common-law master–servant relationship. Asking whether the physicians are “partners” begs the question; titles and employment agreements aren't dispositive. The findings suggested they weren't employees.
An employment agreement isn't dispositive.
The answer depends on control, not shareholder status.
The Court said that question begs the question.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Federal statute's “employee”

q: A law firm calls some lawyers “income partners.” They receive a fixed salary set by the executive committee plus a discretionary bonus, don't share in net profits or losses, make a $10,000 capital contribution returned without adjustment, and can't vote. A malpractice plaintiff sues them as partners. Are they personally liable as partners?
o: No: without a share of profits, losses, or control, they aren't partners.
Yes: the firm calls them partners, so they're liable as partners.
Yes, because each made a $10,000 capital contribution to the firm.
No, because malpractice claims can never reach individual lawyers.
oe: Correct. Davis v. Loftus: substance over form. The book asks whether they might still be liable by estoppel if the firm held them out to clients as partners (UPA § 16; RUPA § 308).
The label doesn't control.
A fixed, returnable contribution doesn't make them co-owners.
Lawyers are liable for their own malpractice; the question was vicarious liability as partners.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Income partners

q: A large firm's self-perpetuating executive committee can fire, demote, and set the pay of any partner; ordinary partners have voted on only one matter in 25 years. The firm demotes 32 partners, who have capital at risk and are liable for firm debts. The EEOC investigates age discrimination. Under Judge Posner's opinion in EEOC v. Sidley Austin, could the 32 be “employees”?
o: Possibly: partners without power over their own fate may be employees.
No: anyone who is a partner under state law is an employer for federal purposes.
Yes, as a matter of law, because a committee set their pay.
No, because personal liability for firm debts is conclusive of partner status.
oe: Correct. Posner reasoned that these partners were “defenseless,” and features like profit sharing and capital ownership have analogues among executives. Easterbrook concurred, applying Darden's common-law test, and would have found them bona fide partners.
Posner rejected that equation.
The court remanded for more facts; it didn't decide.
Posner called it the most partner-like feature but not decisive.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Partners as federal employees

q: A 22-partner farming partnership operates on an oral understanding that interests are bought and sold at book value, that membership is at the managing partner's will, and that a departing partner gets book value as of the prior December 31. The manager expels Hale, a 3% partner, and tenders book value. Hale sues for dissolution and liquidation under the UPA. What result under Frank v. R.A. Pickens?
o: Hale was a partner, but the agreement controls: book value, no liquidation.
Hale can force a liquidation, because the UPA gives every partner that right on dissolution.
Hale wasn't a partner at all, because he started as an employee of the firm.
The expulsion is void, because a partnership agreement must be in writing.
oe: Correct. A partnership “is a contractual relationship that may vary … in an almost infinite variety of ways.” UPA rules apply subject to agreement, so partners may give one partner control over admission and expulsion and set a book-value buyout.
That default (§ 38(1)) yields to the agreement.
The court found he was a partner.
Partnership agreements can be oral.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Agreement over defaults

q: Variation: Hale argues that book value is unfair because the farmland has tripled in market value since it was bought. What does the casebook point out?
o: Book value can badly understate a growing business; agree on an appraisal instead.
Courts always substitute fair market value for book value when the two differ.
Book value always includes the appreciation of land the partnership owns.
Book value is an illegal measure for partnership buyouts.
oe: Correct. The book contrasts book value with appraisal for buyouts and notes its weakness for appreciating assets (see also G & S v. Belman).
Courts enforce the agreed formula.
Book value is kept at cost.
It's a common and enforceable measure.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Book value vs. appraisal
pre: A 22-partner farming partnership operates on an oral understanding that interests are bought and sold at book value, that membership is at the managing partner's will, and that a departing partner gets book value as of the prior December 31. The manager expels Hale, a 3% partner, and tenders book value. Hale sues for dissolution and liquidation under the UPA. What result under Frank v. R.A. Pickens?

q: Under RUPA § 202(c)(3), which recipient of a share of profits is presumed to be a partner?
o: A capital contributor who receives 25% of profits, with nothing else explaining it.
A lender whose interest rate equals 10% of the borrower's profits.
An employee paid a year-end bonus of 5% of the firm's profits.
The seller of a business paid installments out of its profits for its goodwill.
oe: Correct. Profit sharing raises a presumption of partnership unless the profits are paid for a debt, services as an independent contractor or wages, rent, an annuity or retirement benefit, interest on a loan (even if it varies with profits), or the sale of goodwill or other property.
Interest on a loan is an exception.
Wages are an exception.
A sale of goodwill is an exception.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Profit-sharing presumption

q: Two neighbors start selling firewood together, split the work and the profits, and buy a log splitter together. Neither has ever thought of themselves as “partners,” and they would be surprised to hear the word. Is there a partnership?
o: Yes, likely: intent to be “partners” isn't required.
No: a partnership requires the parties to intend to be partners.
No: a partnership requires a written agreement and a state filing.
Yes, but only if they file a partnership tax return.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 202(a). No formalities are required, so inadvertent partnerships are common; statements disavowing a partnership don't bind if the parties intend to do the things that constitute one.
The statute says “whether or not the persons intend.”
General partnerships need neither.
Tax filings are evidence, not a requirement.
topic: Wk 6 · Partner or employee? — Unintended partnership

q: A struggling brokerage gets a $3 million loan of securities from three wealthy investors, who refuse to become partners. In return they get 40% of profits (with a floor and cap) until repayment, the right to be consulted and to veto speculative trades, inspection of the books, an assignment of the partners' interests as security, an option to buy half the firm, and undated resignations from each partner held by the firm's manager. A creditor sues the investors as partners. Under Martin v. Peyton, are they partners?
o: No: the controls were protective, and the investors couldn't run or bind the firm.
Yes: receiving 40% of the profits makes them partners as a matter of law.
Yes: the veto rights gave them control over the firm's business.
No, because their agreement declared that they weren't partners.
oe: Correct. Labels and intent to avoid liability aren't conclusive; the question is whether they in fact associated as co-owners. Here the controls were negative and protective. The court warned that at some point stipulations immaterial separately could cover so wide a field that a partnership exists, but not here.
Profits paid as interest on a loan fall within an exception.
Veto rights let them block, not run, the business.
Declarations aren't conclusive; the substance was examined.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Lender or partner

q: Why did the creditor-lender become a principal in Cargill but the lenders in Martin v. Peyton escape partner status?
o: Cargill actually ran the debtor's business; the Martin lenders could only veto.
Cargill was a corporation and the Martin lenders were individuals.
Cargill's loan was much larger than the Martin lenders' loan.
Agency and partnership use identical tests, and the two cases are inconsistent.
oe: Correct. The casebook draws exactly this contrast.
Entity type wasn't the distinction.
Size wasn't the distinction; control was.
They're reconcilable on control.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Contrast with Cargill

q: According to the casebook's notes on Martin v. Peyton, what would most simply have protected the investors from the risk of partner liability?
o: Have the firm incorporate or form an LLC, so investors' liability is limited.
Lend cash instead of securities, so the deal looks like an ordinary loan.
Take a larger share of profits to compensate for the risk.
Sign the partnership agreement as “silent partners.”
