oe: Correct. The book also notes the securities (not cash) were lent to avoid usury limits, and that an insolvent firm has incentives to gamble with others' money.
Cash would have raised usury problems and wouldn't change partner analysis.
A larger share would make them look more like partners.
That would make them partners.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Planning for investors

q: A produce distributor buys a 40% undivided interest in a farmer's potato crop, advances money, and agrees that net proceeds will be divided “between the partners” and losses shared in the same ratio. The farmer goes bankrupt, and the distributor files as a creditor for its advances. Under Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long, how is it treated?
o: As a partner, not a creditor.
As a secured creditor, because it took a crop mortgage and a note.
As a creditor, because a single crop can't be a partnership business.
As a lender, because it advanced money to the farmer.
oe: Correct. A partnership can be formed for a single venture; intent to do the things constituting a partnership controls regardless of labels. Loss sharing and partnership language distinguished it from Martin v. Peyton, which hurt the distributor in bankruptcy.
The mortgage secured only performance and didn't change the profit-and-loss arrangement.
A single venture can support a partnership.
Advances are consistent with partnership capital.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Shared profits and losses

q: Investors deposit $500,000 relying on a fraudulent financial statement that carries an audit letter from an international accounting firm's Bahamas affiliate. The money vanishes. They sue the firm's U.S. affiliate, arguing that its global brochures (“40,000 professionals worldwide”) made the affiliates look like one partnership. They never saw the brochures before investing. What result under Young v. Jones?
o: No liability: the investors never relied on a representation of partnership.
Partnership by estoppel exists, because the affiliates share a famous name.
A partnership in fact exists, because the affiliates cooperate worldwide.
Liability exists, because public representations bind everyone regardless of reliance.
oe: Correct. The statute requires a representation of partnership made or consented to by the defendant and reliance on it, such as giving credit. The plaintiffs hadn't seen or relied on the brochures, which didn't say the affiliates were one partnership.
A shared name without reliance isn't enough.
The plaintiffs conceded no evidence of an actual partnership.
Even public representations require reliance.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Partnership by estoppel

q: Variation: Suppose the investors had read the U.S. affiliate's brochure stating that “all our offices form one partnership that stands behind every audit,” and deposited the money because of it. Under RUPA § 308, what changes?
o: The U.S. affiliate could be liable as a purported partner.
Nothing: partnership by estoppel never applies to professional firms.
The affiliate becomes an actual partner of the Bahamas firm for all purposes.
Only the Bahamas affiliate could be liable, because it signed the letter.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 308(a) requires reliance on the representation in entering a transaction (broader than UPA § 16's “given credit”); a public representation can bind even toward those unknown to the purported partner.
It applies to anyone who represents or consents to being represented as a partner.
Estoppel liability runs only to those who relied.
The U.S. affiliate's own representation creates its exposure.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Actual reliance
pre: Investors deposit $500,000 relying on a fraudulent financial statement that carries an audit letter from an international accounting firm's Bahamas affiliate. The money vanishes. They sue the firm's U.S. affiliate, arguing that its global brochures (“40,000 professionals worldwide”) made the affiliates look like one partnership. They never saw the brochures before investing. What result under Young v. Jones?

q: How does RUPA § 308 broaden partnership-by-estoppel liability compared with UPA § 16?
o: UPA requires that credit was given; RUPA covers anyone who enters a transaction.
RUPA § 308 eliminates the reliance requirement that UPA § 16 imposed.
UPA § 16 is broader, because it also covers tort victims who relied.
They're identical in substance, differing only in section numbers.
oe: Correct. Both make a public representation actionable even if not communicated directly to the plaintiff.
Reliance remains.
The UPA requires credit extended; RUPA's transaction language is broader.
The wording differs in scope.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — UPA vs. RUPA wording

q: Former partner Wes left the firm two years ago. The firm never filed a statement of dissociation, and Wes did nothing to suggest he was still a partner. A creditor argues Wes is liable as a purported partner because no statement was filed. Under RUPA § 308, is he?
o: No: a person isn't a purported partner merely because no statement of dissociation was filed.
Yes: failing to file a statement of dissociation is a representation of continued partnership.
Yes, for any debt incurred while he's still listed anywhere.
No, because liability for former partners ends the day they leave.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 308(c)–(e): not liable merely for being named in a statement of partnership authority or for a failure to file a statement of dissociation. (His exposure for post-dissociation debts is governed instead by § 703's two-year, no-notice rule.)
Section 308 rejects that.
Liability requires a representation he made or consented to.
Section 703 can impose liability for up to two years in limited cases.
topic: Wk 6 · Lenders & partnership by estoppel — Statements and filings

q: Ana contributes $90,000 and works part time; Ben contributes $10,000 and works full time. They form a RUPA partnership with no agreement about profits, losses, or pay. In year one the firm earns $60,000. How is it divided, and is Ben entitled to a salary?
o: $30,000 each, and no salary.
$54,000 to Ana and $6,000 to Ben, in proportion to their capital.
Equal shares, plus a reasonable salary to Ben for his full-time work.
Whatever a court finds fair given their contributions and their work.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 401(a) (the slides' § 401(b)): equal shares of distributions, losses in the same proportion, regardless of contributions or effort; § 401(j): no remuneration except reasonable compensation for winding up.
Capital doesn't set the default profit share.
No compensation for services by default.
The statute supplies a clear default.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Default profit and loss shares

q: Three equal partners each contribute $50,000. In year one the firm earns $330,000, and each partner draws $90,000. What is each partner's capital account at year end?
oe: Correct. $50,000 contribution + $110,000 share of profit − $90,000 draw = $70,000 (the casebook's Meehan note). Profits increase the account, losses and draws decrease it, and it's kept at cost, not market value.
That ignores the profit allocation and the draw.
That ignores the $90,000 draw.
That's only the profit share.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Capital account after draws

q: In addition to his $20,000 capital contribution, partner Cy lends the partnership $15,000 on the understanding it will be repaid in a year. Which statement is correct?
o: It's a loan to be repaid with interest, not part of Cy's capital.
It's added to Cy's capital account and returned only on liquidation.
Cy may withdraw his $20,000 of capital at any time, but not the loan.
It's void, because partners can't be creditors of their own partnership.
oe: Correct. Advances are something other than capital, with payback expectations (RUPA § 401(f)–(g); UPA § 18(c)). At formation, partners should distinguish capital contributions from loans.
An advance isn't a capital contribution.
A partner can't take back capital before withdrawal or liquidation.
Partners can be creditors; RUPA § 806 pays them along with outside creditors.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Advances vs. capital

q: Partner Dara assigns her right to partnership distributions to her brother as a gift. The brother demands to vote on firm decisions and to inspect the books. Which statement is correct under RUPA?
o: The brother gets only distributions; Dara remains a partner.
The brother becomes a partner with full management and information rights.
The transfer dissociates Dara and dissolves the partnership.
The transfer is void without the unanimous consent of the partners.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 503: a transfer is permitted, doesn't by itself cause dissociation or dissolution, and gives the transferee only distributions (plus a right to seek judicial winding up under § 801(5)). A transferable interest is personal property (§ 502).
Admission requires the consent of all partners (§ 402).
Transfer doesn't cause dissociation or dissolution.
Transfers of the economic interest are permitted.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Transferring an interest

q: Variation: Dara assigns all of her transferable interest to her brother, keeping nothing. The other partners want her out. What can they do?
o: Expel her by unanimous vote of the other partners.
Nothing: a transfer never affects a partner's status.
Expel her by a simple majority vote of the partners.
Sue to have the transfer declared void.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 601(4) permits expulsion by the unanimous vote of the others of a partner who has transferred all (the slides say “substantially all”) of her transferable interest, other than for security or under an unforeclosed charging order.
It doesn't automatically, but it's grounds for unanimous expulsion.
The statute requires the unanimous vote of the others.
The transfer is valid.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Transfer of everything
pre: Partner Dara assigns her right to partnership distributions to her brother as a gift. The brother demands to vote on firm decisions and to inspect the books. Which statement is correct under RUPA?

q: Partner Eli's personal creditor wins a $40,000 judgment against him for an unpaid car loan. Can the creditor seize the partnership's delivery truck to satisfy it?
o: No: its remedy is a charging order on Eli's distributions.
Yes: Eli owns a share of every partnership asset, so his creditor can take that share.
Yes, as long as the truck is worth less than the judgment.
No, and the creditor has no remedy at all against Eli's partnership interest.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 504: a charging order is a lien on distributions; the court may foreclose, but the buyer gets only the transferable interest. This is affirmative asset partitioning (entity shielding): the firm's assets are shielded from owners' personal creditors.
A partner isn't a co-owner of partnership property (§ 501).
Value doesn't matter; partnership property isn't reachable for a partner's personal debt.
The charging order is the remedy.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Charging order

q: Which arrangement illustrates defensive asset partitioning?
o: An LLC member's personal house can't be reached by the LLC's creditors.
A general partner's personal creditor can get only a charging order against the partnership.
Partnership creditors have priority over partners' personal creditors in partnership property.
A general partner is personally liable for the firm's debts.
oe: Correct. Defensive partitioning (limited liability) shields owners' personal assets from the firm's creditors; general partnerships lack it, while LLPs, LLCs, corporations and limited partners have it. Affirmative partitioning (entity shielding) shields firm assets from owners' personal creditors.
That's affirmative partitioning (entity shielding).
That's also entity shielding.
That's the absence of defensive partitioning.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Asset partitioning

q: Fay joins an existing RUPA partnership in March. The firm owes a supplier $50,000 for goods delivered in January, and in June it signs a new $30,000 equipment lease. Both debts go unpaid. For which can the creditors reach Fay's personal assets?
o: Only the June lease.
Both, because partners are jointly and severally liable for all partnership obligations.
Neither, because new partners have limited liability for their first year.
Only the January debt, because she wasn't consulted on the lease.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 306(b). (Her capital in the firm is still at risk for the January debt; UPA § 17 likewise made an incoming partner liable for prior debts only out of partnership property.)
Section 306(b) carves out pre-admission debts.
There's no such grace period.
She's liable for obligations incurred while a partner.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — New partner's liability

q: Variation: As part of buying in, Fay expressly agrees with the outgoing partner to assume and pay all existing partnership debts, including the January supplier bill. Now can the supplier reach her personal assets for that bill?
o: Likely yes: she voluntarily assumed the prior debts.
No: the protection of § 306(b) can never be varied by agreement.
No, because only the outgoing partner can enforce her promise.
Yes, but only up to the amount of her capital contribution.
oe: Correct. The default protects incoming partners, but they can assume prior debts by agreement, as the Shoafs did in Putnam v. Shoaf.
Partners can assume obligations by contract.
Whether the supplier can enforce it directly may depend on third-party-beneficiary rules, but her personal undertaking exists.
An assumption isn't capped by capital.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Assumed debts
pre: Fay joins an existing RUPA partnership in March. The firm owes a supplier $50,000 for goods delivered in January, and in June it signs a new $30,000 equipment lease. Both debts go unpaid. For which can the creditors reach Fay's personal assets?

q: How does RUPA's liability rule for partners differ from the original UPA's?
o: UPA: joint and several for torts, joint for debts. RUPA: joint and several for all.
UPA: joint and several for everything. RUPA: joint liability only.
Both acts give partners limited liability unless they personally guarantee debts.
RUPA abolished partners' personal liability for contract debts.
oe: Correct. Under joint liability all obligors must be sued together; under joint and several liability any one can be sued for the whole and then seek contribution.
Reversed.
General partners are personally liable under both.
Section 306(a) keeps it (absent an LLP filing).
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Joint vs. joint and several

q: Partners Cole and Fritz run a trucking business. Cole's aunt sends him $9,000; he uses $5,000 to buy a used trailer, and the seller's invoice and certificate of title list the business name, “C & F Hauling,” as owner. The trailer is used only in the business. Fritz files for bankruptcy, and his trustee claims the trailer. What result under In re Fulton?
o: Partnership property; Fritz's estate gets only his partnership interest.
Cole's separate property, because his family's money paid for it.
Half Fritz's, because partners hold firm assets as tenants in common.
The aunt's property, because she never made a gift of the money.
oe: Correct. Title in the firm's name, purchase for and use in the business, and the partners' intent at acquisition made it partnership property. A partner has no title to partnership property. The money was Cole's capital contribution, and equity in the trailer is distributed in the UPA § 40(b) order.
The source of Cole's funds doesn't control when title and use point to the firm.
Partners don't own specific partnership assets.
The court found a loan to Cole personally.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — What is partnership property

q: In the book problem after Fulton, the trailer (to which Carroll contributed $4,600 in capital) is sold for $4,000. The partnership owes an outside creditor $1,000, and Carroll personally owes his own creditors $2,000. How are the proceeds applied?
o: $1,000 to the firm's creditor, then $3,000 to Carroll as capital.
$2,000 to Carroll's personal creditors first, then $1,000 to the firm's creditor.
$2,000 to each partner equally, with creditors paid from their shares.
All $4,000 to Carroll, because he paid for the trailer.
oe: Correct. Partnership creditors are paid before capital is returned; Carroll recovers $3,000 of his $4,600 capital; his personal creditors reach only what is distributed to him.
Partnership creditors have priority in partnership property.
Creditors and capital come before any profit split.
The partnership creditor is paid first.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Payout after sale

q: Partner Gia buys a laptop with her own money, in her own name, with nothing on the receipt indicating the partnership, and uses it mostly for partnership work. Under RUPA § 204(d), whose property is it presumed to be?
o: Gia's separate property, despite its partnership use.
Partnership property, because it's used mostly for partnership work.
Owned by all the partners as tenants in partnership.
Partnership property if any partner later reimburses Gia.
oe: Correct. Property acquired in a partner's name, without indicating partner capacity or the partnership and without partnership funds, is presumed separate property even if used for the partnership. Property bought with partnership funds is presumed partnership property.
Use alone doesn't overcome the § 204(d) presumption.
That's the UPA concept, and it applied to partnership property, not separate property.
The presumption looks to acquisition.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Separate-property presumption

q: A partner in a money-losing cotton-gin partnership sells “all my interest in the partnership and its assets” to new partners, who assume the debts; she pays cash to get out and is released. Later the firm discovers that its old bookkeeper embezzled funds, and it recovers $70,000 from banks that honored forged checks. She claims her share. Who gets it?
o: The new partners: she conveyed her whole interest, unknown claims included.
She does: no one can sell a claim nobody knew existed.
She does, because the embezzlement happened while she was a partner.
The banks keep it, because she released the partnership from all claims.
oe: Correct. Putnam v. Shoaf: a partner has no ownership interest in specific partnership assets; the partnership owned the claims. She intended to get out completely, and if the gin had failed she wouldn't have wanted the losses.
Selling one's partnership interest passes everything, including unknown claims.
Timing doesn't matter; the claim belonged to the partnership.
The recovery belongs to the partnership.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Partner's interest, not assets

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the UPA and RUPA on a partner's rights in partnership property?
o: UPA: tenant in partnership. RUPA: not a co-owner at all.
Both acts make partners tenants in common of partnership property.
UPA gives partners no rights in partnership property; RUPA makes them co-owners.
Under RUPA a partner may use firm property for personal purposes if he pays rent.
oe: Correct. Under UPA the incidents of tenancy in partnership (possession for partnership purposes only; not assignable alone; not subject to attachment except on partnership claims) made it close to entity treatment anyway. RUPA § 401(i): use or possess partnership property only on behalf of the partnership.
Neither does.
Reversed.
Use is only on behalf of the partnership, absent agreement.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Co-ownership under UPA vs. RUPA

q: Title to a warehouse is in the name of “Lark & Finch, a partnership.” Partner Lark, without authority, signs a deed in the partnership's name selling the warehouse to Buyer, who pays fair value and has no knowledge or notice that Lark lacked authority. Can the partnership recover the warehouse?
o: No: Buyer is a good-faith purchaser for value without notice.
Yes: a conveyance by one partner without the others' consent is always void.
Yes, because transferring real estate always requires every partner's signature.
No, and Lark has no liability to the partnership either.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 302: property titled in the partnership's name is conveyed by an instrument signed by a partner in that name; the partnership can recover only if the transfer didn't bind it under § 301 and the transferee knew or had notice of the lack of authority.
Any partner can sign a conveyance in the partnership's name.
No such rule exists.
Lark may be liable to the partnership for exceeding authority.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Improper conveyance

q: On dissolution of a UPA partnership, assets are $100,000. It owes outside creditors $60,000, owes partner Hal $20,000 for a loan, and partners' capital contributions total $50,000. In what order are claims paid under UPA § 40(b)?
o: Outside creditors, then Hal's loan, then $20,000 toward capital.
Capital contributions first ($50,000), then the creditors.
Hal's loan first, then the outside creditors, then capital.
All claims share pro rata in the $100,000.
oe: Correct. UPA § 40(b): (I) creditors other than partners; (II) partners other than for capital and profits (loans); (III) partners for capital; (IV) partners for profits. RUPA § 806 combines (I) and (II), paying partner-creditors along with outside creditors.
Creditors come first.
Under UPA, outside creditors rank ahead of partner loans.
There's a strict order.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — UPA liquidation order

q: Three partners in a RUPA partnership disagree: two want to admit Iris, one objects. The agreement says nothing about admission. Can Iris become a partner?
o: Not without all three partners' consent.
Yes, by majority vote, because admitting a partner is an ordinary matter.
Yes, if she makes a capital contribution to the firm.
Yes, if she buys one of the partners' transferable interests.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 402(b)(3); UPA § 18(g): no one becomes a member without the consent of all partners (“pick your partners”).
Admission requires unanimity by default.
Contribution doesn't override the consent requirement; she can even become a partner without contributing (§ 402(c)).
A transferee isn't a partner.
topic: Wk 7 · Partners' interests & property — Admission of new partners

q: Rosa and Tom are equal partners in a corner store with no agreement limiting either's authority. Months ago Rosa told the store's milk supplier that she personally wouldn't be responsible for any more milk. Tom keeps ordering milk, which the store sells. The supplier sues the partnership and Rosa for the unpaid $900. What result?
o: Both are bound: Rosa alone couldn't restrict Tom's ordinary-course authority.
Only Tom is liable, because the supplier knew Rosa objected to more orders.
No one is liable, because the partners were deadlocked on the purchases.
The partnership is liable, but Rosa isn't personally, because she gave notice.
oe: Correct. National Biscuit v. Stroud: each partner is an agent with equal management rights; ordinary differences are decided by a majority, and “Stroud was not, and could not be, a majority of the partners.” With an even split, no restriction can be placed on the power to act. The firm also got the benefit of the goods.
The supplier knew of Rosa's objection, but she lacked the power to limit Tom's authority alone.
Deadlock doesn't strip a partner of authority over ordinary matters as against third parties.
Partners are personally liable for partnership obligations.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Two partners, one objection

q: Two equal partners run a landscaping business. Partner Ken wants to hire a third worker; partner Lou refuses and keeps objecting. Ken hires the worker anyway and pays him $12,000 from his own pocket, then asks the partnership to reimburse him. What result under Summers v. Dooley?
o: No reimbursement: a majority never consented.
Reimbursement, because hiring is an ordinary matter either partner can decide.
Reimbursement, because Lou accepted profits the extra worker helped produce.
Half reimbursement, as a compromise between equal partners.
oe: Correct. Summers: equal management rights mean that between the partners, Ken couldn't impose the expense over Lou's continuing objection. Lou's keeping his share of the profits didn't estop him or ratify the hire.
Between the partners, ordinary matters are decided by a majority, and one of two isn't a majority.
The court rejected that argument.
There's no splitting rule.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Internal reimbursement

q: How does the course reconcile National Biscuit v. Stroud and Summers v. Dooley?
o: National Biscuit governs third-party claims; Summers governs disputes between partners.
The cases are irreconcilable, and Summers effectively overruled National Biscuit.
Both cases hold that one of two partners can never act without the other's consent.
National Biscuit applies to small purchases and Summers applies to large expenses.
oe: Correct. The slides' reconciliation, citing Covalt v. High: if partners are evenly divided, the power to act is suspended internally while the division continues, but the rule differs for transactions with third parties.
They're reconcilable and from different states.
National Biscuit held Freeman's act binding.
The distinction is third parties vs. internal disputes, not amount.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Reconciling the cases

q: Alison, Bill, and Charles are equal partners in a grocery. Charles's son Don works there and performs poorly. Alison and Bill vote to fire Don; Charles objects and tells Don to keep coming in. Who decides?
o: Alison and Bill, as the majority.
Charles, because the employee is his son.
No one, because personnel decisions require unanimity.
A court, because any disagreement among partners needs judicial resolution.
oe: Correct. The casebook's grocery problem. They should notify Don and act through the majority.
Family ties don't change the voting rule.
Ordinary-course decisions require only a majority.
The statute supplies the majority rule.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Majority of three

q: In a five-partner RUPA firm with no agreement on voting, three partners vote to (1) buy a new delivery van and (2) amend the partnership agreement to add a mandatory retirement age. Which decisions are valid?
o: Only the van purchase.
Both, because three of five partners is a majority.
Neither, because every partnership decision requires unanimity.
Only the amendment, because it's a policy decision rather than an ordinary one.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 401(k): ordinary course → majority; outside the ordinary course or an amendment → unanimous. (UPA § 18(h) similarly bars acts in contravention of any agreement without all partners' consent.)
Amendments require unanimity.
Ordinary matters need only a majority.
Reversed.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Ordinary vs. extraordinary

q: Partner Ivy has contributed 80% of the capital of a three-partner firm; the other two contributed 10% each. They disagree on an ordinary business matter, with Ivy outvoted 2–1. Does Ivy's larger contribution give her the deciding vote?
o: No: each partner has one vote.
Yes: votes are weighted by capital contributions by default.
Yes, because the decision affects her capital most.
No, because ordinary matters require unanimity.
oe: Correct. Equality of interest: RUPA § 401(h); UPA § 18(e). Majority means more than half by head count (Frank v. Pickens note).
Not by default.
No such rule exists.
They require a majority.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Majority by head count

q: Under UPA § 9(3), which act can a majority of partners NOT take, absent authorization by all partners?
o: Submitting a partnership claim to arbitration.
Buying the ordinary inventory the business sells.
Hiring a cashier at the going wage.
Paying the monthly electric bill.
oe: Correct. UPA § 9(3): less than all partners lack authority to assign property in trust for creditors, dispose of goodwill, do an act making it impossible to carry on the ordinary business, confess a judgment, or submit a claim to arbitration.
An ordinary-course act.
An ordinary-course act.
An ordinary-course act.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Acts requiring all partners

q: A limited partnership's agreement bars its general partner from borrowing above an approved budget without the limited partners' written consent. The general partner signs a $1 million construction loan, far above budget. The bank never saw the agreement, and no one told it of the limit. The LP defaults and argues the bank should have investigated the GP's authority. What result under RNR Investments?
o: The LP is bound: the bank lacked knowledge or notice of the limit.
The LP isn't bound, because banks must read partnership agreements before lending.
The LP isn't bound, because the loan exceeded the approved budget.
The LP is bound, but only for the budgeted amount of the loan.
oe: Correct. RNR's two steps: (1) was the GP apparently carrying on business in the usual way? (2) did the third party know or have notice of the restriction? Third parties have no duty to inquire “even if they have some reason to question it.” The LP could have filed a statement of authority or notified the bank.
RNR rejected that duty.
An internal limit doesn't bind a third party without knowledge or notice.
Apparent authority bound it for the whole loan.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Third party with no notice

q: Variation: Before closing, a limited partner phones the bank's loan officer and explains that the GP can't borrow beyond the budget without written consent. The bank lends anyway. Is the LP bound?
o: No: the bank had notice of the limit.
Yes: oral notice is never effective; only a filed statement counts.
Yes, because construction loans are always in the ordinary course.
No, and the bank must also pay damages to the limited partners.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 301(1) and ULPA § 402: knowledge or notice of the limit defeats apparent authority.
Notice can come from direct notification.
Ordinary course matters only if the third party lacks notice of the limit.
The question is only whether the LP is bound.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Bank told of the limit
pre: A limited partnership's agreement bars its general partner from borrowing above an approved budget without the limited partners' written consent. The general partner signs a $1 million construction loan, far above budget. The bank never saw the agreement, and no one told it of the limit. The LP defaults and argues the bank should have investigated the GP's authority. What result under RNR Investments?

q: A partnership files a statement of partnership authority stating that no partner may transfer the firm's real estate without all partners' signatures, and records it in the county real-property records. It also states that no partner may buy equipment over $10,000. A partner signs a $15,000 equipment purchase with a vendor who never saw the filing. Which limit binds third parties?
o: Only the recorded real-estate limit.
Both, because a public filing gives notice to everyone.
Neither, because statements of authority have no legal effect.
Only the equipment limit, because it involves goods.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 303(d), (g): grants of authority in a filed statement are conclusive for those who give value in reliance, but limitations aren't notice to third parties, except a limit on transferring real property that is recorded in the real property records.
Only the recorded real-property limitation works that way.
They have effect, mainly for grants and recorded real-property limits.
Reversed.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Statement of authority

q: After her shift, a partner in a pizza restaurant comes back with her toddler because her co-partner needs help, sets the child on the counter while making pizzas, and the child's hand is crushed in the dough press. The child sues the partnership, which seeks indemnity from the partner-mother. What result under Moren v. Jax Restaurant?
o: The partnership is liable and can't get indemnity from her.
The partnership is liable but may recover fully from her, because she was negligent.
The partnership isn't liable, because caring for a child isn't partnership business.
Only the partner is liable, because partnerships can't commit torts.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 305(a) makes the partnership liable for a partner's wrongful act in the ordinary course of business; § 401(c) gives partners a right to indemnity from the partnership, not the reverse. Mixed personal motives don't take conduct out of the ordinary course.
The partnership has no indemnity claim against a partner for ordinary-course conduct.
She was making pizzas, the core of the business.
Partnerships are liable for partners' ordinary-course torts.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Partner's tort and indemnity

q: Variation: The person who set the child on the counter was a non-partner employee cook, not a partner. Could the partnership seek indemnity from her?
o: Potentially yes: an employee stays liable for her own torts.
No: employees and partners are treated identically on indemnity.
No, because employees are never liable for workplace accidents.
Yes, and her claim against the partnership would be identical to a partner's.
oe: Correct. The casebook contrasts partnership law (§ 401(c)) with agency law, where the employee stays liable (R3d § 7.01) and an employer may in theory recover from the employee, though it rarely does.
Partners have a statutory indemnity right that employees don't.
Employees are liable for their own torts.
Employees don't get § 401(c) indemnity.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Employee instead of partner
pre: After her shift, a partner in a pizza restaurant comes back with her toddler because her co-partner needs help, sets the child on the counter while making pizzas, and the child's hand is crushed in the dough press. The child sues the partnership, which seeks indemnity from the partner-mother. What result under Moren v. Jax Restaurant?

q: A senior partner who founded and chaired a firm's Washington office objects when the executive committee merges the firm with another, makes his office co-chaired, and moves it. The partnership agreement, which he signed, gives the executive committee authority over “all questions of firm policy” and lets a majority approve amendments and admissions. He sues for breach of contract and fiduciary duty, arguing a merger needed unanimous consent. What result under Day v. Sidley & Austin?
o: Summary judgment for the firm: the agreement controls, and no disclosure duty was breached.
Judgment for Day: a merger is outside the ordinary course and always needs every partner's consent.
Judgment for Day, because partners must disclose all information about changes in the firm.
Judgment for the firm, because founding partners lose their rights after ten years.
oe: Correct. Statutory rules apply “subject to any agreement,” so no unanimity or veto applied. Fiduciary cases concern secret profits, usurped opportunities, and competition; the court found no duty to disclose changes in internal structure. Day “may be suffering from a bruised ego.”
That default yields to the partnership agreement.
The court found no such duty on these facts.
No such rule exists.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Agreement over statute

q: Under the UPA (1914) and RUPA, what information must a partnership give its partners?
o: UPA § 20: on demand. RUPA § 408: material information, even unasked.
Only information about each partner's own distributions.
Nothing beyond the annual tax forms each partner receives.
Everything, without limit, even after a partner leaves the firm.
oe: Correct. Day discussed UPA § 20. RUPA § 408 also lets partners inspect and copy the books, which are kept at the principal office; the agreement can't unreasonably restrict information rights (§ 105(c)(4)).
Information rights are broader.
Both acts give broader rights.
Dissociated partners have limited access.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Information rights

q: A profitable RUPA partnership decides not to distribute any profits this year. A partner demands her share in cash. Is she entitled to it?
o: No: there's no right to an interim distribution.
Yes: partners are entitled to their share of profits as soon as they're earned.
Yes, as long as she gives 30 days' written notice.
Only in kind, not in cash.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 405: distributions before dissolution are in equal shares, there's no right to an interim distribution unless the partnership decides, and no right to distributions in kind.
Profits are allocated to capital accounts but needn't be distributed.
No such rule exists.
Distributions are in money unless agreed.
topic: Wk 7 · Management & authority — Interim distributions

q: Under a 20-year joint venture, Sloan manages a leased office building and Mead supplies half the money; profits are shared. Four months before the lease ends, the landlord, who also owns the adjoining lots, offers Sloan a much bigger deal: a new long-term lease of the building plus the adjoining lots, with a new tower to be built. Sloan signs it through his own company and tells Mead nothing. Under Meinhard v. Salmon, what is Mead entitled to?
o: An equitable interest in the new lease.
Nothing: the venture was limited to the original lease, which was about to expire.
Nothing, because Sloan didn't commit any conscious fraud.
Only damages equal to Mead's share of the old lease's profits.
oe: Correct. Cardozo: co-venturers owe “the duty of the finest loyalty … Not honesty alone, but the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive.” Salmon appropriated the opportunity “in secrecy and silence.” The new lease was an extension and enlargement of the old subject matter; Meinhard got half (with Salmon keeping control through one extra share).
That was Judge Andrews's dissent.
No fraud was found; the breach was the failure to disclose.
Cardozo imposed a constructive trust on the new lease.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Managing co-venturer's opportunity

q: Variation: The landlord instead offers Sloan a lease on a building across the city, unconnected to the venture's property, and Sloan takes it without telling Mead. Is Sloan likely liable?
o: Probably not: the new lease lacks a nexus to the venture.
Yes: every opportunity a managing co-venturer learns of belongs to the venture.
Yes, because the same landlord offered both leases.
No, because Sloan's duties ended when the original lease expired.
oe: Correct. Meinhard required a connection: the new lease was an extension and enlargement of the venture's property. The organizational-opportunity factors include nexus, how the fiduciary learned of it, use of firm assets, and the venture's scope.
Cardozo limited the rule by nexus.
Same source helps but isn't enough without nexus to the venture's subject.
The question is nexus, not expiration.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Distant opportunity
pre: Under a 20-year joint venture, Sloan manages a leased office building and Mead supplies half the money; profits are shared. Four months before the lease ends, the landlord, who also owns the adjoining lots, offers Sloan a much bigger deal: a new long-term lease of the building plus the adjoining lots, with a new tower to be built. Sloan signs it through his own company and tells Mead nothing. Under Meinhard v. Salmon, what is Mead entitled to?

q: According to Cardozo in Meinhard, what was the least Salmon should have done?
o: Tell Meinhard about the offer so either could compete for it.
Turn down the new lease entirely and walk away from the deal.
Give Meinhard the entire new lease as a matter of course.
Ask a court for permission before signing the new lease.
oe: Correct. Cardozo said Salmon “might have warned Meinhard that the plan had been submitted, and that either would be free to compete,” leaving open whether Salmon, if he then won, would hold the lease for the venture. Disclosure equalizes opportunity, and a heavier duty rests on the managing partner.
Cardozo didn't require refusal.
Meinhard got half, not all.
No court approval was required.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Minimum duty

q: If you represented Salmon before the venture was formed, which clause would best protect him?
o: Each venturer may pursue renewals or related deals for himself after the term.
All fiduciary duties of every kind between the venturers are waived.
Meinhard, rather than Salmon, will be the managing venturer.
All disputes between the venturers will be decided by Judge Cardozo.
oe: Correct. The book asks what each side would want: Salmon, freedom to take new opportunities after the term; Meinhard, a right of first refusal or disclosure. RUPA § 105 allows such limits on loyalty if not manifestly unreasonable.
A complete elimination of loyalty and care isn't permitted under the uniform acts.
That wouldn't protect Salmon's freedom to take opportunities.
Not a serious drafting solution.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Planning around Meinhard

q: Four investors pool money from a shared account, buy three five-year oil and gas leases titled in one investor's company, and plan to resell them for a profit. Months before the leases expire, two of them secretly buy “top leases” on the same land that take effect when the originals expire. Under Sandvick v. LaCrosse, what was the relationship, and was there a breach?
o: A joint venture, and the secret top leases breached the duty of loyalty.
A partnership, but no breach, because top leases are separate property interests.
No relationship at all, because title was held in one investor's company.
A joint venture, but joint venturers owe each other no fiduciary duties.
oe: Correct. Buying the leases was a single act, not a “series of acts directed toward an end,” so no partnership. But the joint-venture elements were met, partnership law (including § 409 loyalty) applies, and the top leases were effectively extensions that created a conflict of interest. The others should have had a chance to participate.
No partnership (single act), and the top leases breached loyalty.
Title in one member's company is consistent with a joint venture.
Joint venturers owe the same duties as partners (Meinhard).
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Joint venture vs. partnership

q: Which is NOT one of the joint-venture elements listed in Sandvick?
o: Equal contributions of the same kind by each party.
A proprietary interest and right of mutual control over the engaged property.
An express or implied agreement to share profits.
An express or implied contract showing a joint venture was formed.
oe: Correct. Contributions need not be equal or of the same nature. The elements: (1) contribution of money, property, time, or skill to a common undertaking; (2) a proprietary interest and right of mutual control over the property; (3) an agreement to share profits (usually but not necessarily losses); (4) an express or implied contract forming the venture.
A listed element.
A listed element.
A listed element.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Joint venture elements

q: A family oil partnership's written agreement says each partner may freely pursue business for his own account “even though such business may be in conflict or competition with the partnership,” and the partnership has no claim to it. At a meeting, the partners discuss buying a tract of land but defer the decision. Two partners then buy it themselves. Under Singer v. Singer, did they breach a duty?
o: No: the agreement allowed competition, and no partnership asset was taken.
Yes: partners can never compete with their own partnership.
Yes, because the partnership had discussed buying the land at a meeting.
Yes, because the competition clause was void as against public policy.
oe: Correct. The clause was drafted “to promote spirited, if not outright predatory competition.” The partnership hadn't acquired the land, so the partners were free to buy it. Partners can contract around loyalty if not manifestly unreasonable (RUPA § 105(d)(3)).
The default can be changed by agreement.
Discussion without acquisition didn't cross the agreement's line.
The court enforced it.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Contracting around loyalty

q: A consulting firm's stock plan lets it redeem retired officers' shares “at any time” at book value. While negotiating a sale of a division that will multiply the share price, the firm redeems two retirees' shares at pre-sale book value, adding millions to the remaining owners' proceeds. The retirees sue for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and of fiduciary duty. What did the majority in Nemec v. Shrader hold?
o: Both fail: the contract authorized the redemption and governs the dispute.
The implied covenant claim succeeds, because redeeming just before a sale is always bad faith.
The fiduciary claim succeeds, because officers always owe each other fiduciary duties.
Both succeed, because book value is never a fair price for shares.
oe: Correct. The implied covenant is a “cautious enterprise” that fills only gaps the parties didn't anticipate; one can't base a claim on conduct the agreement authorizes. Redemption served a legitimate interest. The dissent would have required the power to be exercised reasonably and in good faith.
The majority rejected that argument.
The contract governed, displacing the overlapping fiduciary claim.
Parties can make good and bad bargains.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Implied covenant and redemption

q: A retired law partner receives a pension that ends if the firm dissolves without a successor. The firm's managing council makes a merger and spending decisions that prove disastrous, and the firm dissolves; the pension stops. He sues the council for negligent mismanagement, alleging no fraud or self-dealing. What result under Bane v. Ferguson?
o: No claim: duties run to current partners, and negligence is protected.
A claim, because the council owed duties to everyone with an interest in the firm.
A claim, because UPA § 9(3)(c) forbids acts making it impossible to carry on the business.
A claim, because ordinary negligence breaches a partner's duty of care.
oe: Correct. Bane ceased to be a partner on retiring; withdrawal ended the relationship as to him. UPA § 9(3)(c) protects partners, not third parties. Even fiduciaries aren't liable for mere negligence (cf. RUPA § 409(c)).
Duties run to current partners.
That provision protects partners, not retirees.
Partners' duty of care requires gross negligence or worse.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Duty to retired partners

q: A partner makes a careless but good-faith decision to sign a supply contract at a price slightly above market, costing the firm $15,000. Is she liable to the partnership under RUPA § 409(c)?
o: No: ordinary negligence doesn't breach a partner's duty of care.
Yes: partners owe the same duty of reasonable care that agents owe.
Yes, because any loss caused by a partner must be reimbursed.
No, because partners never owe each other a duty of care.
oe: Correct. Ordinary negligence isn't a breach. Contrast an agent's duty of reasonable care (R3d § 8.08).
Partners' standard is lower.
Liability requires a breach.
They do, at the gross-negligence level.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Standard of care

q: Two people orally agree to build a data-analytics business as equal partners. After a year of shared work and costs, one of them, without warning, cuts the other off from the servers and code, incorporates a new company, and takes in investors. Do the excluded partner's claims survive a motion to dismiss under Second Measure v. Kim?
o: Yes: he can't dissolve to grab the business; duties to account continue.
No: an oral partnership agreement can't be enforced.
No: once a partner dissolves the partnership, all fiduciary duties end.
No, because incorporating the business converted the partnership into a corporation.
oe: Correct. Some duties, such as not competing, end at dissolution (RUPA § 409(b)(3)), but the duty to account for property, profits and opportunities continues through winding up. “A partner may not dissolve a partnership to gain the benefits of the business for himself, unless he fully compensates his copartner” (Leff; Page).
Partnerships can be formed orally.
Duties to account continue through winding up.
Incorporating a new company doesn't extinguish the partner's claims.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Duties during winding up

q: Two partners decide to leave their law firm and take clients. They secretly line up office space and prepare lists of cases. When a partner asks one of them directly whether he's leaving, he says no, three times. After giving notice, they immediately send clients one-sided letters on firm letterhead and delay giving the firm their list of cases until they've collected most consents. Under Meehan v. Shaughnessy, where is the breach?
o: In lying when asked and unfairly gathering client consents, not in preparing.
In leasing new office space before giving the firm notice.
In leaving at all, because partners must stay until the firm consents.
Nowhere, because clients always choose their own lawyers.
oe: Correct. Meehan: departing partners may prepare, but must answer truthfully on demand (UPA § 20) and must not gain an unfair advantage in competing for clients. They held profits from unfairly removed cases in constructive trust for the old firm.
Logistical preparation isn't a breach.
Partners may leave.
Clients' freedom of choice doesn't excuse unfair solicitation.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Grabbing and leaving by partners

q: Before giving notice, two departing partners prepare a memo listing their department's associates and staff with salaries, billing rates and billable hours, and give it to their new firm, which interviews those employees. Under Gibbs v. Breed, Abbott & Morgan, did they breach a duty?
o: Yes: handing over confidential staff data and recruiting before notice was a breach.
No: salary information is widely known, so sharing it is harmless.
No: partners owe fiduciary duties to the firm's employees, not to the firm.
Yes, and the firm automatically recovers all its lost profits through dissolution.
oe: Correct. Recruitment of firm employees is permitted on a more limited basis than client solicitation, generally only after notice. The breach parallels Bancroft-Whitney for agents.
That was the dissent's view.
They owe duties to the firm.
The court vacated that damages award for lack of causation.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Recruiting with confidential data

q: A law firm's agreement lets two-thirds of the senior partners expel any partner without cause. The firm expels a partner who reported, in good faith, that the managing partner was overbilling a client; an investigation found no overbilling. She sues for breach of fiduciary duty. Under Bohatch v. Butler & Binion, what result?
o: No fiduciary duty not to expel her.
She wins, because expelling a whistleblower always breaches fiduciary duty.
She wins, because expulsion of a partner always requires cause.
The expulsion is void because her report turned out to be wrong.
oe: Correct. The court recognized no duty not to expel a partner for reporting suspected overbilling (her contract recovery rested on other grounds). Lawlis similarly held that a no-cause expulsion under the agreement is in good faith if nothing due is wrongfully withheld.
The majority rejected that; the dissent would have imposed damages.
The agreement allowed no-cause expulsion.
The report's accuracy didn't change the result.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Expulsion

q: A partner wants to sell the partnership a building she owns. Under RUPA § 409 (2013), which step would protect her from a loyalty claim?
o: Full disclosure, then authorization of the deal by all the partners.
A clause in the partnership agreement eliminating the duty of loyalty entirely.
Approval of the deal by any single other partner.
Keeping the deal confidential so that no dispute arises.
oe: Correct. § 409(f) allows all partners to authorize or ratify a specific act after full disclosure; § 409(g) makes fairness a defense to a self-dealing claim; § 409(e) says furthering one's own interest isn't by itself a breach.
The agreement can't eliminate loyalty, only alter specific aspects if not manifestly unreasonable.
Authorization must come from all the partners (or a method the agreement specifies).
Secrecy is the problem, not the solution.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Ratification and fairness

q: Which term may a RUPA partnership agreement validly include?
o: A term naming activities that don't violate loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable.
A term eliminating the partners' obligation of good faith and fair dealing.
A term exonerating partners from liability for their intentional misconduct.
A term barring any partner from ever withdrawing from the partnership, rightfully or not.
oe: Correct. § 105(d)(3). The agreement may not eliminate loyalty or care, eliminate good faith and fair dealing, exonerate bad faith or knowing violations of law, unreasonably restrict information rights, or vary the power to dissociate or the judicial expulsion and dissolution grounds.
Prohibited by § 105(c)(6).
Prohibited by § 105(c)(8).
The power to dissociate can't be varied (§ 105(c)(9)).
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — Limits of waiver

q: While her partnership is operating, a partner in a catering firm quietly starts catering weddings for her own account in the same city. The agreement is silent. Which duty does this most directly breach?
o: The duty not to compete before dissolution.
The duty of care, because she neglected the firm's business.
The duty to render information on demand.
No duty, because competition is allowed unless the agreement forbids it.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 409(b)(3). She'd also have to account for any profits from the partnership's business or opportunities (§ 409(b)(1)).
Competition is a loyalty problem.
That's a separate duty.
Not competing is the default.
topic: Wk 8 · Partners' fiduciary duties — No competing before dissolution

q: Under the UPA (1914), a five-partner accounting firm's junior partner retires on good terms. What is the technical effect?
o: The partnership dissolves.
Nothing; the partnership continues as an entity without him.
The partnership terminates immediately and must stop all business.
He remains a partner until the firm's assets are sold.
oe: Correct. UPA § 29 defines dissolution as the change in the partners' relation caused by any partner ceasing to be associated in carrying on the business. Adding a partner doesn't dissolve. Dissolution is only the beginning of the end.
That's RUPA's approach.
Dissolution starts winding up; termination comes later.
He ceases to be associated; winding up follows.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Aggregate dissolution

q: Two partners agree to run a cafeteria for the 30-year term of its lease. Four years in, the money partner, unhappy with profits, announces that he dissolves the partnership. Under the UPA and Collins v. Lewis, what happens?
o: The partnership dissolves, but wrongfully, and he owes damages.
Nothing happens; a term partnership can't be dissolved before its term ends.
The partnership dissolves rightfully, because any partner may withdraw at any time.
He can withdraw only with a court's permission.
oe: Correct. “There always exists the power, as opposed to the right, of dissolution.” Express-will dissolution before the term ends is premature and wrongful but effective (UPA § 31(2)).
The power to dissolve can't be eliminated by agreement.
That's true only of at-will partnerships.
The power exists without court approval.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Power vs. right

q: Variation: Instead, the money partner asks the court to order dissolution because the cafeteria isn't profitable, but the jury finds the unprofitability was caused by his own unreasonable demands and refusal to fund. What result?
o: Denied: he can't get judicial dissolution for problems he caused.
Granted, because unprofitability is always grounds for dissolution.
Granted, and the managing partner must pay damages.
Denied, and he can never leave the partnership.
oe: Correct. Collins v. Lewis: the managing partner was competent; Collins couldn't get judicial dissolution caused by his own breach.
Not when the petitioner caused it.
The other partner wasn't at fault.
He retains the power to dissolve, at the risk of damages.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Judicial dissolution for one's own conduct
pre: Two partners agree to run a cafeteria for the 30-year term of its lease. Four years in, the money partner, unhappy with profits, announces that he dissolves the partnership. Under the UPA and Collins v. Lewis, what happens?

q: Two brothers form an oral linen-supply partnership with no stated term. One brother's corporation lends it $47,000. After years of losses, just as the business turns profitable, the lending brother announces he is dissolving it. The other argues the partnership was for a term: until the debt was repaid from profits. Under Page v. Page, what result?
o: At will, so he may dissolve, but only in good faith.
For a term until the loan was repaid, so dissolution is wrongful.
At will, so he may dissolve for any reason, including to take the business.
Dissolution requires both brothers' consent.
oe: Correct. A shared hope that the business will pay for itself doesn't create a definite term or particular undertaking. But the power must be exercised in good faith: “a partner may not dissolve a partnership to gain the benefits of the business for himself, unless he fully compensates his copartner.”
The court found it at will.
Good faith limits the power.
An at-will partner can dissolve by express will.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Implied term

q: In which situation is a court most likely to find an implied term, making early dissolution wrongful?
o: A partner lends the business money to be repaid from its profits.
The partners share a hope that the business will succeed.
The partners have worked together for many years.
The partners sign a lease for their shop with no stated duration.
oe: Correct. Owen v. Cohen found an implied term from such an arrangement; slide notes add terms implied until a sum is earned, investments recouped, debts paid, or property sold on favorable terms. Page distinguished a mere hope that the business would pay for itself.
A common hope doesn't create a term.
Duration of the past relationship doesn't imply a future term.
No term arises from that.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Implicit term found

q: A bowling-alley partner repeatedly humiliates his co-partner in front of staff and customers, refuses to work, takes money without consent, and pushes to open a gambling room. The co-partner seeks judicial dissolution. What result under Owen v. Cohen?
o: Dissolution granted for persistent misconduct.
Denied: personal friction between partners is never grounds for dissolution.
Denied, because the partnership had no stated term.
Granted, but the co-partner's loan may be repaid only from future profits.
oe: Correct. Under UPA § 32, petty but persistent mistreatment can justify dissolution. The co-partner's loan is repaid first from the sale proceeds. (These grounds now appear in RUPA § 801(4).)
Persistent misconduct affecting the business is.
Judicial dissolution is available in any partnership.
The court ordered it repaid first from the sale.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Judicial dissolution for misconduct

q: Which event does NOT cause dissolution of a UPA (1914) partnership?
o: The admission of a new partner.
A partner's death.
A partner's bankruptcy.
The expiration of the agreed term.
oe: Correct. Dissolution follows a partner's ceasing to be associated. Causes include express will, expulsion under the agreement, death, bankruptcy, expiration of the term or undertaking, illegality, and court decree (§§ 31–32).
Death dissolves a UPA partnership.
Bankruptcy dissolves it (as in Fulton).
Expiration dissolves it automatically.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Causes of dissolution

q: After a UPA partnership dissolves, partner Ned signs a new five-year supply contract with a longtime supplier who doesn't know of the dissolution, which hasn't been advertised. Is the partnership bound?
o: Likely yes, toward a prior creditor without notice of the dissolution.
No: dissolution ends every partner's authority immediately and completely.
No, because a new long-term contract is never appropriate after dissolution.
Yes, and Ned has no liability to his partners for signing it.
oe: Correct. UPA § 33 ends actual authority except to wind up; § 35 preserves power to bind prior creditors without notice and those who knew of the partnership if dissolution wasn't advertised. Notice to creditors is the protection.
Apparent authority can survive toward those without notice.
It's not appropriate for winding up, but § 35 may still bind the firm toward this supplier.
A partner who exceeds winding-up authority may be liable to the others.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Authority after dissolution

q: Under UPA § 38(2), when a partner wrongfully dissolves a partnership, what may the innocent partners do?
o: Continue the business, paying his interest less damages, without goodwill.
Force the wrongdoer to remain a partner until the agreed term ends.
Take the wrongdoer's interest for free, as damages for the breach.
Only liquidate the business and split the proceeds among all partners.
oe: Correct. Pav-Saver v. Vasso applied this: the innocent partner continued the business and kept using the contributed patents, and the wrongdoer's interest was valued without goodwill.
The power to dissolve can't be taken away.
They must pay its value less damages.
They may continue instead.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Wrongful dissolution consequences

q: A partner in a three-person memorabilia store dies; there's no continuation agreement. The survivors inventory the stock, have it valued at book value, offer the estate its share, and start a new store. The widow demands a liquidation sale to find the business's true value. Under Creel v. Lilly, must they liquidate?
o: No: a good-faith winding up that pays the estate its share is enough.
Yes: under UPA § 38(1), any partner's estate can always force a sale.
Yes, and the estate also gets a share of the new store's profits.
No, because a deceased partner's estate has no rights at all.
oe: Correct. Creel: forced liquidation is harsh and gives the estate too much leverage; the court's approach fits RUPA's entity theory. Disotell similarly allowed a fair-market-value buyout instead of a sale.
Courts increasingly allow alternatives to a fire sale.
The court denied a share of the successor's profits.
The estate gets its share.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Liquidation not required

q: Two brothers dissolve their milk-hauling partnership and agree to auction its assets, including the key hauling contract, to each other. One brother wins the auction, but the other has meanwhile applied in his own name to the dairy co-op, which awards him the contract, leaving the partnership's assets nearly worthless. Under Monin v. Monin, is he liable?
o: Yes: his duties continued through winding up.
No: dissolution ends all fiduciary duties between partners.
No, because the dairy co-op made its choice freely.
Yes, but only for nominal damages.
oe: Correct. Monin: damages were the difference between the winning bid and what the assets were worth without the contract.
Duties continue through winding up.
That was the dissent's view.
Damages were substantial ($64,000).
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Duties during wind-up

q: In a judicial dissolution, the two majority partners of a shopping-center partnership bid for the property at the court-ordered sale. The minority partner objects that they froze him out. Under Prentiss v. Sheffel, may they bid?
o: Yes: without bad faith, they may bid.
No: majority partners can never bid at a dissolution sale.
Yes, but only if they pay double the appraised value.
No, because a freeze-out always occurs in such cases.
oe: Correct. The exclusion came from an inability to function together, not a scheme. The minority partner could bid too.
The court allowed it.
No such rule exists.
The court found no bad-faith freeze-out.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissolution under the UPA (1914) — Insiders at the sale

q: In a RUPA at-will partnership of four, partner Uma gives notice that she is withdrawing. The other three want to keep the business going. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Her notice dissolves the firm by default, unless the agreement provides for a buyout.
Her withdrawal has no effect until the other partners consent to it.
The firm must buy her out in every case; a RUPA partnership never dissolves on withdrawal.
She remains a partner until the business is sold.
oe: Correct. RUPA separates dissociation from dissolution, but § 801(1) makes express-will dissociation from an at-will partnership a dissolution event by default. Partners can and usually do agree otherwise, and then § 603 sends the case to an Article 7 buyout.
A partner has the power to dissociate at any time.
Absent agreement, an at-will partner's withdrawal triggers dissolution.
She is dissociated on notice.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Withdrawal from an at-will firm

q: A partner rightfully dissociates from a RUPA term partnership that continues. Absent agreement, how is the buyout price set under § 701(b)?
o: The greater of liquidation or going-concern value, plus interest.
Her capital account at book value on the date she leaves the firm.
Whatever price the remaining partners consider fair to her.
Liquidation value only, without any interest.
oe: Correct. The partnership must buy her interest; damages for wrongful dissociation would be offset (§ 701(c)). Unlike UPA § 38(2)(c)(II), there's no goodwill deduction.
Book value is a common agreed formula, not the statutory default.
The statute sets the default formula.
The greater of liquidation or going-concern value, with interest.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Buyout price

q: Partners agree to remain partners for five years to develop a resort. In year two, partner Vic withdraws by express will; no other partner has left. Under RUPA § 602, what's the status of his dissociation?
o: Wrongful, and he's liable for damages.
Rightful, because any partner may withdraw at any time.
Ineffective, because a term partnership can't be left early.
Wrongful only if the agreement expressly forbids withdrawal.
oe: Correct. § 602(b)(2)(i). He still had the power to dissociate (§ 602(a)). Consequences: damages offset against his buyout, payment deferred until the term ends absent proof of no undue hardship (§ 701(h)), and no right to take part in winding up (§ 802(c)).
He has the power, but not the right, in a term partnership.
The power to dissociate can't be eliminated.
Withdrawing early from a term partnership is wrongful by statute.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Wrongful dissociation

q: Variation: Vic withdraws 60 days after another partner died. Is his withdrawal wrongful?
o: No: withdrawal within 90 days of a death isn't wrongful.
Yes: the term hasn't expired, so any early withdrawal is wrongful.
Yes, because a partner's death automatically ends a term partnership.
No, but only if the deceased partner's estate consents.
oe: Correct. § 602(b)(2)(i). Such a withdrawal also counts toward the half of the remaining partners who may choose to wind up the term partnership within 90 days (§ 801(2)(A)).
The statute has a 90-day exception.
Death alone doesn't end it; the others may vote within 90 days.
The estate's consent isn't required.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — 90-day exception
pre: Partners agree to remain partners for five years to develop a resort. In year two, partner Vic withdraws by express will; no other partner has left. Under RUPA § 602, what's the status of his dissociation?

q: A wrongfully dissociating partner demands immediate payment of her buyout from a term partnership with three years left. What's her position under § 701(h)?
o: She waits until the term ends, unless she shows no undue hardship.
She's paid within 120 days, like any other dissociated partner.
She forfeits her entire interest in the partnership as a penalty.
She's paid immediately, but without any interest.
oe: Correct. The slides: a wrongful dissociator may have to wait, but the longest a non-wrongful dissociator must wait is 120 days (§ 701(e)).
That's for non-wrongful dissociators.
She's paid, less damages.
Payment is deferred, with interest.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Waiting for payment

q: In a family farming partnership, one son refuses to cooperate on any decision, tells each partner they'll die in turn and he'll be “the last man standing,” threatens that “paybacks are hell,” and communicates only through his lawyer. Business is at a standstill. The family asks the court to remove him. Under Giles v. Giles Land Co., what result?
o: Judicial expulsion of the son, followed by a buyout.
No relief: family disputes are personal and unrelated to the partnership business.
Dissolution of the entire partnership and sale of the family land.
No court role: expulsion requires the unanimous vote of the other partners.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 601(5)(C) (and alternatively (5)(A)). Dissolution case law applies because RUPA's dissociation grounds were modeled on the UPA's dissolution grounds; in a family partnership, family disputes relate to the business.
In a family partnership, they're related.
RUPA's tool lets the court remove one partner instead.
Judicial expulsion is a separate route (§ 601(5)).
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Judicial expulsion

q: Which event does NOT dissociate a partner under RUPA?
o: A creditor's charging order against the partner's interest.
The partner's death.
The partner's becoming a debtor in bankruptcy.
The partner's expulsion under the partnership agreement.
oe: Correct. Transfer of a transferable interest, a charging order, adding a partner, and ordinary disagreements don't cause dissociation (though transfer of all of an interest can support unanimous expulsion, and serious conduct can support judicial expulsion).
A § 601(7) event.
A § 601(6) event.
A § 601(3) event.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Not dissociation

q: Partner Will dissociates from a continuing RUPA partnership in January; no statement of dissociation is filed. In June, Will signs a contract in the partnership's name with a vendor who has dealt with the firm for years, doesn't know he left, and reasonably believes he's still a partner. Is the partnership bound?
o: Likely yes, and Will is liable to the firm for any resulting damage.
No: a dissociated partner can never bind the partnership.
Yes, and Will has no liability to the partnership.
No, because the vendor should have checked the state's filings.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 702. Filing a statement of dissociation (§ 704) would give everyone notice 90 days after filing (§ 103(d)). Will's management rights ended on dissociation (§ 603(b)).
Section 702 provides lingering power for two years.
He's liable for damage caused.
No statement was filed, and the vendor lacked notice.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — After dissociation

q: Partner Xia dissociates in March. The partnership owes a bank on a loan signed the prior December. Is Xia released from the bank loan?
o: No: dissociation doesn't discharge her existing liabilities.
Yes: dissociation ends all of a partner's personal liability.
Yes, as long as she files a statement of dissociation.
No, and she can never be released from it by anyone.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 603(c) and § 703(c)–(d). The partnership must indemnify her against partnership liabilities in a buyout (§ 701(d)).
Past liabilities remain.
The statement affects future obligations, not past ones.
She can be released by the creditor's agreement or material alteration.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Old debts

q: A six-partner term partnership loses one partner to death. How can the partnership be dissolved before the term expires under RUPA § 801(2)?
o: By a 90-day vote of half the others, by all partners' agreement, or at term's end.
Automatically, because a partner's death always dissolves a partnership.
Only by a court order entered on some partner's application.
By a vote of the deceased partner's estate within 90 days.
oe: Correct. § 801(2). Otherwise the partnership continues and buys out the deceased partner's interest. A term partnership can't be forced into liquidation by one partner leaving prematurely.
That's the UPA rule, not RUPA's.
Court order is one route (§ 801(4)) but not the only one.
The estate doesn't decide.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Term partnership dissolution

q: A partnership agreement states that “no partner may seek judicial dissolution for any reason.” A partner later shows that the firm's economic purpose is likely to be unreasonably frustrated. Can she get judicial dissolution?
o: Yes: the agreement can't vary the judicial dissolution grounds.
No: partners may waive any statutory right by agreement.
Yes, but only with the consent of a majority of the partners.
No, because economic frustration isn't a ground for dissolution.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 105(c)(11); the slides note that § 801(1)–(3) can be modified but not § 801(4)–(5).
Some rights are mandatory.
Judicial dissolution on these grounds isn't subject to a vote.
It is one (§ 801(4)).
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Non-waivable grounds

q: A creditor holds a charging order on a partner's interest in an at-will partnership. When may it seek judicial dissolution?
o: At any time, if winding up is equitable.
Never, because transferees have no rights against the partnership.
Only with the consent of all the partners.
Only after the debtor partner dies.
oe: Correct. § 801(5): a transferee may apply after the term ends (for a term partnership) or at any time (if at will at the time of the transfer or charging order).
They have the § 801(5) right.
The court decides on equitable grounds.
Death isn't required.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Transferee's petition

q: After a RUPA partnership dissolves, a partner signs a contract to open a new branch location. The landlord doesn't know of the dissolution, and no statement of dissolution was filed. Which statement is correct?
o: The firm may be bound toward the landlord, and the partner is liable to it.
The partnership is bound, and the partner has no liability for signing it.
The partnership isn't bound, because dissolution ends all partners' authority.
Signing the lease converts the dissolution into a continuation of the business.
oe: Correct. §§ 802, 804–805: a partnership continues after dissolution only to wind up; acts not appropriate for winding up bind only toward those without notice. A filed statement of dissolution gives everyone notice 90 days later.
Section 805 makes him liable.
Apparent authority survives toward those without notice.
Partners can choose to continue only by the means the statute or agreement allows.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Winding up

q: A partner's wrongful dissociation caused the partnership's dissolution. May she participate in winding up?
o: No: a wrongful dissociator can't participate.
Yes: all partners participate in winding up.
Yes, and she controls the process.
Only if she pays her damages first.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 802(c). Partners who do wind up may receive reasonable compensation (§ 401(j)).
Wrongful dissociators are excluded.
She has no right to participate.
Payment doesn't restore the right.
topic: Wk 8 · Dissociation & dissolution under RUPA — Who participates in winding up

q: Kira puts up $20,000 for a home-remodeling venture; Lee contributes only his work as estimator and foreman, without salary. They agree to split profits equally and never discuss losses. A year later the venture has lost $16,000, leaving $4,000. Kira sues Lee for half the loss, $8,000. Under Kovacik v. Reed, what result?
o: Lee owes nothing.
Lee owes $8,000: under UPA § 18(a), losses are shared like profits.
Lee owes $8,000 minus the value of his labor.
Lee owes $16,000, because he managed the work that lost the money.
oe: Correct. Kovacik: each loses his own contribution, one his money and the other his labor, and agreeing to split profits equally implies they valued the contributions as equal. Kira bears the $16,000 capital loss and takes the $4,000 left.
That's the statutory default, which Kovacik declined to apply.
Kovacik didn't net out labor; it treated the labor as his lost contribution.
Nothing makes the services partner bear all the loss.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Money partner vs. services partner

q: Variation: Apply the UPA's default rules (§§ 18(a), 40) instead of the Kovacik exception to the same facts. What would Lee owe?
o: Nothing, because he had no capital account.
$2,000, half of the remaining assets.
oe: Correct. The slides' default chart: losses are shared like profits, return of capital has priority, so the services partner must pay in his half of the capital loss to equalize.
Under the default he must contribute to cover his share of the loss.
The calculation is half the loss, not half the remainder.
He bears only his half.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Statutory default math
pre: Kira puts up $20,000 for a home-remodeling venture; Lee contributes only his work as estimator and foreman, without salary. They agree to split profits equally and never discuss losses. A year later the venture has lost $16,000, leaving $4,000. Kira sues Lee for half the loss, $8,000. Under Kovacik v. Reed, what result?

q: In which situation would courts most likely NOT apply the Kovacik rule, so the services partner shares capital losses?
o: The services partner drew a weekly salary.
The parties never discussed losses.
The services partner worked full time.
The money partner contributed more than $10,000.
oe: Correct. Courts don't apply Kovacik where the services partner was compensated for his work or made any capital contribution, even a nominal one.
That's the Kovacik situation itself.
Full-time work without pay fits Kovacik.
Amount of capital doesn't trigger an exception.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Exceptions to Kovacik

q: Variation: Lee contributed $500 of his own money along with his services. Does Kovacik still protect him?
o: Probably not: any capital contribution takes him outside it.
Yes: a $500 contribution is too small to matter.
Yes, but only if he also drew no salary from the venture.
No, and he must now bear the entire loss himself.
