oe: Correct. The slide's second exception.
Even nominal capital takes the case outside Kovacik.
The capital contribution alone defeats the exception.
He'd share losses per the default, not bear all of them.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Nominal capital
pre: In which situation would courts most likely NOT apply the Kovacik rule, so the services partner shares capital losses?

q: How does RUPA treat the Kovacik rule?
o: Its § 401 comment rejects Kovacik: losses follow profits.
It codifies Kovacik in § 401 for services-only partners.
It leaves loss sharing entirely to the courts to decide case by case.
It requires losses to be shared by the ratio of capital contributed.
oe: Correct. The comment continues UPA § 18(a)'s rules “where one or more of the partners contribute no capital, although there is case law to the contrary,” citing Kovacik. The lesson: always draft a loss-sharing clause.
It rejects it.
It supplies a default.
Losses follow distribution shares by default.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — RUPA's response

q: What concern does the professor's note raise about the Kovacik rule?
o: It may encourage risk-taking by the services partner.
It makes capital partners too cautious to invest in new ventures.
It forces services partners to borrow money to cover their share of losses.
It conflicts with the statute of frauds for partnership agreements.
oe: Correct. The note suggests that bargaining parties would likely land somewhere between Kovacik and equal sharing, but the hypothetical-bargain model alone doesn't say where.
The concern is about the services partner's incentives.
Kovacik relieves services partners of capital losses.
Not relevant.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Incentives

q: Which is NOT among the three possible loss-allocation rules listed on the Kovacik slides?
o: Allocate all capital losses to the partner who managed the business.
All capital losses borne by the capital partner alone (Kovacik).
Capital losses shared in the same proportion as profits (the statute).
Capital losses allocated by the ratio of capital contributions.
oe: Correct. The listed options: (1) all capital losses borne by the capital partner alone (Kovacik); (2) capital losses shared like profits (the statute); (3) capital losses allocated by the ratio of capital contributions.
Listed.
Listed.
Listed.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Possible rules

q: A limited partnership's general partner develops a drug habit and behaves erratically. The other general partner sues to dissolve the partnership and buy him out. Before judgment, the troubled partner dies. The agreement says that on a general partner's death the others may continue and must buy his interest at his capital account plus his average profits for the prior three years. His estate argues the lawsuit had already dissolved the partnership, so the agreement's buyout clause no longer applies. What result under G & S Investments v. Belman?
o: The buyout clause applies.
The partnership dissolved when the suit was filed, so the estate gets liquidation value.
The clause is void, because the partner died during the litigation.
The court must set a fair price because the partner was ill.
oe: Correct. Dissolution occurs by decree or other acts, not by filing suit (Cooper v. Isaacs). The partner's wrongful conduct also permitted continuation under UPA §§ 32 and 38.
Filing doesn't dissolve.
Death is exactly the clause's trigger.
The court enforced the agreed formula.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Filing doesn't dissolve

q: Variation: The deceased partner's capital account on the books is negative $44,000, though his share of the apartment complex's market value is about $77,000. The estate asks the court to read “capital account” as market value. What result?
o: The clause is enforced as written, at book value.
The court substitutes market value because the result is unfair.
The estate gets nothing, because the account is negative.
The court splits the difference between book and market value.
oe: Correct. G & S: the term is unambiguous under GAAP (contributions plus profits minus losses and distributions), kept at cost; the agreement is valid even if the price differs from actual value. “It is not the province of this court to act as a post-transaction guardian for either party.” The estate received about $4,900.
Courts won't rewrite the deal based on later notions of fairness.
The formula also added average profits, producing a small payment.
No splitting rule exists.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Capital account at cost
pre: A limited partnership's general partner develops a drug habit and behaves erratically. The other general partner sues to dissolve the partnership and buy him out. Before judgment, the troubled partner dies. The agreement says that on a general partner's death the others may continue and must buy his interest at his capital account plus his average profits for the prior three years. His estate argues the lawsuit had already dissolved the partnership, so the agreement's buyout clause no longer applies. What result under G & S Investments v. Belman?

q: A partner contributes $100,000, is allocated $30,000 of profit, and takes a $10,000 distribution. Meanwhile the partnership's real estate doubles in market value. What is her capital account?
o: $240,000, reflecting the doubled value.
oe: Correct. The book's G & S example: contributions plus profit share minus distributions. Losses can even drive an account negative while the property appreciates, which is why book-value formulas can be dangerous.
Capital accounts don't track market value.
That ignores the distribution.
That ignores profit and distribution.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Capital account and appreciation

q: You're drafting a buy-sell agreement for a two-owner business. Which question belongs on the course's drafting checklist?
o: What happens if an obligated buyer refuses, or if there's only an option?
Which partner's spouse will manage the business after a divorce?
Whether the buyout price will be kept confidential from the IRS.
Which court will decide every future dispute over the buyout price.
oe: Correct. The checklist: triggers (death, disability, will of the partner); whether there's an obligation or an option and whose; consequences of refusal; procedures for offering to buy or sell (e.g., a shotgun clause); treatment of IP contributions (Pav-Saver); how to set the price; method of payment; and outstanding partnership debts.
Divorce is a trigger to plan for, but the checklist doesn't hand management to spouses.
Not on the list.
Not on the list (dispute resolution can be drafted, but it isn't a checklist item).
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Drafting triggers

q: A buyout clause lets either partner name a price per unit, after which the other must either buy the first partner's interest or sell his own at that price. What is this mechanism, and why does it tend to produce a fair price?
o: A shotgun clause: the first mover must be willing to buy or sell at its own price.
A right of first refusal, which lets the first partner match outside offers.
A book-value formula, which uses the capital accounts to set price.
A charging order, which lets creditors force a sale of the interest.
oe: Correct. The casebook describes the first mover setting a price to buy or sell, or forcing the other side to set it.
A right of first refusal responds to a third party's offer.
No formula is involved.
Charging orders are a creditor's remedy.
topic: Wk 8 · Loss sharing & buyout agreements — Shotgun clause

q: A buy-sell agreement requires the firm to buy out a partner who dies. What funding device do the slides suggest for that trigger?
o: Firm-owned life insurance.
A pension plan.
Disability insurance.
A charging order on the estate.
oe: Correct. The slides pair triggers with funding: death → firm-owned life insurance; retirement → a pension plan such as a 401(k); disability → disability insurance; divorce → see Alaska Plastics; miscellaneous → a valuation formula.
That's for retirement.
That's for disability.
Charging orders are creditors' remedies.

q: Why do the slides cite Alaska Plastics in connection with buy-sell agreements?
o: An ex-spouse may end up with an illiquid stake and no buyer.
It held buy-sell agreements unenforceable in a divorce.
It approved book value as the measure in every divorce case.
It required firm-owned life insurance for every partner.
oe: Correct. Buy-sell agreements create a market for the interests of inactive owners and let remaining owners control who joins.
That isn't its point on the slide.
Not the point.
That's the death trigger.

q: Which is NOT among the purposes of buy-sell agreements listed in the slide notes?
o: Guaranteeing that the business will always be profitable.
Providing an orderly transfer of interests on death, retirement, or disability.
Letting the remaining owners retain control and choose new owners.
Creating a market at a fair price for inactive owners' interests.
oe: Correct. The purposes: provide an orderly transfer on death, retirement, disability and other events; let remaining owners keep control and avoid conflicts with new owners; transfer the business to the right family members; and create a market at a fair price for inactive owners' interests.
Listed.
Listed.
Listed.

q: Pine Ridge Apartments, LP has one general partner, Pine GP LLC, and twelve limited partners who invested money and take no part in management. The LP defaults on a $2 million loan. Who is personally liable?
o: Only the general partner.
All the partners, jointly and severally.
The limited partners, because they supplied the capital.
No one, because an LP is a kind of corporation.
oe: Correct. In an LP, general partners manage and have full liability; limited partners have no daily responsibilities and no liability beyond their investment. Using an entity as general partner gives managers limited liability too.
Limited partners are shielded.
Supplying capital doesn't create liability.
An LP isn't a corporation; its general partner is liable.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Limited partner liability

q: Two people are limited partners in an LP and are also the officers, directors, and shareholders of its only general partner, a corporation, through which they run the LP day to day. The LP breaches a supply contract; the creditor knew it was dealing with the corporate GP and never asked for guarantees. Under Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, are the two personally liable as general partners?
o: No: they acted only as agents of the corporate general partner.
Yes: limited partners who control the business always lose their shield.
Yes, because a corporation can't serve as an LP's sole general partner.
No, because limited partners can never be liable for anything.
oe: Correct. The statute permits a corporation as sole general partner; undercapitalization concerns are handled by veil piercing; and the creditor could have demanded personal guarantees.
Their control was exercised in their corporate capacities.
Frigidaire held it could.
Under older ULPA versions they could be, if they took part in control.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Corporate general partner

q: Under ULPA (2001, amended 2013) § 303(a), a limited partner regularly advises the general partner and votes on major decisions. Does she risk personal liability for the LP's debts?
o: No: the modern act substantially eliminates that risk.
Yes: any participation in control makes a limited partner a general partner.
Yes, but only to creditors who knew of her participation.
Only if she contributed services instead of money.
oe: Correct. Under earlier ULPA versions, a limited partner who “took part in the control of the business” could be liable; § 303(a) removes that risk.
That was the old control rule.
That was a limitation under older versions; the 2001 act goes further.
The form of contribution doesn't matter.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Control rule today

q: A law firm registers as an LLP by filing a statement of qualification. Partner Ann commits malpractice; partner Bob had nothing to do with the matter. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Bob isn't liable just for being a partner; Ann is liable for her own malpractice.
Both Ann and Bob are personally liable, as in any general partnership.
Neither is liable; the LLP shields everyone, including the wrongdoer.
Bob is personally liable unless he signed a release before the malpractice occurred.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 306(c): debts incurred while an LLP are solely the LLP's, and a partner isn't liable “solely by reason of being or acting as a partner”; a partner stays liable for her own torts. LLPs are popular with law, accounting and architecture firms.
The LLP shield protects Bob.
Partners remain liable for their own torts.
No release is needed.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — LLP shield

q: What does a limited liability limited partnership (LLLP) add to an ordinary LP?
o: General partners are shielded too.
Limited partners may manage the business.
No state filing is required.
The entity becomes a corporation.
oe: Correct. ULPA §§ 102(10), 404(c). On the chart, an LLLP files a certificate, has two classes, gives limited liability to all, and gives control to general partners.
Control remains with general partners.
LLLPs file.
It remains a partnership.

q: Which factor is NOT on the course's list of 1980s trends that drove the spread of limited liability forms?
o: The repeal of the federal income tax on corporations.
The savings and loan crisis.
Rapidly rising liability insurance premiums.
The IRS's increased willingness to grant pass-through treatment to unincorporated entities with limited liability.
oe: Correct. No such repeal happened. The listed trends: growth of very large professional partnerships; repeal of tax rules favoring professional corporations; mass financial torts against lawyers and accountants; the Texas real estate collapse; the savings-and-loan crisis; rising liability insurance premiums; and IRS willingness to give pass-through treatment to entities with limited liability.
Listed.
Listed.
Listed.

q: An LP agreement lets the general partners buy partnership land “in their sole discretion” without limited partners' consent. The GPs buy a parcel at an appraised price, but never told the appraiser the land had just been conditionally rezoned, raising its value. Under Jerman v. O'Leary, can they be liable?
o: Yes: they still had to pay fair value and disclose all facts bearing on value.
No: a “sole discretion” clause eliminates the general partners' fiduciary duties.
No, because most of the limited partners approved the purchase.
Yes, but only if they resold the land at a profit.
oe: Correct. The court read fiduciary duties into the permissive clause and found that withholding the rezoning from the appraiser could support bad faith. Compare Delaware's contract-first approach in Sonet.
Jerman held otherwise.
Approval after incomplete disclosure doesn't cure the breach.
Liability doesn't depend on resale.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Sole discretion clause

q: A publicly traded Delaware LP's agreement lets the general partner propose a conversion in its sole discretion, subject to approval by two-thirds of unitholders. A unitholder sues, claiming the GP's share of the deal is unfair self-dealing. Under Sonet v. Plum Creek, what result?
o: Dismissed: the agreement controls, and the remedy is the ballot box.
Judgment for the unitholder: GPs always owe full fiduciary duties regardless of the agreement.
Dismissed, because unitholders have no rights of any kind in an LP.
Judgment for the unitholder under the implied covenant of good faith.
oe: Correct. Delaware analyzes the agreement first and resorts to fiduciary defaults only if it's silent or ambiguous. El Paso and Haynes v. Kinder Morgan reinforce that investors must read the agreement; the implied covenant remains as a backstop (Dieckman).
Delaware lets the agreement modify them.
They had the voting right the agreement gave them.
The covenant fills only gaps; the agreement addressed the matter.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Delaware contractarianism

q: An LP agreement bars limited partners from offering “Cellular Service,” defined by a specific FCC regulation, in the LP's markets, but expressly lets partners engage in other businesses of every kind. A limited partner begins offering a newer wireless service governed by a different regulation. Under Cincinnati SMSA, did it breach?
o: No: the court won't expand an unambiguous noncompete.
Yes: the implied covenant bars any competition with the partnership.
Yes, because the new service is economically similar.
No, because limited partners owe no duties of any kind.
oe: Correct. Implying terms is a “cautious enterprise” for rare cases of compelling fairness; precise terms control (cf. Nemec).
The agreement expressly allowed other businesses.
Economic similarity doesn't override the precise definition.
The question was the scope of the contractual noncompete.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Implied covenant and noncompete

q: Mo is one of five members of a manager-managed LLC; he holds no office and has no role in operations. He signs a $40,000 equipment lease in the LLC's name. The lessor argues that, like a general partner, Mo can bind the company. Is that right?
o: No: membership alone doesn't make him an agent.
Yes: every LLC member, like every partner, is an agent of the company.
Yes, if the LLC is member-managed rather than manager-managed.
No, and no LLC member can ever bind the company.
oe: Correct. ULLCA (2006) § 301(a), unlike RUPA § 301 for partners. Authority comes from actual or apparent authority and any § 302 statement of authority.
That's the key difference from partnerships.
Even then, membership alone doesn't make one an agent under the 2006 act; authority comes from agency law.
Members can bind it with actual or apparent authority.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Members aren't automatic agents

q: A two-member LLC never holds meetings, keeps no minutes, and mixes its records casually. A creditor argues the members are personally liable because the LLC ignored formalities. Under ULLCA § 304, what's the rule?
o: Ignoring formalities isn't a ground for personal liability.
Ignoring formalities automatically pierces the veil.
LLC members are always personally liable like general partners.
Veil piercing is unavailable for LLCs.
oe: Correct. Company debts are solely the company's; members and managers aren't liable solely by reason of their status.
The statute says otherwise.
They have limited liability.
The slide notes piercing as the exception.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Liability shield

q: An LLC's operating agreement doesn't say whether it is member-managed or manager-managed. The members disagree about an ordinary purchase (3 to 2 in favor) and about amending the operating agreement (4 to 1 in favor). What results under ULLCA § 407?
o: Member-managed: the purchase passes, the amendment fails.
Manager-managed by default, and both pass.
Both pass, because each has a majority.
Neither passes, because every LLC decision needs unanimity.
oe: Correct. The default is member-managed; ordinary-course differences are decided by a majority of members, while acts outside the ordinary course and amendments need all members (the same in manager-managed LLCs for those matters).
Member-managed is the default.
Amendments need unanimity.
Ordinary matters need only a majority.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Management defaults

q: In a manager-managed LLC, a passive member who isn't a manager opens a competing business. Has she breached a fiduciary duty under ULLCA § 409?
o: Not merely as a member: in a manager-managed LLC, duties fall on managers.
Yes: every LLC member owes a duty not to compete.
Yes, because the operating agreement can't eliminate members' duties.
No, because LLCs have no fiduciary duties at all.
oe: Correct. § 409(i). In a member-managed LLC, members owe partner-like loyalty (including no competing before dissolution) and care (no gross negligence or worse).
Not in a manager-managed LLC.
The statute itself allocates duties to managers.
Managers (and members in member-managed LLCs) owe duties.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — LLC fiduciary duties

q: An LLC's members vote to distribute $500,000 even though the company can't pay its debts as they come due. A creditor goes unpaid. Who can be liable?
o: Members or managers who consented, for the excess.
No one, because members have limited liability.
Only the LLC, which already has no money.
All members equally, whether or not they consented.
oe: Correct. ULLCA §§ 405–406: no distribution if the company would be insolvent (unable to pay debts as they come due, or assets less than liabilities plus preferences).
Improper distributions are an exception.
Consenting members or managers can be personally liable.
Liability falls on those who consented in breach.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Improper LLC distributions

q: A member of an LLC withdraws. The operating agreement says nothing about buyouts. What does the 2006 ULLCA provide?
o: No buyout: she keeps her economic interest as a transferee.
The LLC must buy her out at the greater of liquidation or going-concern value.
The LLC dissolves automatically.
She keeps full management rights until she sells her interest.
oe: Correct. § 603(a)(3); a key contrast with RUPA § 701's buyout. A member has the power to withdraw at any time, but withdrawal may be wrongful (before winding up completes, or in breach of the agreement).
That's RUPA's partnership rule.
Dissociation doesn't dissolve the LLC.
Management rights end on dissociation.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — No mandatory buyout

q: A creditor of an LLC's only member forecloses on its charging order against her interest. What does the buyer get under ULLCA § 503?
o: The whole interest, and the buyer becomes a member.
Only a right to distributions, as in any other LLC.
The LLC's assets directly.
Nothing, because LLC interests can't be foreclosed.
oe: Correct. Ordinarily a charging order is the exclusive remedy and gives only distributions; foreclosure against a sole member is the exception.
The sole-member case is the exception.
The creditor reaches the interest, not the assets.
They can.
topic: Wk 8 · LPs, LLPs & LLCs — Charging order exception

q: Which term may an LLC operating agreement NOT include under ULLCA § 105?
o: A term varying the grounds on which a court may dissolve the LLC.
A term identifying specific activities that don't violate loyalty.
A term making the LLC manager-managed.
A term setting a disinterested-approval procedure for conflicts.
oe: Correct. The agreement can't eliminate loyalty or care (beyond § 105(d)), good faith and fair dealing, exonerate bad faith or knowing violations, unreasonably restrict information or the right to sue, or vary judicial dissolution grounds. It may alter aspects of loyalty and care if not manifestly unreasonable.
Allowed if not manifestly unreasonable.
Allowed.
Allowed.
